lessons.title: The Fall of the Sikh State: From Ranjit Singh's Death to Annexation
lessons.summary: The disintegration of the ਸਰਕਾਰ-ਏ-ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ after 1839 and the road to the First Anglo-Sikh War.

lessons.title: The First Anglo-Sikh War and the Treaty of Lahore
lessons.summary: The campaign of 1845–46, the great battles, and the humiliating peace that left the Sikh state nominally intact but fatally weakened.

lessons.title: The Second Anglo-Sikh War and the Annexation of Punjab
lessons.summary: The revolt at Multan, the battles of Chillianwala and Gujrat, and Lord Dalhousie's proclamation of annexation in March 1849.

lessons.title: Colonial Restructuring: Land, Canals, and the Punjab School
lessons.summary: How the British remade annexed Punjab through the 'Punjab School' of paternalist administration, land settlement, and the canal colonies.

lessons.title: The Manufacture of the Martial Race and the Sikh Soldier
lessons.summary: The colonial theory of 'martial races', the recruitment of Sikhs into the Indian Army, and the enforced maintenance of Khalsa identity in the ranks.

lessons.title: The Paradox of 1857: Sikh Loyalism and the Great Rebellion
lessons.summary: Why most Sikhs supported the British during the 1857 uprising, and the long consequences of that choice for Sikh-British relations.

lessons.title: Early Reform: The Nirankari and Namdhari (ਕੂਕਾ) Movements
lessons.summary: The first nineteenth-century movements to purify Sikh practice — Baba Dyal's Nirankaris and Baba Ram Singh's Namdharis — and the 1872 Malerkotla tragedy.

lessons.title: The ਸਿੰਘ ਸਭਾ Revival and the Contest over Sikh Identity
lessons.summary: The founding of the Singh Sabha in 1873, the threat of conversion, and the modernizing program of education, print, and reform.

lessons.title: ਤੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ versus ਸਨਾਤਨ ਸਿੱਖੀ: Defining the Boundaries
lessons.summary: The internal struggle within the Singh Sabha over Sikh identity, culminating in the victory of the Tat Khalsa and the slogan 'We are not Hindus'.

lessons.title: The ਗ਼ਦਰ Party and Transnational Sikh Radicalism
lessons.summary: The emigration of Punjabi Sikhs to North America, the racism they faced, the Komagata Maru, and the founding of the revolutionary Ghadar Party in 1913.

lessons.title: ਜਲ੍ਹਿਆਂਵਾਲਾ ਬਾਗ਼ and the Rupture of 1919
lessons.summary: The Rowlatt Act, the Vaisakhi massacre at Jallianwala Bagh on 13 April 1919, and the shattering of Sikh and Indian faith in British rule.

lessons.title: From Reform to Institution: The ਅਕਾਲੀ ਦਲ and the SGPC
lessons.summary: The culmination of seventy years of reform and resistance in the Gurdwara Reform Movement, the founding of the SGPC and the Shiromani Akali Dal, and the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

courses.title: The Historical Rehatnamas: Codes of Sikh Conduct
courses.source: Rehatnamas, compiled by Piara Singh Padam
courses.summary: A scholarly survey of the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ — the early codes of Sikh conduct attributed to the Khalsa era. This course examines the ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ, ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ, ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ, ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ, ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ and related ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ, their disputed dates, the textual and authenticity debates surrounding them, what they reveal about eighteenth-century Sikh practice, the contradictions among them, and the central methodological problem of distinguishing genuine Guru-era injunctions from later sectarian and Brahmanical additions — culminating in how these texts were sifted to produce the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ.
outcomes: Identify the major historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ, their attributed authors, and their approximate dates of composition
Analyze the textual-critical debates over the authenticity, interpolation, and dating of each ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ
Explain what the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ collectively reveal about eighteenth-century Khalsa belief and practice
Compare and contrast the contradictory injunctions found across different ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
Evaluate the methodological problem of separating genuine ਗੁਰੂ-era ਰਹਿਤ from later ਬ੍ਰਾਹਮਣਵਾਦੀ and sectarian accretions
Trace how the historical ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ were critically sifted to produce the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ (1945)

lessons.title: Introduction: What Is a ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ?
lessons.summary: Defines the genre of the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ, situates it within the formation of Khalsa identity, and lays out the central problems of dating and authenticity that the course addresses.

lessons.title: The ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and Bhai Nand Lal's Verse Rehat
lessons.summary: Examines the earliest layer of rehat literature attributed to Bhai Nand Lal, including the ਤਨਖਾਹਨਾਮਾ and the prose ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਨ-ਉੱਤਰ, and the debates over their genuineness.

lessons.title: The ਚੌਪਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ: The Great Compendium
lessons.summary: A detailed study of the longest and most complex rehatnama, attributed to Chaupa Singh Chhibbar, its Chhibbar-Brahman bias, and its layered composition.

lessons.title: The ਦੇਸਾ ਸਿੰਘ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ: Verse Discipline of the Eighteenth Century
lessons.summary: Studies the verse rehatnama attributed to Desa Singh, its systematic treatment of daily discipline and the five Ks, and its place in the maturing Khalsa.

lessons.title: The ਦਯਾ ਸਿੰਘ and ਪ੍ਰਹਿਲਾਦ ਰਾਇ ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
lessons.summary: Surveys two further codes — that attributed to Bhai Daya Singh of the Panj Piare and the short Prahlad Rai text — and their distinctive emphases and problems.

lessons.title: The ਸਾਖੀ ਰਹਿਤ and the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ
lessons.summary: Examines anecdote-based rehat texts and the contested Prem Sumarag, a code reflecting a 'Sanatan' vision of Sikh society and its debated dating.

lessons.title: The Problem of ਅੰਤਰ-ਪਾਠ: Interpolation and Brahmanical Accretion
lessons.summary: A methodological lesson on how interpolations entered the rehatnamas, how scholars detect them, and the special problem of Brahmanical material contradicting Gurbani.

lessons.title: Contradictions Across the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ
lessons.summary: Catalogues and analyzes the substantive contradictions among the codes and what they reveal about the contested, evolving nature of Khalsa discipline.

lessons.title: What the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ Reveal About Eighteenth-Century Sikh Practice
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the codes as social-historical evidence for how the eighteenth-century Khalsa actually lived, worshipped, ate, dressed, and organized itself.

lessons.title: The Four ਕੁਰਹਿਤ, ਤਨਖਾਹ, and the Disciplinary Order of the ਪੰਥ
lessons.summary: Focuses on the disciplinary machinery of the rehat — the cardinal transgressions, the system of penalties, and the corporate authority that enforced them.

lessons.title: From Manuscript to ਮਰਯਾਦਾ: Sifting the Tradition
lessons.summary: Traces how the diverse historical rehatnamas were critically sifted by the Singh Sabha reformers and the SGPC to produce the modern Sikh Rahit Maryada of 1945.

lessons.title: Conclusion: Reading the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮੇ Critically
lessons.summary: Draws together the course's methods and findings, articulates a mature critical posture toward the rehat tradition, and closes with the Works Cited.

courses.title: ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ: Seat of Sikh Sovereignty
courses.summary: A comprehensive intermediate course on ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, the supreme temporal seat of the Sikh Panth founded by Guru Hargobind Ji in 1609 facing ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ. The course traces the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ, the institution of the five ਤਖ਼ਤ, the tradition of ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ and ਗੁਰਮਤਾ, the governance of the Panth through ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ during the ਮਿਸਲ period, the trauma of 1984, and contemporary debates over Panthic authority. Students examine the architectural and theological symbolism of the Takhat, its relationship to the ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ–ਗੁਰੂ ਪੰਥ doctrine, and its evolving role as the conscience and sovereign voice of the Khalsa.
outcomes: Explain the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ and how Guru Hargobind Ji embodied temporal and spiritual sovereignty in the founding of ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ in 1609.
Identify the five ਤਖ਼ਤ of the Sikh Panth, their historical origins, and their distinct jurisdictions.
Analyze the function of ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ, ਗੁਰਮਤਾ, and ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ as instruments of collective Panthic governance.
Describe the role of ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ during the ਮਿਸਲ period and the rise of Sikh political power in eighteenth-century Punjab.
Critically evaluate the events of 1984 and Operation Bluestar and their lasting impact on the institution and the Sikh psyche.
Assess contemporary controversies over the authority, autonomy, and reform of ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ in the modern era.
references: Singh, Mohinder. The Akali Movement. Delhi: Macmillan, 1978.

lessons.title: Introduction: The Throne of the Timeless One
lessons.summary: Orientation to the course, the meaning of ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ, and why a religion of saints built a throne of sovereignty.

lessons.title: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ: The Doctrine of Twin Sovereignty
lessons.summary: The theological and political meaning of the two swords of Guru Hargobind Ji and the integration of spiritual and temporal power.

lessons.title: 1609: The Founding by Guru Hargobind Ji
lessons.summary: The historical circumstances, date, and significance of the construction of Akal Takhat opposite Harmandir Sahib.

lessons.title: Architecture and Symbolism of the Takhat
lessons.summary: The physical form of Akal Takhat, its relationship to Harmandir Sahib, and the layered symbolism of the complex.

lessons.title: The Five ਤਖ਼ਤ of the Panth
lessons.summary: The historical origins, locations, and jurisdictions of the five supreme seats of Sikh authority.

lessons.title: ਹੁਕਮਨਾਮੇ: Edicts and Panthic Authority
lessons.summary: The tradition of authoritative edicts issued from the Takhats, their history, force, and limits.

lessons.title: ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and ਗੁਰਮਤਾ: Collective Governance

courses.title: Prem Sumarag: The Path of Love — An 18th-Century Sikh Manual
courses.summary: An advanced study of the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ (Prem Sumarag Granth), an enigmatic 18th-century Sikh prose manual of remarkable social vision. Working closely with W.H. McLeod's critical translation and analysis, the course examines the text's progressive ethics — widow remarriage, female education, ਜਾਤਿ (caste) equality, economic justice, and ਲੰਗਰ — alongside its detailed ਰਹਿਤ (code of conduct), its disputed authorship and dating, and its place within the wider ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ literature. Students learn to read the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ as both a normative blueprint for the ਖਾਲਸਾ panth and a window onto how 18th-century Sikhs imagined an ideal society grounded in ਪ੍ਰੇਮ (love).
outcomes: Situate the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ within the genre of ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ literature and the broader textual history of the early ਖਾਲਸਾ.
Critically evaluate the scholarly debates over the text's authorship, dating, and recensions, drawing on W.H. McLeod and later critics.
Analyze the manual's progressive social ethics — including widow remarriage, female education, and the rejection of ਜਾਤਿ hierarchy — and assess their historical significance.
Explain the text's prescriptions for the four great life-cycle rites (birth, ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ initiation, marriage, and death) and daily ਰਹਿਤ.
Interpret the ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਸੁਮਾਰਗ's vision of an ideal Sikh polity, including economic justice, ਦਸਵੰਧ, and community organization.
Apply careful methods of reading a normative source — distinguishing prescription from description — to questions of Sikh history and ethics today.

courses.title: Tankhahnama: Penalties and Accountability in Sikh Ethics
courses.source: Tankhahnama attributed to Bhai Nand Lal and others
courses.summary: An intermediate study of the ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ tradition within Sikh ethics: the literature of transgression and penance attributed to ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ and circulated under the authority of ਗੁਰੂ ਗੋਬਿੰਦ ਸਿੰਘ ਜੀ. The course examines what constitutes a ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹ, the ਕੁਰਹਿਤਾਂ that sever a person from the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ, the corporate role of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ in adjudicating accountability, the place of ਅਰਦਾਸ and ਸੇਵਾ in restoration, and how this restorative model differs structurally from Christian confession and Islamic hudood. Students engage the ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ corpus critically, weighing questions of attribution, textual transmission, and the codification of these norms in the modern ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ.
outcomes: Define ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹ as a category of ethical accountability and distinguish it from sin, crime, and punishment in other religious-legal systems
Trace the textual history of the ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ within the broader ਰਹਿਤਨਾਮਾ corpus and evaluate questions of attribution to ਭਾਈ ਨੰਦ ਲਾਲ
Identify and explain the four ਕੁਰਹਿਤਾਂ (ਬੱਜਰ ਕੁਰਹਿਤਾਂ) that result in apostasy from the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ
Describe the corporate, restorative role of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ in adjudicating a ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹ and prescribing ਸੇਵਾ
Compare and contrast Sikh ethical accountability with Christian confession and Islamic hudood
Connect the historical ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ tradition to its modern codification in the Akal Takht-sanctioned ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ

lessons.summary: Defines the ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹ as restorative discipline, locates the ਤਨਖ਼ਾਹਨਾਮਾ within Sikh ethics, and previews the full course.

courses.title: ੴ ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ: The Mool Mantar as Complete Theology
courses.source: Mool Mantar analysis in SGGS and scholarly commentaries
courses.summary: The ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ is the theological seed (ਬੀਜ ਮੰਤਰ) from which the entire ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ unfolds. Standing at the very opening of the scripture, before ਜਪੁ ਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ and before every ਰਾਗ, it functions as a compressed and complete statement of Sikh doctrine concerning the nature of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. This intermediate-level course examines each term of the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ — ੴ, ਸਤਿ ਨਾਮੁ, ਕਰਤਾ ਪੁਰਖੁ, ਨਿਰਭਉ, ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ, ਅਕਾਲ ਮੂਰਤਿ, ਅਜੂਨੀ, ਸੈਭੰ, and ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ — not as isolated attributes but as a single, integrated theological architecture. Each lesson reads a term against the religious and philosophical inheritance of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Punjab, showing how ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਾਹਿਬ's formulation simultaneously affirms a radical monotheism and quietly displaces competing doctrines of avatar, ritual mediation, and fear-based devotion. Drawing on the commentarial tradition of ਭਾਈ ਵੀਰ ਸਿੰਘ, the ਫਰੀਦਕੋਟ ਟੀਕਾ, and modern academic scholarship, students learn to treat the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ as a complete theology that is also a lived ਸਿਮਰਨ. By the course's end, a student should be able to expound any single term and demonstrate how it depends on and illuminates the others.
outcomes: Recite and accurately parse the complete ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ, identifying each term as a discrete theological claim within an integrated whole.
Explain the numeral-letter construction of ੴ and articulate why ਗੁਰੂ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਾਹਿਬ chose this novel symbol rather than inherited devotional formulae.
Distinguish the Sikh conception of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ as ਅਜੂਨੀ and ਸੈਭੰ from doctrines of incarnation, avatar, and creator-deities in the surrounding religious landscape.
Analyze how ਨਿਰਭਉ and ਨਿਰਵੈਰੁ reframe the relationship between the devotee and the Divine away from fear and propitiation toward love and remembrance.
Interpret ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ as a doctrine of grace and assess its implications for ritual, caste mediation, and the role of the ਗੁਰੂ.
Engage primary commentarial sources and modern scholarship to construct a coherent, evidence-based account of the ਮੂਲ ਮੰਤਰ as complete theology.
references: Singh, Vir. Santhya Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1958.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.

lessons.summary: Interprets ਗੁਰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ as the doctrine of grace through the Guru, contrasting it with salvation through ritual works alone.

courses.title: Sikhi in the Punjab: The Homeland and Its Living Tradition
courses.summary: This course examines the Punjab as the geographical, cultural, and spiritual cradle of the Sikh tradition, tracing how the land of the five rivers shaped the lives of the ten Gurus and the institutions they founded. Students explore the rupture of the 1947 Partition, the sacred geography of Harmandir Sahib and the Takhts, and the social challenges facing Punjab today. The course argues that land, memory, and faith are deeply intertwined in Sikh identity.
outcomes: Explain why the Punjab is understood as the birthplace and homeland of Sikhi and how its rivers, agriculture, and trade routes shaped early Sikh society.
Map the physical geography associated with the ten Gurus, including key sites such as Nankana Sahib, Kartarpur, Goindval, Amritsar, and Anandpur Sahib.
Analyze the impact of the 1947 Partition on Sikh communities, sacred sites, and the demographic landscape of the divided Punjab.
Describe the institutional significance of ਹਰਿਮੰਦਰ ਸਾਹਿਬ, Anandpur Sahib, and the five Takhts in contemporary Sikh life.
Evaluate the contemporary social and political challenges of Punjab, including the drug epidemic, farmer protests, and political tensions.
Articulate how attachment to land and place informs Sikh identity, memory, and devotional practice.

courses.title: Sikhi in the Deccan: Nanded, Hazur Sahib, and the Southern Legacy
courses.summary: This course examines the southern frontier of Sikh history, centered on the town of Nanded on the banks of the Godavari River in present-day Maharashtra, where Guru Gobind Singh Ji spent his final months in 1708 and conferred eternal Guruship upon Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. It traces the rise of Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib as one of the five seats of Sikh temporal authority and explores how geography, distance from Punjab, and local Maharashtrian culture produced a distinctive regional expression of Sikhi. Students will learn how the Nanded sangat preserved and adapted Khalsa traditions over three centuries.
outcomes: Reconstruct the historical circumstances of Guru Gobind Singh Ji's journey to and final months in the Deccan in 1708.
Explain the significance of the conferral of Guruship upon ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ ਜੀ at Nanded and its lasting doctrinal weight.
Describe the institutional development of Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib among the five Takhts of the Panth.
Analyze the distinctive ritual, maryada, and Nihang-influenced traditions of the Nanded sangat and how they differ from Punjab norms.
Evaluate how the Deccan plateau's geography and distance from Punjab shaped a durable Maharashtrian Sikh identity.
Assess the scholarly debates surrounding regional diversity and the construction of Sikh tradition outside the Punjab heartland.

courses.title: Sikhi in East Africa: Kenya, Uganda, and the Indian Ocean Sikh Diaspora
courses.summary: This course examines the formation, flourishing, and forced transformation of the Sikh community in East Africa, from the laborers and artisans who built the Uganda Railway in the 1890s to the prosperous gurdwara-centered communities of colonial Kenya and Uganda. It traces how East African Sikhs preserved Panthic identity far from Punjab, navigated the 1972 Uganda expulsion under Idi Amin, and became a distinctive "twice-migrant" diaspora whose Swahili-Punjabi culture reshaped Sikh communities in Britain and Canada.
outcomes: Explain the labor migration that brought Sikh artisans and railway workers to the East Africa Protectorate between 1896 and 1901 and situate it within wider Indian Ocean networks.
Analyze how East African Sikhs built durable community institutions, including gurdwaras, schools, and welfare societies, that sustained ਪੰਥ identity in a colonial setting.
Assess the causes and consequences of the 1972 Uganda expulsion and its place in the politics of Africanization.
Evaluate the concept of the "twice-migrant" community and how East African Sikh settlement patterns shaped diasporic life in the United Kingdom and Canada.
Describe the distinctive Swahili-Punjabi cultural synthesis expressed in language, cuisine, dress, and gurdwara practice.
Critically read primary and secondary sources on the Asian presence in East Africa with attention to caste, class, and gender.

courses.title: Sikhi in Britain: From Soldiers to Citizens
courses.summary: This course traces the British Sikh story from the regiments of the British Indian Army through the mass labour migrations that followed the Partition of 1947 to the formation of one of Europe's most visible diaspora communities. It examines the landmark legal struggles, the building of monumental gurdwaras, the layered question of British Sikh identity, and the unresolved politics of the diaspora.
outcomes: Explain the role of Sikh soldiers in the British Indian Army during the First and Second World Wars and assess its legacy for later migration.
Trace the post-1947 settlement patterns of Sikhs in Wolverhampton, Southall, and Birmingham and the labour economy that shaped them.
Analyse the legal significance of Mandla v Dowell Lee (1983) for the recognition of Sikhs as an ethnic group under the Race Relations Act.
Evaluate how British Sikhs negotiate overlapping identities as British Asian, Punjabi, and ਸਿੱਖ.
Assess the development of Sikh political representation and institutional life in Britain, including the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha Southall.
Critically discuss the Khalistan debate as it has played out within the British Sikh diaspora.

courses.title: Sikhi in Canada: The Largest Sikh Diaspora Outside India
courses.summary: This course traces the Sikh presence in Canada from the first arrivals in 1897 through the trauma of the Komagata Maru and the long struggle for inclusion, to the contemporary reality of one of the most influential Sikh communities in the world. Students examine settlement patterns in British Columbia and Ontario, the politics of Canadian multiculturalism, and the remarkable civic and political prominence Sikhs have achieved. The course balances celebration of integration with honest analysis of racism, the Air India tragedy, and diaspora nationalism.
outcomes: Reconstruct the chronology of Sikh migration to Canada from 1897 through the present, situating it within imperial and immigration history.
Analyze the Komagata Maru incident of 1914 as a defining episode of exclusion and Sikh political resistance.
Explain the rise of Surrey, British Columbia and Brampton, Ontario as demographic and cultural centres of Sikh Canada.
Evaluate the participation of Sikhs in Canadian political life, including figures such as Jagmeet Singh and numerous members of Parliament and cabinet.
Assess the legacy of the Air India bombing of 1985 and the contours of Khalistan diaspora politics in Canada.
Discuss how Canadian multiculturalism shaped the public expression of Sikh identity, including the use of the ਖੰਡਾ in civic and electoral contexts.

courses.title: Sikhi in the United States: From Bhai Jawala Singh to the Sikh Coalition
courses.summary: This course traces the history of Sikhs in the United States from the pioneering Punjabi agriculturalists who arrived in California in the early twentieth century through the convert communities, post-1984 refugees, and civil-rights advocates of the present day. Students examine how American law, racism, and migration shaped a distinctive and internally diverse Sikh American identity. The arc runs from Bhai Jawala Singh's Stockton Gurdwara of 1912 to the legal advocacy of the Sikh Coalition after 9/11.
outcomes: Reconstruct the migration history of early Punjabi Sikh pioneers to California and the western United States between the 1890s and the 1910s.
Analyze how the Alien Land Laws, immigration exclusion, and anti-Asian racism constrained the lives and landholding of early Sikh settlers.
Explain the founding and significance of the Stockton Gurdwara (1912) as the first Sikh institution in North America.
Evaluate, with scholarly neutrality, the controversial figure of Yogi Bhajan and the 3HO movement of ਗੋਰੇ ਸਿੱਖ (white Sikhs).
Assess the impact of post-1984 political migration and the 9/11 hate-crime wave, including the murder of Balbir Singh Sodhi.
Describe the emergence of organized Sikh American advocacy and a growing political voice through bodies such as the Sikh Coalition.

courses.title: Sikhi in Southeast Asia: Malaysia, Singapore, and the Sikh Spread East
courses.summary: This course traces the migration, settlement, and transformation of Sikh communities across the Malay Peninsula and Singapore from the late nineteenth century to the present. It examines how Sikh police, soldiers, and watchmen of British Malaya built enduring gurdwara networks, and how Sikhs negotiated a distinctive "Punjabi-Malaysian" identity within Malay-cultural and Chinese-majority societies. Students will analyze the sociology of a small but resilient diaspora shaped by tropical climate, colonial labor regimes, and post-colonial nation-building.
outcomes: Reconstruct the colonial-era migration of Sikhs to British Malaya and Singapore as police, soldiers, and watchmen during the 1880s and after.
Explain the institutional role of the Sri Guru Singh Sabha Malaysia and the broader gurdwara network in sustaining community cohesion.
Analyze how tropical climate, Malay culture, and a Chinese-majority society reshaped everyday Sikh practice and the maintenance of ਖਾਲਸਾ identity.
Assess the transition from colonial subjecthood to the post-independence category of "Punjabi-Malaysian" and Singaporean Sikh citizenship.
Evaluate the sociological literature on the Sikh diaspora as it applies to the Southeast Asian case.
Compare the trajectories of the Malaysian and Singaporean Sikh communities within their differing national frameworks.

courses.title: Sikhi in Australia: The Southern Hemisphere's Fastest-Growing Sikh Community
courses.summary: This course traces the Sikh presence in Australia from the camel-driving pioneers of the nineteenth-century outback through the exclusionary decades of the White Australia Policy to the post-1970s migrations that have made Sikhs one of the continent's fastest-growing faith communities. Students examine how a distinctly Australian Sikh identity has taken shape at the meeting point of laid-back Antipodean culture and Punjabi heritage, and how Sikhs have entered rural agriculture, parliamentary politics, interfaith dialogue, and civic festival life. The course combines sociological analysis with historical narrative to map a diaspora that is at once deeply rooted and rapidly expanding.
outcomes: Reconstruct the history of Sikh cameleers and early settlers in the Australian outback between the 1860s and 1920s.
Analyze the mechanisms and consequences of the White Australia Policy for South Asian and Sikh migration.
Explain the post-1970s immigration waves that produced the contemporary Sikh communities of Melbourne and Sydney.
Evaluate the formation of an Australian Sikh identity that blends Punjabi heritage with local civic culture and the keeping of ਕਕਾਰ.
Assess Sikh contributions to Australian rural farming, parliamentary representation, and interfaith civic life.
Interpret Baisakhi and Diwali celebrations in Australia as public civic festivals rather than purely private observances.

courses.title: Sikhi in Germany and Continental Europe: A New Community in an Old Land
courses.summary: This course examines the formation and consolidation of Sikh communities in Germany and across continental Europe, tracing the arc from a tiny post-war presence to substantial congregations built largely by asylum seekers fleeing the violence of 1984 and its aftermath. It analyzes how European models of secularism, citizenship, and integration interact with the Sikh commitment to a visible religious identity, especially the dastaar. Students will engage with legal disputes over turbans in schools and identity documents, transnational Sikh networks, and the comparative politics of religious visibility in France, Belgium, Italy, and beyond.
outcomes: Reconstruct the demographic history of Sikh settlement in Germany and continental Europe from the post-WWII period through the asylum waves of the 1980s and 1990s.
Compare European models of secularism, including French laïcité and German state-church arrangements, and analyze their consequences for the public expression of Sikh identity.
Evaluate the legal and political struggles over the ਦਸਤਾਰ in schools, photo identity documents, and workplaces across European jurisdictions.
Map transnational Sikh networks linking gurdwaras and advocacy bodies in Germany, France, Belgium, and Italy.
Assess how second-generation European Sikhs negotiate ਸਿੱਖੀ identity within secular, plural societies.
Critically read primary and scholarly sources on Sikh migration, representation, and minority rights in Europe.

courses.title: Sikhi in Latin America: Chile, Argentina, and the Yogi Bhajan Legacy
courses.summary: This course examines the emergence of Sikh communities in Latin America, focusing on Chile and Argentina, where the Healthy, Happy, Holy Organization (3HO) and Sikh Dharma International established convert-led congregations through the network of Harbhajan Singh Khalsa Yogiji (Yogi Bhajan). Students will analyze how a Kundalini-yoga-inflected, Spanish-speaking form of Sikh practice took root amid Catholic cultural heritage, and how this distinctive expression relates to, and sometimes diverges from, mainstream Punjabi Sikh tradition. The course foregrounds the diversity of the global Sikh panth and the sociological questions raised by religious conversion across linguistic and cultural frontiers.
outcomes: Trace the historical development of 3HO and Sikh Dharma International communities in Chile and Argentina and their connection to Yogi Bhajan's transnational network.
Analyze how Spanish-speaking converts encounter ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ across language and cultural barriers, and the strategies used to make scripture accessible.
Compare Kundalini-influenced Sikh Dharma practice with mainstream Punjabi Sikh practice, identifying points of convergence and divergence.
Evaluate how Latin American Catholic cultural heritage shapes the reception and reinterpretation of Sikh philosophy.
Assess scholarly debates surrounding the authenticity, controversy, and legitimacy of convert-led Sikh movements.
Articulate the sociological significance of the global ਪੰਥ as a diverse, multinational community.

courses.title: Charitropakhyan: Theology and Interpretation in Dasam Granth
courses.summary: An expert-level seminar on the ਚਰਿਤ੍ਰੋਪਾਖਿਆਨ, the longest and most controversial composition in the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ. The course situates its 405 tales of ਮਾਇਆ, deception, and worldly cunning within the older Indic and Persian narrative traditions of ਨੀਤਿ-ਸ਼ਾਸਤ੍ਰ and Kalila wa Dimna, examines the centuries-long debate over its authorship, recovers its theological aim of cultivating ਬਿਬੇਕ (discernment) against worldly illusion, and confronts the modern misuse of decontextualized stories. Students engage the full critical bibliography from Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Robin Rinehart, Pashaura Singh, and others.
outcomes: Locate the ਚਰਿਤ੍ਰੋਪਾਖਿਆਨ within the structure of the ਦਸਮ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ and within world traditions of moral-narrative literature (ਨੀਤਿ-ਸ਼ਾਸਤ੍ਰ, Kalila wa Dimna, Tutinama).
Critically evaluate the principal scholarly positions on the authorship of the text, distinguishing devotional, sceptical, and historical-critical arguments.
Analyze the frame narrative of ਰਾਜਾ and ਮੰਤ੍ਰੀ and explain how it governs the meaning of the embedded tales.
Interpret individual ਚਰਿਤ੍ਰ in light of the composition's stated didactic purpose rather than reading them in isolation.
Articulate the theology of ਬਿਬੇਕ and detachment from ਮਾਇਆ that the text dramatizes.
Identify how the closing ਬੇਨਤੀ ਚੌਪਈ functions theologically and liturgically within Sikh practice.
Diagnose and respond to common forms of misreading, mistranslation, and polemical misuse of the text.
Construct a methodologically responsible reading practice for difficult premodern devotional literature.
references: Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. Albany: State University of New York Press, 2005.
Rinehart, Robin. Debating the Dasam Granth. New York: Oxford University Press, 2011.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
Rinehart, Robin. "Strategies for Interpreting the Dasam Granth." In Sikhism in Global Context, edited by Pashaura Singh, 135-160. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2011.
Mann, Gurinder Singh. "Sources for the Study of Guru Gobind Singh's Life and Times." Journal of Punjab Studies 15, nos. 1-2 (2008): 229-284.
McLeod, W. H. Textual Sources for the Study of Sikhism. Manchester: Manchester University Press, 1984.
Fenech, Louis E. The Sikh Zafar-namah of Guru Gobind Singh: A Discursive Blade in the Heart of the Mughal Empire. New York: Oxford University Press, 2013.

courses.title: Family and Relationships in Sikhi
courses.summary: A Sikh-centered course on the foundations of healthy family life and relationships — covering the values of respect, compassion, communication, and seva that the Gurus modeled and Gurbani teaches, applied to modern family dynamics.
outcomes: Understand the Sikh perspective on family as a sacred space where spiritual growth happens.
Learn how seva, selfless service, is lived in the home without losing yourself.
Develop communication and conflict-resolution skills grounded in Gurbani values.
Apply Gurbani teachings to parenting challenges and raising spiritually-rooted children.
Deepen your understanding of marriage as an equal partnership in Sikhi.
Build connections across generations and anchor your family to Sikh roots and community.

courses.title: Guru Angad Dev Ji: The Second Master's Life and Ministry
courses.summary: This course examines the life, discipleship, and Guruship of Guru Angad Dev Ji (1504–1552), the second Guru of the Sikhs. Students will trace his origins as Lehna, a devoted Vaishnav, through his transformation into the chosen successor of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Key themes include tests of devotion, the meaning of the name Angad, and the institutional contributions that shaped the young Panth.
outcomes: Identify the key biographical events in the life of Guru Angad Dev Ji from birth to Guruship
Explain the significance of the name Angad and its theological meaning within Sikh tradition
Describe the tests administered by Guru Nanak Dev Ji to Lehna and their spiritual significance
Analyze the institutional contributions of Guru Angad Dev Ji to the early Sikh Panth
Evaluate primary and secondary source accounts of the Second Guru's ministry
Connect the life of Guru Angad Dev Ji to broader themes of selfless service and succession

lessons.title: Conflicts and Challenges: Baba Sri Chand and Continuity
lessons.summary: The tensions within the early Panth regarding the Udasi order, Baba Sri Chand's claims, and how Guru Angad Dev Ji navigated these challenges.

courses.title: Gurmukhi Script: Guru Angad Dev Ji's Gift to the Panth
courses.summary: This course examines the Gurmukhi script — its origins, structure, standardization under Guru Angad Dev Ji, and its profound role in Sikh identity and literacy. Students will learn the historical context of script development in Punjab, the theological significance of writing as a form of service to Gurbani, and how Gurmukhi became the medium through which the Sikh scriptural tradition was preserved and transmitted.
outcomes: Describe the historical origins and antecedents of the Gurmukhi script in the context of Punjabi writing systems
Explain the role of Guru Angad Dev Ji in standardizing and teaching Gurmukhi
Identify the theological significance of Gurmukhi as the script of the Guru's mouth
Analyze how Gurmukhi literacy supported the preservation and transmission of Gurbani
Compare Gurmukhi with related scripts such as Sharada, Takri, and Devanagari
Evaluate the contemporary significance of Gurmukhi as a marker of Sikh identity and cultural heritage

courses.title: Guru Angad Dev Ji's Saloks: Wisdom in Few Words
courses.summary: This course examines the sixty-two saloks composed by Guru Angad Dev Ji and preserved in the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Saloks are brief, aphoristic verses in which profound spiritual and moral wisdom is concentrated into a few lines. Students will engage closely with the themes, imagery, and theological teaching of these compositions, understanding them in their scriptural context and as expressions of the Second Guru's spiritual vision.
outcomes: Identify and describe the literary form of the salok within the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
Analyze the primary spiritual themes found in Guru Angad Dev Ji's compositions
Explain the theological concepts of haumain (ego), naam (divine name), and sewa as developed in these saloks
Interpret selected saloks using traditional and scholarly commentaries
Connect the teachings of the saloks to the broader Sikh theology of liberation
Demonstrate how Guru Angad Dev Ji's voice complements and extends the teachings of Guru Nanak Dev Ji

lessons.summary: Guru Angad Dev Ji's teaching on Naam — the divine Name — as the transformative practice that dissolves ego and leads to liberation.

lessons.summary: Guru Angad Dev Ji's teaching on the indispensable role of the Guru in guiding the soul toward liberation.

lessons.title: Conclusion: The Voice of Guru Angad Dev Ji

courses.title: Langar, Sangat, and the Expansion of Community Under Guru Angad Dev Ji
courses.summary: This course examines the development of the Langar and Sangat institutions under Guru Angad Dev Ji's ministry at Khadur Sahib, with particular attention to the role of Mata Khivi. Students will explore how communal eating and congregational worship functioned as engines of social equality and community formation in sixteenth-century Punjab, and trace the theological foundations of these institutions in Sikh teaching.
outcomes: Describe the historical origins and development of the Langar institution in Sikh tradition
Explain Mata Khivi's recorded contribution to the Langar at Khadur Sahib
Analyze how Langar and Sangat functioned as practices of social equality in caste-stratified Punjab
Connect the Langar institution to the Sikh theological principles of seva, equality, and community
Trace the expansion of these institutions from Guru Nanak Dev Ji through Guru Angad Dev Ji to subsequent Gurus
Evaluate the significance of communal institutions for the formation of Sikh identity
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1962.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. Vol. 2. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

lessons.title: Introduction: Food, Equality, and Community
lessons.summary: An introduction to the Langar institution, its social and theological significance, and the scope of this course.

lessons.title: The Social Context: Caste, Food, and Pollution in Sixteenth-Century Punjab
lessons.summary: The social norms around food, purity, and caste hierarchy that the Langar institution challenged in Guru Angad Dev Ji's time.

lessons.title: Langar's Origins: Guru Nanak Dev Ji and Kartarpur
lessons.summary: The establishment of the Langar institution by Guru Nanak Dev Ji at Kartarpur and its foundational principles.

lessons.title: Guru Angad Dev Ji Takes Over: Langar at Khadur Sahib
lessons.summary: How Guru Angad Dev Ji expanded and institutionalized the Langar at Khadur Sahib, building on the foundation established at Kartarpur.

lessons.title: Mata Khivi: The Celebrated Administrator of the Langar
lessons.summary: The life and contribution of Mata Khivi, wife of Guru Angad Dev Ji, who is uniquely celebrated in the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji for her role in managing the Langar.

lessons.title: Pangat: Sitting in Equal Rows
lessons.summary: The practice of pangat — sitting in rows to receive Langar — as a social and theological practice of equality.

lessons.title: Sewa in the Langar: Who Cooks and Why It Matters
lessons.summary: The practice of voluntary service in the Langar as a spiritual discipline and its theological significance.

lessons.title: The Theology of Langar: Feeding the Divine in Every Person
lessons.summary: The theological foundations of the Langar in Sikh teaching about the divine presence in all human beings.

lessons.title: Sangat: The Congregation That Gathers
lessons.summary: The Sangat institution — the holy congregation — its character, practices, and theological significance in early Sikh community life.

lessons.title: Sangat and Social Transformation in Early Sikh History
lessons.summary: How the Sangat functioned as an agent of social transformation in the stratified society of sixteenth-century Punjab.

lessons.title: Expansion Under Later Gurus
lessons.summary: How the Langar and Sangat institutions were further developed by subsequent Gurus, particularly Guru Amar Das Ji and Guru Ram Das Ji.

lessons.title: Langar and Sangat in the Contemporary World
lessons.summary: The Langar and Sangat institutions in the contemporary global Sikh community, including responses to humanitarian crises and new contexts.

courses.title: Physical Fitness and the Akhara: Guru Angad Dev Ji's Embodied Legacy
courses.summary: This course examines Guru Angad Dev Ji's establishment of the akhara — a wrestling and physical fitness gymnasium — at Khadur Sahib, and its significance for Sikh understandings of the body, health, and spiritual practice. Students will explore the theological basis for physical cultivation in Sikhism, the historical context of the akhara tradition in Punjab, and how Guru Angad Dev Ji's embodied legacy connects to the later development of the Khalsa ideal of the saint-soldier.
outcomes: Describe the historical akhara institution and its place in Punjabi cultural life
Explain Guru Angad Dev Ji's establishment of an akhara at Khadur Sahib and its significance
Analyze the Sikh theological basis for physical cultivation as part of spiritual life
Connect the akhara tradition to the later development of the Khalsa ideal
Evaluate how Guru Angad Dev Ji's approach to the body differed from ascetic traditions of the period
Identify practical principles for physical health derived from Sikh spiritual teaching

lessons.title: Introduction: The Body in Sikh Spiritual Life
lessons.summary: An introduction to how the body is understood in Sikh theology and why Guru Angad Dev Ji's akhara represents a distinctive vision of embodied spirituality.

lessons.title: The Akhara in Punjab: Cultural and Historical Background
lessons.summary: The akhara as a pre-existing institution in Punjabi and North Indian culture, and its transformation under Guru Angad Dev Ji's ministry.

lessons.title: Asceticism and Its Critique in Gurbani
lessons.summary: The critique of ascetic withdrawal in Gurbani and how it provides the theological context for Guru Angad Dev Ji's positive valuation of the body.

lessons.title: Guru Angad Dev Ji Establishes the Akhara at Khadur Sahib
lessons.summary: The historical account of the akhara established by Guru Angad Dev Ji and its role in the Khadur Sahib community.

lessons.title: Wrestling, Games, and Physical Training in the Guru's Community
lessons.summary: The specific activities practiced at the akhara, their cultural context, and their place in the life of the Khadur Sahib community.

lessons.title: The Body as Instrument of Sewa
lessons.summary: The Sikh theological understanding of the body as an instrument for selfless service, and how this grounds the value of physical cultivation.

lessons.title: Physical Discipline and Mental Discipline: The Connection
lessons.summary: The relationship between physical training and mental/spiritual discipline in Sikh tradition and general human psychology.

lessons.title: The Saint-Soldier Ideal: Seeds in the Akhara
lessons.summary: How Guru Angad Dev Ji's akhara tradition planted seeds for the later development of the saint-soldier ideal in Sikh tradition.

lessons.title: Health, Disease, and Spiritual Practice in Sikh Teaching
lessons.summary: How Sikh theological teaching addresses physical health, illness, and the relationship between bodily and spiritual wellbeing.

lessons.title: The Khalsa and Martial Arts: A Longer Trajectory
lessons.summary: The development of Sikh martial arts traditions from the akhara through the Khalsa to contemporary practices.

lessons.title: Contemporary Sikh Physical Culture
lessons.summary: How Sikh communities today maintain traditions of physical culture, sports, and health as expressions of religious identity.

lessons.title: Conclusion: An Integrated Vision of Human Flourishing
lessons.summary: A synthesis of the course's themes, reflecting on Guru Angad Dev Ji's akhara as an expression of a holistic Sikh vision of human life.

courses.title: Historical Sources: The Suraj Prakash Account of the Second Guru
courses.summary: This advanced course examines the Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth (Suraj Prakash) by Kavi Santokh Singh as a primary source for the history of Guru Angad Dev Ji. Students will learn to read hagiographic literature critically, understand the text's literary conventions, compare its account with other sources, and develop skills for evaluating historical claims in a tradition where history and theology are closely intertwined.
outcomes: Describe the Suraj Prakash as a text — its author, composition, structure, and literary conventions
Apply critical historical methods to hagiographic sources about Guru Angad Dev Ji
Compare the Suraj Prakash account of key events with other Sikh historical sources
Identify where sources agree, where they differ, and how scholars evaluate competing accounts
Explain the distinction between theological narrative and historical claim in hagiographic literature
Demonstrate skills of source analysis applicable to other Sikh historical texts
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1962.
McLeod, W. H. Early Sikh Tradition: A Study of the Janam-Sakhis. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1980.

Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham, MD: Rowman and Littlefield, 2014.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. Vol. 2. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

lessons.title: Introduction: What Is the Suraj Prakash?
lessons.summary: An introduction to the Suraj Prakash as a text, its place in Sikh literary tradition, and what it offers the student of Sikh history.

lessons.title: Kavi Santokh Singh: Author and Context
lessons.summary: The life, training, and perspective of Kavi Santokh Singh, the author of the Suraj Prakash.

lessons.title: The Structure of the Suraj Prakash
lessons.summary: The organizational structure of the Suraj Prakash, its major sections, and the specific sections devoted to Guru Angad Dev Ji.

lessons.title: Literary Conventions of the Hagiographic Genre
lessons.summary: The conventions of Sikh hagiographic literature that shape how the Suraj Prakash presents the life of Guru Angad Dev Ji.

lessons.title: The Suraj Prakash Account: Guru Angad Dev Ji's Early Life
lessons.summary: A detailed examination of how the Suraj Prakash describes Guru Angad Dev Ji's birth, family, and life before meeting Guru Nanak Dev Ji.

lessons.title: The Encounter with Guru Nanak Dev Ji in the Suraj Prakash
lessons.summary: How the Suraj Prakash narrates the first meeting of Lehna with Guru Nanak Dev Ji and its theological significance.

lessons.title: The Tests and Their Narrative Function
lessons.summary: The famous test narratives in the Suraj Prakash and how scholars analyze them as both historical record and theological construction.

lessons.title: The Succession Narrative in the Suraj Prakash
lessons.summary: How the Suraj Prakash narrates the formal succession of Guru Angad Dev Ji and what this narrative reveals about Sikh understanding of Guruship.

lessons.title: Comparing Suraj Prakash with Other Sources
lessons.summary: A methodological comparison of the Suraj Prakash account of Guru Angad Dev Ji's life with other available sources.

lessons.title: Historical-Critical Method and Hagiographic Sources
lessons.summary: An introduction to the methods historians use to evaluate hagiographic sources like the Suraj Prakash.

lessons.title: What the Suraj Prakash Cannot Tell Us — and What It Can
lessons.summary: A calibrated assessment of the historical value and limitations of the Suraj Prakash as a source for Guru Angad Dev Ji's life.

lessons.title: Conclusion: Reading Hagiography Wisely
lessons.summary: A synthesis of the course's approach to the Suraj Prakash, with guidelines for continuing to read hagiographic sources wisely.

courses.title: Guru Amar Das Ji: Life, Discipleship, and Calling
courses.summary: This course examines the remarkable life of Guru Amar Das Ji (1479–1574), who became a devoted Sikh disciple at the age of sixty-one and received the Guruship at seventy-three. Students will trace his biography from his early Vaishnav practice through his transformation under Guru Angad Dev Ji, his ministry at Goindval, and his legacy as a Guru who demonstrated that spiritual transformation is possible at any stage of life.
outcomes: Describe the key biographical events in Guru Amar Das Ji's life from birth through Guruship
Explain the significance of Guru Amar Das Ji's late-life discipleship and what it teaches about spiritual awakening
Identify the major contributions of Guru Amar Das Ji to Sikh institutional development
Analyze how Guru Amar Das Ji's personal history shaped his ministry's emphasis on inclusivity
Evaluate the sources available for Guru Amar Das Ji's life and their reliability
Connect Guru Amar Das Ji's biography to the broader development of the Sikh Panth in the sixteenth century
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1962.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion: Its Gurus, Sacred Writings and Authors. Vol. 2. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.

Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. London: Bloomsbury, 2013.

lessons.title: Introduction: Never Too Late — The Lesson of Guru Amar Das Ji's Life
lessons.summary: An overview of Guru Amar Das Ji's life and the central lesson it carries: that spiritual awakening and transformation can occur at any age.

lessons.title: Punjab in the Mid-Sixteenth Century
lessons.summary: The political, social, and religious landscape of Punjab in the mid-sixteenth century — the context of Guru Amar Das Ji's ministry.

lessons.title: Amar Das Ji's Early Life and Vaishnav Practice
lessons.summary: Guru Amar Das Ji's origins, family background, and decades of Vaishnav religious practice before his encounter with Sikhism.

lessons.title: The Encounter with Bibi Amro and the Shabad
lessons.summary: The transformative moment when Amar Das heard Bibi Amro singing a shabad of Guru Nanak Dev Ji, which drew him to seek Guru Angad Dev Ji.

lessons.title: Becoming a Disciple of Guru Angad Dev Ji
lessons.summary: Amar Das Ji's journey to Khadur Sahib, his first encounter with Guru Angad Dev Ji, and the beginning of his discipleship.

lessons.title: Devoted Service at Khadur Sahib: The Water-Carrier
lessons.summary: The iconic narrative of Amar Das Ji's water-carrying sewa for Guru Angad Dev Ji and its spiritual significance.

lessons.title: The Succession: Receiving the Guruship at Age 73
lessons.summary: The circumstances of Guru Amar Das Ji's selection as the Third Guru and the theological significance of his advanced age at succession.

lessons.title: Establishing Goindval as the New Center
lessons.summary: How Guru Amar Das Ji built Goindval into the new center of Sikh life, including the construction of the baoli and the Langar.

lessons.title: The Emperor Akbar and the Langar Test
lessons.summary: The famous account of Emperor Akbar's visit to Guru Amar Das Ji and the requirement to eat in Langar first.

lessons.title: Festival Days as Sikh Gathering Points
lessons.summary: Guru Amar Das Ji's designation of Baisakhi, Maghi, and Diwali as Sikh community gathering days and the significance of this institutional innovation.

lessons.title: Guru Amar Das Ji's Family and Succession to Guru Ram Das Ji
lessons.summary: The family of Guru Amar Das Ji and the succession to Guru Ram Das Ji, including the selection of his son-in-law.

lessons.title: Legacy: What Guru Amar Das Ji's Life Teaches
lessons.summary: A synthesis of Guru Amar Das Ji's contributions and the enduring lessons of his life for the Sikh community.

courses.title: Anand Sahib: The Song of Bliss — A Deep Study
courses.summary: This course offers a deep study of Anand Sahib — the forty-stanza composition by Guru Amar Das Ji that has become one of the most central texts in daily Sikh practice. Students will examine the composition's themes of spiritual bliss, its poetic structure, its place in the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the theological concepts it develops, and its role in Sikh liturgical practice from birth to death.
outcomes: Describe the composition Anand Sahib — its structure, raag, and place in the Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
Explain the concept of anand (bliss) as developed in this composition and in broader Sikh theology
Analyze the forty stanzas of Anand Sahib in terms of their themes and theological content
Identify the Sikh liturgical contexts in which Anand Sahib is recited
Connect the themes of Anand Sahib to the broader Gurbani teachings of Guru Amar Das Ji
Evaluate how Anand Sahib reflects Guru Amar Das Ji's spiritual vision and biographical experience
references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. 10 vols. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962–1964.

lessons.title: Introduction to Anand Sahib
lessons.summary: An overview of Anand Sahib as a composition, its place in Sikh liturgy, and the scope of this course.

lessons.title: The Raag Ramkali and Musical Context
lessons.summary: The musical context of Anand Sahib — the Raag Ramkali, its characteristics, and how the musical setting shapes the composition's spiritual impact.

lessons.summary: A close study of the opening stanza of Anand Sahib and its declaration of divine bliss.

lessons.title: The Divine Sound: Panch Shabad
lessons.summary: The mystical teaching of Anand Sahib about the divine sound heard within — the panch shabad — and its significance in Sikh theology.

lessons.title: The Guru as the Path to Anand
lessons.summary: Anand Sahib's teaching on the indispensable role of the Guru in enabling the experience of divine bliss.

lessons.title: The Organs of Perception and the Divine
lessons.summary: How Anand Sahib uses the human body's organs of perception as metaphors and vehicles for divine experience.

lessons.title: The Mind and Its Transformation
lessons.summary: How Anand Sahib addresses the transformation of the mind through the Guru's grace — from restlessness to bliss.

lessons.title: Death, Liberation, and Bliss
lessons.summary: How Anand Sahib addresses death and the prospect of liberation as dimensions of the bliss it describes.

lessons.title: The Congregation of Saints
lessons.summary: Anand Sahib's teaching on the role of the holy congregation (sadhsangat) in enabling and sustaining the experience of bliss.

lessons.title: The Final Stanzas: The Source of All Bliss
lessons.summary: The concluding stanzas of Anand Sahib and their synthesis of the composition's theological teaching.

lessons.title: Anand Sahib in Sikh Liturgical Life
lessons.summary: The many liturgical contexts in which Anand Sahib is recited or sung, from daily worship to life-cycle ceremonies.

courses.title: Guru Amar Das Ji: Social Reforms — Caste, Sati, Purdah, and Widow Remarriage
courses.summary: This course examines the social reform agenda of Guru Amar Das Ji, focusing on his challenges to four major oppressive practices of sixteenth-century Punjab: the caste system, sati (widow immolation), purdah (the veiling and seclusion of women), and the prohibition on widow remarriage. Students will explore both the theological foundations and the practical implementation of these reforms, situating them in their historical context and tracing their ongoing significance.
outcomes: Describe the social practices of sati, purdah, and caste discrimination in sixteenth-century Punjab
Explain Guru Amar Das Ji's theological critique of each of these practices
Analyze how Guru Amar Das Ji's reforms were implemented institutionally through the Langar and Manji system
Evaluate the historical impact of these reforms on Sikh community life and women's status
Connect Guru Amar Das Ji's social reform agenda to broader Sikh theological principles of equality and human dignity
Assess the legacy of these reforms for contemporary Sikh social ethics

lessons.summary: The practice of purdah in sixteenth-century Punjab and Guru Amar Das Ji's challenge to it through open congregational practice.

lessons.title: The Guru's Open Congregation: Challenging Purdah
lessons.summary: How the structure of Sikh congregational life under Guru Amar Das Ji functioned as an ongoing challenge to the purdah system.

lessons.title: Caste Discrimination and the Sikh Critique
lessons.summary: The caste system as encountered by Guru Amar Das Ji and the Sikh theological critique of caste-based hierarchy.

lessons.title: Langar as Anti-Caste Practice
lessons.summary: How the Langar institution under Guru Amar Das Ji functioned specifically as a practice of anti-caste equality.

lessons.title: Widow Remarriage: Social Prohibition and Sikh Support
lessons.summary: Guru Amar Das Ji's support for widow remarriage against the prevailing social prohibition.

lessons.title: The Manji System and Women's Leadership
lessons.summary: How Guru Amar Das Ji's Manji system created formal roles for women's religious leadership within the Sikh Panth.

lessons.title: Gurbani on Gender Equality
lessons.summary: A survey of Gurbani's teachings on women and gender equality, with particular attention to Guru Amar Das Ji's compositions.

lessons.title: Legacy and Ongoing Significance
lessons.summary: The lasting impact of Guru Amar Das Ji's social reforms on the Sikh community and their ongoing relevance for contemporary Sikh social ethics.

courses.title: The Manji System: Guru Amar Das Ji and Scaling the Panth's Institutions
courses.summary: This course examines the Manji system established by Guru Amar Das Ji — a network of 146 district-level community leaders that organized the geographically expanding Sikh Panth in the sixteenth century. Students will trace the origins, structure, and function of the system, its relationship to other Sikh institutional innovations, and its significance as an early model of distributed religious organization.
outcomes: Describe the Manji system — its origin, structure, and the role of the Manji leaders
Explain why Guru Amar Das Ji created the Manji system and what organizational problem it addressed
Analyze how the Manji system functioned alongside the Langar, Sangat, and Baoli in building the Sikh Panth
Evaluate the inclusivity of the Manji system with respect to caste and gender
Compare the Manji system to the Piri system established under Guru Ram Das Ji
Assess the long-term impact of the Manji system on Sikh community organization

lessons.summary: How Manji leaders served as missionaries spreading the Sikh message across Punjab and beyond.

lessons.title: Comparison with the Piri System
lessons.summary: A comparison between the Manji system and the Piri system established under Guru Ram Das Ji, and what changed between them.

lessons.title: Criticisms and Limitations of the Manji System
lessons.summary: An honest assessment of the limitations and problems that emerged in the Manji system over time.

lessons.title: Legacy and Impact
lessons.summary: The long-term impact of the Manji system on Sikh institutional development and its lessons for community organization.

courses.title: The Baoli at Goindval and Sacred Geography
courses.summary: This course examines the baoli (step-well) constructed at Goindval under Guru Amar Das Ji and its significance as a sacred site, a center of pilgrimage, and an expression of Sikh theology about sacred space and geography. Students will explore the construction of the baoli, the spiritual practice associated with its eighty-four steps, and how Goindval became an early Sikh pilgrimage center that offered an alternative to the dominant Hindu and Muslim sacred geography of northern India.
outcomes: Describe the physical structure and location of the Goindval baoli
Explain the symbolic significance of the eighty-four steps and their connection to Sikh theology
Analyze how the Goindval baoli functioned as an early Sikh pilgrimage site
Compare the Sikh concept of sacred space with Hindu and Muslim sacred geography
Evaluate the relationship between the baoli and the Guru's teachings about inner versus outer practice
Trace the development of Sikh sacred geography from Goindval through the Golden Temple at Amritsar

lessons.title: The Step-Well Tradition in South Asia
lessons.summary: The vav or baoli as an architectural tradition in South Asia, and the cultural and religious significance of step-wells.
