Singh, Trilochan, et al., trans. Selections from the Sacred Writings of the Sikhs. London: George Allen and Unwin, 1960.
Kohli, Surindar Singh. Janam Sakhi Traditions. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1969.

lessons.title: The Awakening at Sultanpur: Context and Call
lessons.summary: Examination of Guru Nanak's years at Sultanpur Lodhi, his role as a store-keeper under Nawab Daulat Khan Lodi, and the transformative experience at the Bein river that preceded the First Udasi.

lessons.title: Sources for the First Udasi: Janamsakhis and Sri Nanak Prakash
lessons.summary: Critical evaluation of the primary sources documenting the First Udasi, including the Puratan, Miharban, and Bala Janamsakhi traditions, and Santokh Singh's Sri Nanak Prakash.

lessons.title: Departing East: Eminabad and the Shadow of Babar
lessons.summary: The First Udasi's early eastward stages, including the famous encounter at Saidpur during Babar's invasion and the Babarvani compositions as historical witness.

lessons.title: Hardwar: Challenging Ritual at the Ganges
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's arrival at Hardwar and his famous challenge to the ritual of throwing water toward the rising sun, establishing the principle of meaningful over mechanical worship.

lessons.title: Benaras: Dialogue with Brahmanical Learning
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's time at Benaras, the center of Sanskrit learning and Hindu religious authority, and his recorded dialogues with Brahmin scholars and pandits.

lessons.title: Gaya and the Pilgrimage Circuit
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak at Gaya, the Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage center associated with ancestral rites, and his continuing challenge to formalistic religion along the eastern pilgrimage circuit.

lessons.title: Jagannath Puri: The Arti Sakhi
lessons.summary: One of the most celebrated episodes of the First Udasi — Guru Nanak at the Jagannath temple at Puri, where he pointed to the cosmic arti of the natural world rather than the temple ceremony.

lessons.title: Eastward to Dhubri and Assam
lessons.summary: The easternmost reaches of the First Udasi, including the encounter with Kauda in Assam and scholarly evaluation of these accounts from the distant east.

lessons.title: Bhai Mardana: Companion, Musician, and Theological Foil
lessons.summary: A focused study of Bhai Mardana's role throughout the First Udasi — as rababi musician, as a Muslim companion in Hindu territories, and as the narrative voice of human limitation in the Janamsakhis.

lessons.title: Sabads Composed During the First Udasi
lessons.summary: A survey of Gurbani compositions associated with the First Udasi period, including Asa raag sabads, the Babarvani, and the Aarti — examined for their theological themes and geographic context.

lessons.title: Geography and Chronology: Scholarly Debates
lessons.summary: An overview of scholarly debates about the precise dating, duration, and geographic route of the First Udasi, including challenges of reconciling janamsakhi accounts with independent historical evidence.

lessons.title: Legacy of the First Udasi in Sikh Tradition
lessons.summary: The First Udasi's enduring impact on Sikh theology, practice, and community identity — from the establishment of sangats along the route to the theological themes encoded in the journey's major sakhis.

courses.title: The Second Udasi: Guru Nanak's Journeys South — Deccan, Tamil Nadu, and Sri Lanka
courses.summary: This course traces Guru Nanak's second great journey southward through the Deccan plateau, Tamil Nadu, Rameshwaram, and across to Sri Lanka (Lanka), following janamsakhi accounts and Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Nanak Prakash. Students examine Guru Nanak's encounters with Nath yogis, Shaivite and Vaishnava communities, and diverse regional spiritual traditions. The course critically evaluates how these southern journeys expanded the geographic and theological scope of early Sikhism.
outcomes: Identify the major geographic stages of the Second Udasi through the Deccan and peninsular India
Analyze Guru Nanak's theological engagements with Shaivite and Vaishnava traditions in South India
Compare different janamsakhi accounts of the Sri Lanka encounter and assess their historicity
Explain how the Second Udasi extended Guru Nanak's social and spiritual mission beyond the Punjab-Gangetic sphere
Evaluate the Nath yogi tradition as a theological interlocutor for Guru Nanak during the southern journey
Assess the significance of the Second Udasi for the development of Sikh universalism
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Nanak Prakash. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1843.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Grewal, J. S. Guru Nanak in History. Chandigarh: Panjab University, 1969.
Kohli, Surindar Singh. Janam Sakhi Traditions. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1969.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Lorenzen, David N. The Kapalikas and Kalamukhas: Two Lost Shaivite Sects. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1972.
McLeod, W. H., trans. and ed. The B40 Janam-Sakhi. Amritsar: Guru Nanak Dev University, 1980.

lessons.title: Setting Out South: Routes and Motivations of the Second Udasi
lessons.summary: Contextualizing the Second Udasi's southward direction, its approximate dating, and the religious landscape of the Deccan and South India that Guru Nanak entered.

lessons.title: Through the Deccan: Nanded and Bidar
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's passage through the Deccan plateau, including stops at Nanded and Bidar, and encounters with the religious and political communities of the Bahmani successor states.

lessons.title: The Nath Yogi Tradition: A Theological Interlocutor
lessons.summary: An examination of the Nath yogi tradition that Guru Nanak engaged throughout his journeys, its theology of bodily practice and immortality, and how Guru Nanak's debates with Nath yogis shaped key compositions.

lessons.title: Shri Rangam and the Vaishnava South
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's encounter with the major Vaishnava temple tradition at Shri Rangam on the Kaveri river, and his engagement with South Indian Bhakti traditions.

lessons.title: Rameshwaram: The Southern Pilgrimage Extreme
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's arrival at Rameshwaram, the southernmost major Hindu pilgrimage site, and his engagement with the pilgrimage traditions at the very tip of the subcontinent.

lessons.title: Crossing to Lanka: The Janamsakhi Accounts
lessons.summary: A critical examination of the janamsakhi accounts of Guru Nanak's journey to Sri Lanka, their literary structure, and what they reveal about the tradition's understanding of the Second Udasi's southern extent.

lessons.title: The Shiv Nath Encounter in Lanka
lessons.summary: The janamsakhi accounts of Guru Nanak's meeting with Shiv Nath in Lanka, the theological content of their exchange, and what this encounter reveals about the Second Udasi's engagement with Shaivite traditions.

lessons.title: Shaivite Traditions and Guru Nanak's Response
lessons.summary: An examination of the Shaivite traditions Guru Nanak encountered in the south — their theology, practice, and social structure — and how his compositions engage Shaivite vocabulary and concepts.

lessons.title: Compositions Associated with the Second Udasi
lessons.summary: A survey of Gurbani compositions associated by tradition with the Second Udasi period, examining their theological themes and connections to the southern journey's geographic and cultural context.

lessons.title: Social Encounters in the South: Caste and Community
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's engagement with caste and social hierarchy during the Second Udasi, including encounters with lower-caste communities and his challenge to untouchability in the southern context.

lessons.title: The Return Journey: Communities Founded
lessons.summary: The Second Udasi's northward return from Lanka through the Deccan, and the communities of followers established along the route that would sustain the growing Sikh movement.

lessons.title: Legacy of the Second Udasi
lessons.summary: The Second Udasi's enduring contributions to Sikh tradition — theological, geographical, and institutional — and its place in the larger narrative of Guru Nanak's mission.

courses.title: The Third Udasi: Guru Nanak's Journeys North — Kashmir, Sumer Parbat, and Tibet
courses.summary: This course traces Guru Nanak's third great journey northward into Kashmir, the Himalayan peaks, and the Tibetan plateau, following janamsakhi accounts and Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Nanak Prakash. Students examine the Sidh Gosht dialogue tradition, Guru Nanak's encounters with Brahmin scholars in Kashmir, and the theological significance of the mountaintop encounters with Nath Siddhs. The course evaluates the scholarly debate over whether the Sidh Gosht represents a historical encounter or a literary-theological dialogue.
outcomes: Identify the major geographic stages of the Third Udasi through Kashmir, the Himalayas, and the Tibetan region
Analyze the Sidh Gosht as both potential historical event and theological composition
Explain the theological debate between Guru Nanak and the Nath Siddhs over the path to liberation
Compare Guru Nanak's encounter with Brahmin Pandit Brahm Das in Kashmir with his earlier Brahmanical encounters
Evaluate the scholarly debate over the literal versus literary character of the Sumer Parbat encounter
Assess how the Third Udasi's northern journey completed Guru Nanak's engagement with all major Indian spiritual traditions
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Nanak Prakash (part of Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth, composed 1843). Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1900.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Grewal, J. S. Guru Nanak in History. Chandigarh: Panjab University, 1969.
Kohli, Surindar Singh. Janam Sakhi Traditions. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1969.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
White, David Gordon. The Alchemical Body: Siddha Traditions in Medieval India. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1996.
Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962.

lessons.title: The Third Udasi: Setting Out North
lessons.summary: Contextualizing the Third Udasi's northward direction, its approximate dating, and the spiritual landscape of Kashmir and the Himalayan region that Guru Nanak entered.

lessons.title: Kashmir: The Valley of Brahmanical Learning
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's arrival in the Kashmir valley, its distinctive intellectual culture of Sanskrit scholarship and Shaiva philosophy, and the theological landscape he encountered there.

lessons.title: Pandit Brahm Das and the Kashmir Encounter
lessons.summary: The janamsakhi accounts of Guru Nanak's encounter with the learned Kashmir Brahmin Pandit Brahm Das, the theological content of their exchange, and its significance for the Third Udasi.

lessons.title: Into the Himalayas: Routes and Reality
lessons.summary: The geographic reality of travel into the Himalayan region, the routes available to Guru Nanak, and the historical and physical context for the Third Udasi's mountain journeys.

lessons.title: The Nath Siddh Tradition at Its Northern Strongholds
lessons.summary: An examination of the Nath Siddh tradition as it existed in the Himalayan region — its theology, practice communities, and relationship to the philosophical traditions of Kashmir.

lessons.title: Sumer Parbat: The Sacred Mountain
lessons.summary: The janamsakhi accounts of Guru Nanak's arrival at Sumer Parbat, the gathering of the 84 Siddhs, and the setting of the great dialogue that produced the Sidh Gosht.

lessons.title: The 84 Siddhs: Dialogue at the Summit
lessons.summary: The specific exchanges between Guru Nanak and the 84 Siddhs at Sumer Parbat as recorded in the janamsakhi tradition, examining their structure and theological content.

lessons.title: The Sidh Gosht: Text, Context, and Interpretation
lessons.summary: A scholarly examination of the Sidh Gosht as a Gurbani composition — its structure, its place in the Guru Granth Sahib, and the scholarly debate over its relationship to the Third Udasi's historical encounters.

lessons.title: Key Theological Arguments of the Sidh Gosht
lessons.summary: A detailed examination of the Sidh Gosht's major theological arguments — on liberation, the Guru, the householder path, and the relationship between effort and grace.

lessons.title: Tibet and the Northern Extreme
lessons.summary: The janamsakhi accounts of Guru Nanak's journey beyond the Himalayan passes into the Tibetan region, and the Buddhist traditions he would have encountered there.

lessons.title: Compositions Associated with the Third Udasi
lessons.summary: A survey of Gurbani compositions associated with the Third Udasi period, with particular attention to the Sidh Gosht and compositions in Ramkali raag.

lessons.title: Legacy of the Third Udasi
lessons.summary: The Third Udasi's enduring contributions to Sikh tradition — the Sidh Gosht as scriptural legacy, the householder theology, and the completion of the northern arc of Guru Nanak's universal mission.

courses.title: The Fourth Udasi: Guru Nanak's Journeys West — Sindh, Mecca, Medina, and Baghdad
courses.summary: This course traces Guru Nanak's fourth and final great journey westward through Sindh, Pak Pattan, Mecca, Medina, Baghdad, and Kabul, following janamsakhi accounts and Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Nanak Prakash. Students examine the most famous episodes of the Udasi tradition — the Mecca Kaaba sakhi, the meeting with Bahlol Dana in Baghdad — and analyze what these encounters reveal about Guru Nanak's theology of divine omnipresence and his engagement with Islam at its most sacred sites.
outcomes: Identify the major geographic stages of the Fourth Udasi westward to the Arab world and back
Analyze the Mecca Kaaba sakhi and its theological significance for understanding divine omnipresence
Explain Guru Nanak's engagement with Islamic spiritual traditions including Sufi mysticism
Compare Guru Nanak's approach to Muslim audiences with his earlier encounters with Hindu and yogi traditions
Evaluate the historicity of the Mecca and Baghdad episodes using multiple janamsakhi sources
Assess the Fourth Udasi's contribution to the development of Sikh universalism and the settlement at Kartarpur
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Nanak Prakash. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1843.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Grewal, J. S. Guru Nanak in History. Chandigarh: Panjab University, 1969.
Kohli, Surindar Singh. Janam Sakhi Traditions. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1969.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Schimmel, Annemarie. Mystical Dimensions of Islam. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975.
McLeod, W. H., trans. and ed. The B40 Janam-Sakhi. Amritsar: Guru Nanak Dev University, 1980.

lessons.title: Setting Out West: The Fourth Udasi's Context
lessons.summary: Contextualizing the Fourth Udasi's westward direction, its approximate dating, and the Islamic world that Guru Nanak entered — from the Sindh to the Arabian peninsula.

lessons.title: Sindh and Pak Pattan: The Faridian Connection
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's passage through Sindh and his visit to Pak Pattan — the shrine of Baba Farid, one of the great Sufi saints of Punjab — and the connection between Guru Nanak's teaching and the Faridian Sufi tradition.

lessons.title: Westward Through Persia: The Route to Arabia
lessons.summary: The Fourth Udasi's westward route through Persia and the broader cultural and religious landscape Guru Nanak traversed on the way to Mecca.

lessons.title: Arrival at Mecca: The City at the Center of Islam
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's arrival at Mecca — the holiest city of Islam — and the religious and social world he encountered at the annual pilgrimage.

lessons.title: The Kaaba Sakhi: Feet Toward the Qibla
lessons.summary: The most famous episode of the Fourth Udasi — Guru Nanak sleeping with his feet toward the Kaaba, the exchange with the qazi Rukn al-Din, and the miraculous turning of the Kaaba.

lessons.title: The Theological Heart of the Mecca Episode
lessons.summary: A deeper examination of the theological claims embedded in the Mecca Kaaba sakhi — divine omnipresence, the insufficiency of directional prayer, and Guru Nanak's synthesis of Islamic and universal spiritual values.

lessons.title: Medina: The City of the Prophet
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's visit to Medina, the second holiest city of Islam and the burial place of the Prophet Muhammad, and the significance of this visit in the Fourth Udasi narrative.

lessons.title: Baghdad: Meeting Bahlol Dana
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's arrival at Baghdad, the former center of the Islamic caliphate, and his meeting with Bahlol Dana — the God-intoxicated majzub mystic — and the theological significance of this encounter.

lessons.title: The Baghdad Miracle: Calling Across Worlds
lessons.summary: The famous Baghdad miracle account in the Janamsakhis — Guru Nanak's prayer call that was heard in both the upper and lower worlds — and its theological significance.

lessons.title: The Return: Kabul and the Khyber Pass
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's return journey from Baghdad through the Persian world, Khorasan, Kabul, and finally through the Khyber Pass back to Punjab.

lessons.title: The Settlement at Kartarpur
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's founding of the community of Kartarpur after completing the Fourth Udasi — the model village that embodied his social and spiritual vision and became the prototype of later Sikh institutions.

lessons.title: Legacy of the Fourth Udasi and the Complete Udasi Journey
lessons.summary: The Fourth Udasi's enduring contributions to Sikh tradition and a synthetic assessment of all four udasis as a complete arc of universal spiritual mission.

courses.title: Japji Sahib: A Deep Study
courses.summary: This course offers a deep theological and literary study of Japji Sahib, Guru Nanak's foundational composition that opens the Guru Granth Sahib and is recited daily by Sikhs. Each of the 38 pauris (stanzas) and the Mool Mantar are examined for their theological content, linguistic structure, and place in Sikh spiritual practice. The course draws on Prof. Sahib Singh's authoritative commentary and grounds Japji's teaching in Guru Nanak's broader theological vision.
outcomes: Explain the theological content of the Mool Mantar as a foundational statement of Sikh theology
Analyze the major theological themes of Japji — hukam, seva, nadar, and sahaj — across the 38 pauris
Identify the five khands (realms) of spiritual progression described in the final pauris
Apply textual analysis methods to interpret Gurmukhi passages from Japji with accuracy
Compare the Japji's theology of divine sovereignty with parallel concepts in other Indian religious traditions
Evaluate the role of Japji in Sikh daily life and its function as the opening composition of the Guru Granth Sahib
references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962.
Singh, Manmohan, trans. Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Amritsar: SGPC, 1969.
Macauliffe, Max Arthur. The Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1909.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Singh, Trilochan, et al., trans. Selections from the Sacred Writings of the Sikhs. London: George Allen and Unwin, 1960.

lessons.title: Introduction to Japji Sahib: Structure, Context, and Daily Practice
lessons.summary: An overview of Japji Sahib's place in the Guru Granth Sahib, its structure of Mool Mantar, 38 pauris, and closing slok, and its central role in Sikh daily practice.

lessons.title: The Mool Mantar: Theology in Fourteen Words
lessons.summary: A detailed examination of the Mool Mantar — the foundational theological statement of Sikhism — analyzing each of its terms and their significance for Sikh theological self-understanding.

lessons.title: The Opening Slok: How Does One Become Truthful?
lessons.summary: Examination of Japji's opening slok, which poses the central question: if truth is the highest value, how does one become truthful? — and Guru Nanak's answer through the concept of Hukam.

lessons.title: Pauris 1–6: Hukam and the Divine Order
lessons.summary: Analysis of Japji's first six pauris, which develop the concept of Hukam (divine order) and establish the impossibility of approaching the divine through ritual or intellectual effort alone.

lessons.title: Pauris 7–15: The Infinity of the Divine and Human Limitation
lessons.summary: Analysis of Japji's middle section (pauris 7–15), which meditates on the infinite scope of the divine reality and the radical limitation of human knowing.

lessons.title: Pauris 16–19: The Praise of the Divine Name
lessons.summary: Analysis of the section of Japji focused on the Naam (Divine Name) — what it is, how it is received, and what happens to those who dwell in it.

lessons.title: Pauris 20–27: The Qualities of the Truthful
lessons.summary: Analysis of Japji's extended reflection on the qualities of the truthful (sachiar) — those who have genuinely aligned with the Hukam — and what their lives look like.

lessons.title: Pauris 28–32: The Cosmic Vision
lessons.summary: Analysis of Japji's cosmic passages — pauris 28–32 — which describe the infinite scope of the divine creation and the Guru's role in guiding the soul through it.

lessons.title: Pauris 33–37: The Five Khands
lessons.summary: Detailed examination of Japji's most systematic theological section — the description of the five khands (realms/spheres) through which the soul progresses on its journey to the divine.

lessons.title: The Final Slok: The Closing Teaching
lessons.summary: Examination of Japji's closing slok, which summarizes the entire path in an extended metaphor of the spiritual journey as a process of making oneself a vessel for the divine.

lessons.title: Japji's Theological Vision: Synthesis
lessons.summary: A synthetic overview of Japji Sahib's complete theological vision — its doctrine of the divine, its soteriology, its ethics, and its relationship to the broader Sikh theological tradition.

lessons.title: Japji in Sikh Life and Scholarship
lessons.summary: The role of Japji in Sikh daily life and practice, its place in scholarly commentary, and contemporary approaches to its study and teaching.

courses.title: Asa Di Var: Morning Prayer and Social Vision
courses.summary: This course offers a comprehensive study of Asa Di Var, Guru Nanak's ballad in Asa raag that is sung as the morning prayer in gurdwaras worldwide. The course examines each of the 24 pauris and their accompanying slokas, exploring the composition's powerful social critique of caste, ritual, and religious hypocrisy alongside its positive vision of truthful living, honest labor, and the community of the Naam. Special attention is given to the composition's structure as a var (ballad) and its relationship to the Bhagat bani slokas interspersed throughout.
outcomes: Identify the structure of Asa Di Var as a var with 24 pauris and interspersed slokas
Analyze Guru Nanak's social critique of caste hierarchy, ritual Brahminism, and religious hypocrisy in the text
Explain the positive social vision encoded in Asa Di Var — honest labor, community, and the dignity of truthful living
Examine the theological relationship between the pauris of Guru Nanak and the Bhagat slokas included in the composition
Compare Asa Di Var's social teaching with other Bhakti movement critiques of caste and ritual
Evaluate the role of Asa Di Var in Sikh morning practice and its musical tradition
references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962.
Singh, Manmohan, trans. Sri Guru Granth Sahib. Amritsar: SGPC, 1969.

Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Loehlin, C. H. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa Brotherhood. Lucknow: Lucknow Publishing House, 1971.

lessons.title: Introduction to Asa Di Var: Structure, Setting, and Significance
lessons.summary: Overview of Asa Di Var's structure as a var, its place in the Guru Granth Sahib, and its role in Sikh morning worship practice.

lessons.title: The Var Form: Ballad as Theological Vehicle
lessons.summary: Examination of the var (ballad) form in Punjabi literature, its traditional functions, and how Guru Nanak adapted it for theological and social critique.

lessons.title: Opening Slokas: Setting the Stage
lessons.summary: Examination of the slokas that open Asa Di Var, establishing its theological premises and the questions it will address.

lessons.title: Pauris 1–4: The Divine Order and Human Striving
lessons.summary: Analysis of the first four pauris of Asa Di Var, which establish the divine order, the inadequacy of ritual, and the path of genuine spiritual practice.

lessons.title: Pauris 5–8: The Critique of Caste
lessons.summary: Analysis of the sections of Asa Di Var that directly address the caste system — one of Guru Nanak's most sustained and direct engagements with this social institution.

lessons.title: Pauris 9–12: Honest Labor and the Ethics of Living
lessons.summary: Examination of Asa Di Var's positive ethical vision, centered on the concepts of kirat karo (honest labor), vand chhako (sharing), and the dignity of productive work.

lessons.title: Pauris 13–16: The Hypocrisy of Religious Pretense
lessons.summary: Asa Di Var's powerful critique of religious hypocrisy (pakhand) — examining those who perform religion as a social display rather than as genuine inner practice.

lessons.title: Pauris 17–20: The Community of the Naam
lessons.summary: Analysis of the section of Asa Di Var focused on the sangat (holy congregation) and the community of Naam practitioners as the context for genuine spiritual development.

lessons.title: Pauris 21–24: The Final Vision of Truthful Living
lessons.summary: Analysis of Asa Di Var's final pauris, which present the complete vision of the truthful life — its characteristics, its relationship to the divine, and its social expression.

lessons.title: The Bhagat Slokas: Kabir and the Tradition of Critique
lessons.summary: Examination of the slokas by Bhagat Kabir and others interspersed in Asa Di Var, and what their inclusion tells us about Guru Nanak's theological vision and the Guru Granth Sahib's compilation.

lessons.title: Asa Di Var's Social Vision: A Theological Analysis
lessons.summary: A synthetic analysis of Asa Di Var's social vision — examining the relationship between its theology and its social ethics, and its significance for Sikh social thought.

lessons.title: Asa Di Var in Sikh Morning Practice
lessons.summary: The role of Asa Di Var in Sikh morning worship, its musical tradition, and how the experience of singing and hearing the composition shapes Sikh community life.

courses.title: Sidh Gosht: Guru Nanak's Dialogue with the Siddhs
courses.summary: This advanced course offers a close reading of the Sidh Gosht, Guru Nanak's extended philosophical dialogue with the Nath Siddhs preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib in Ramkali raag. Students examine each of the composition's pauris for their theological arguments about liberation, the Guru, the householder path, the nature of the self, and the relationship between human effort and divine grace. The course requires familiarity with Nath yogi terminology and Sikh theological concepts introduced in earlier courses.
outcomes: Analyze the structure of the Sidh Gosht as a theological dialogue and identify its major argumentative stages
Explain the Nath Siddh tradition's position on liberation and how Guru Nanak systematically challenges it
Defend Guru Nanak's theology of the householder path against the Siddhs' preference for renunciation
Interpret the Sidh Gosht's key theological terms — shabad, sahaj, gurprasad, anhad — in their proper theological context
Evaluate the scholarly debate over the Sidh Gosht's relationship to a historical encounter versus a literary dialogue
Apply the Sidh Gosht's theology to contemporary questions about the relationship between effort and grace in spiritual practice
references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
White, David Gordon. The Alchemical Body: Siddha Traditions in Medieval India. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1996.
Briggs, George Weston. Gorakhnath and the Kanphata Yogis. Calcutta: YMCA Press, 1938.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Grewal, J. S. Guru Nanak in History. Chandigarh: Panjab University, 1969.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Sidh Gosht: Genre, Structure, and Context
lessons.summary: Overview of the Sidh Gosht as a theological dialogue — its genre, its place in the Guru Granth Sahib, and the historical and intellectual context for its composition.

lessons.title: The Nath Siddh Tradition: Background for the Dialogue
lessons.summary: A focused review of the Nath Siddh tradition's theology and practice — the interlocutor that Guru Nanak engages in the Sidh Gosht — to enable close reading of the dialogue.

lessons.title: The Siddhs' Opening Challenges
lessons.summary: Close reading of the Siddhs' opening questions in the Sidh Gosht — who are you, why are you here, what path do you follow — and Guru Nanak's initial responses.

lessons.title: Guru Nanak's Defense of the Householder Path
lessons.summary: Close reading of Guru Nanak's defense of the householder path in the Sidh Gosht, and the theological argument for why the grihasta life can be the genuine spiritual path.

lessons.title: The Shabad Guru: Redefining the Guru
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's revolutionary redefinition of the Guru concept in the Sidh Gosht — from a human teacher to the divine Word — and its implications for Sikh theology.

lessons.title: The Ocean of Existence: Bhavjal and Its Crossing
lessons.summary: The Sidh Gosht's central metaphor — the bhavjal (ocean of existence) — and the debate between Nath and Sikh approaches to crossing it.

lessons.title: Effort and Grace: The Central Soteriological Debate
lessons.summary: The Sidh Gosht's core theological tension — between Nath yogic self-sufficiency and Guru Nanak's insistence on divine grace — examined in detail.

lessons.title: Sahaj: Natural Ease as the Mark of Liberation
lessons.summary: The Sidh Gosht's development of the concept of sahaj (natural ease/equipoise) as the characteristic quality of genuine liberation — in contrast to the Nath tradition's emphasis on achieved states.

lessons.title: The Anhad Naad: Inner Sound as Spiritual Sign
lessons.summary: The Sidh Gosht's treatment of the anhad naad (unstruck sound) as a sign of spiritual progress — comparing the Nath and Sikh understandings of this inner phenomenon.

lessons.title: The True Yogi: Guru Nanak's Counter-Portrait
lessons.summary: Guru Nanak's positive counter-portrait of the true yogi in the Sidh Gosht — against the Nath ideal of the accomplished ascetic — and its characteristics.

lessons.title: Nirgun and Sargun in the Sidh Gosht
lessons.summary: The Sidh Gosht's philosophical treatment of the relationship between the formless (nirgun) and with-form (sargun) aspects of the divine — one of its most sophisticated theological contributions.

lessons.title: The Sidh Gosht's Legacy in Sikh Theology
lessons.summary: The Sidh Gosht's enduring contributions to Sikh theology — the Shabad Guru doctrine, the householder theology, the nirgun-sargun synthesis — and its place in the Sikh scriptural canon.

courses.title: Guru Nanak's Social Revolution: Caste, Gender, and Equality
courses.summary: This course examines Guru Nanak's revolutionary social teachings on caste, gender, and human equality — situating these teachings in the historical context of early sixteenth-century Punjab and assessing their long-term impact on Sikh community life. Students examine primary textual evidence from Gurbani, the institutional innovations of the udasi period (sangat, langar, pangat), and scholarly assessments of how Guru Nanak's social vision compared to and differed from the broader Bhakti movement. Special attention is given to how these teachings were received by different communities and how they have been implemented — and sometimes compromised — in subsequent Sikh history.
outcomes: Explain the caste system of early sixteenth-century Punjab and the specific social context into which Guru Nanak spoke
Analyze Gurbani evidence for Guru Nanak's teachings on caste, gender, and human dignity
Compare Guru Nanak's social critique with that of contemporaneous Bhakti and Sufi reformers
Evaluate the institutional innovations of sangat, langar, and pangat as implementations of the social vision
Assess the historical record of how Sikh communities have lived up to — and fallen short of — Guru Nanak's egalitarian vision
Apply Guru Nanak's social teachings to contemporary questions of discrimination and social justice
references: Singh, Giani Ditt. The Sikhs and Their Religion. Lahore: Khalsa Press, 1899.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Grewal, J. S. Guru Nanak in History. Chandigarh: Panjab University, 1969.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.
Jodhka, Surinder S. Caste. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2012.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Barrier, N. G., ed. The Sikhs and Their Literature. New Delhi: Manohar, 1970.

lessons.title: The Social World Guru Nanak Was Born Into
lessons.summary: A description of the caste hierarchy, gender roles, and social institutions of early sixteenth-century Punjab that formed the context for Guru Nanak's social teachings.

lessons.title: The Theological Foundation of Social Equality
lessons.summary: Examination of the theological basis for Guru Nanak's social egalitarianism — rooted in the doctrine of divine immanence and the equal presence of the divine light in every human being.

lessons.title: Gurbani on Caste: A Textual Examination
lessons.summary: A close reading of specific Gurbani passages that directly address caste — examining what Guru Nanak actually says and what it means in theological and social context.

lessons.title: The Langar: Equality Made Concrete
lessons.summary: The history and theology of the langar (free community kitchen) as Guru Nanak's most influential institutional expression of his egalitarian social vision.

lessons.title: Pangat: The Practice of Sitting Together
lessons.summary: The practice of pangat (sitting in a row to eat together) as the langar's social expression — its anti-caste significance and how it embodied Guru Nanak's theological vision.

lessons.title: Guru Nanak and Women: Theological Affirmation
lessons.summary: Examination of Guru Nanak's theological affirmation of women's full spiritual equality, grounded in the doctrine of divine immanence and expressed in specific Gurbani compositions.

lessons.title: The Composition About Women: So Kiyo Manda Akhiye
lessons.summary: A close reading of the Guru Granth Sahib composition that most directly addresses women's status and dignity — often cited as Guru Nanak's most explicit affirmation of gender equality.

lessons.title: Bhai Lalo and the Ethics of Honest Living
lessons.summary: Re-examination of the Bhai Lalo/Malik Bhago sakhi from the First Udasi as the founding narrative of Guru Nanak's social ethic of honest labor and economic justice.

lessons.title: The Bhakti Comparison: What Was Distinctive About Guru Nanak
lessons.summary: A comparative examination of Guru Nanak's social vision alongside the broader Bhakti movement, identifying both common ground and what was distinctive about Guru Nanak's approach.

lessons.title: Historical Reception: Who Was Attracted and Why
lessons.summary: An examination of the historical evidence about who was attracted to Guru Nanak's community during the udasis and at Kartarpur, and what this reveals about the social reception of his egalitarian teaching.

lessons.title: Implementation and Compromise: The Long Historical Record
lessons.summary: An honest assessment of how Sikh communities have implemented — and sometimes compromised — Guru Nanak's egalitarian social vision across five centuries.

lessons.title: Guru Nanak's Social Vision and Contemporary Sikhism
lessons.summary: The relevance of Guru Nanak's social teachings to contemporary Sikhism — from ongoing challenges of caste discrimination to contemporary social justice movements.

courses.title: The Janamsakhis: Devotional Biography and Historical Method
courses.summary: This advanced course examines the Janamsakhi tradition — the devotional biography collections that preserve the life of Guru Nanak — as both historical sources and literary-theological documents. Students learn to distinguish the major Janamsakhi traditions (Puratan, Miharban, Bala, and Gyan Ratanavali), evaluate their relative historical reliability, and apply critical methods to extract historical content from devotional narrative. The course also examines Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Nanak Prakash as a nineteenth-century synthesis of the tradition.
outcomes: Identify and distinguish the major Janamsakhi traditions by their date, authorship, and theological orientation
Apply W. H. McLeod's critical method for evaluating Janamsakhi historical reliability
Analyze the literary structure and theological purposes of key Janamsakhi sakhis
Compare how different Janamsakhi traditions narrate the same events and assess what the differences reveal
Evaluate the Sri Nanak Prakash of Kavi Santokh Singh as a nineteenth-century synthesis of earlier traditions
Defend a position on the appropriate use of Janamsakhi evidence in Sikh historical scholarship
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Nanak Prakash. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1843.
McLeod, W. H. Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
McLeod, W. H., trans. and ed. The B40 Janam-Sakhi. Amritsar: Guru Nanak Dev University, 1980.
Kohli, Surindar Singh. Janam Sakhi Traditions. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1969.
Grewal, J. S. Guru Nanak in History. Chandigarh: Panjab University, 1969.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Loehlin, C. H. The Granth of Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa Brotherhood. Lucknow: Lucknow Publishing House, 1971.

lessons.title: Introduction: What Is a Janamsakhi?
lessons.summary: An introduction to the Janamsakhi genre — its literary character as devotional biography, its relationship to similar hagiographic traditions, and why its critical evaluation matters for Sikh history.

lessons.title: The Puratan Janamsakhi: The Oldest Tradition
lessons.summary: An examination of the Puratan (ancient) Janamsakhi tradition — its manuscript history, its distinctive features, and its relative historical value.

lessons.title: The Miharban Janamsakhi: Sectarian Biography
lessons.summary: Examination of the Miharban Janamsakhi — composed by a member of a rival Sikh sect — its distinctive theological agenda, and what it contributes to our understanding of the tradition.

lessons.title: The Bala Janamsakhi: Tradition and Controversy
lessons.summary: The controversial Bala Janamsakhi tradition — presenting itself as narrated by Guru Nanak's companion Bhai Bala — and the scholarly debate about its authenticity and historical value.

lessons.title: The Gyan Ratanavali and Other Traditions
lessons.summary: Overview of the Gyan Ratanavali and other Janamsakhi traditions not yet covered, and their contribution to the overall picture of Guru Nanak's life.

lessons.title: Sri Nanak Prakash: The Nineteenth-Century Synthesis
lessons.summary: A close examination of Kavi Santokh Singh's Sri Nanak Prakash as a nineteenth-century synthesis of the Janamsakhi tradition — its sources, its literary character, and its historical value.

lessons.title: W. H. McLeod's Critical Method
lessons.summary: An examination of W. H. McLeod's influential critical method for evaluating Janamsakhi historical evidence, including his criteria for relative historical reliability and the responses his work has generated.

lessons.title: The Sakhi as Literary Form: Structure and Purpose
lessons.summary: An analysis of the individual sakhi as a literary form — its typical narrative structure, its theological purposes, and how understanding the form enriches reading individual episodes.

lessons.title: Miracle Stories: Theological Function and Historical Evaluation
lessons.summary: A focused examination of the miracle stories in the Janamsakhis — their literary and theological functions, and how scholars evaluate them historically.

lessons.title: Geographic Evidence in the Janamsakhis
lessons.summary: The geographic dimension of Janamsakhi evidence — how the travel accounts of the udasis compare with known historical geography, and what the consistency or inconsistency of geographic details reveals.

lessons.title: Comparing Janamsakhi Accounts: A Case Study
lessons.summary: A detailed case study comparing how different Janamsakhi traditions narrate the same event — using the Mecca Kaaba episode as the example — to illustrate the critical method in practice.

lessons.title: The Janamsakhis in Sikh Scholarship and Practice
lessons.summary: The role of the Janamsakhis in Sikh scholarly tradition and devotional practice — how the community has used these texts and how this usage shapes their reception.

courses.title: Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji: Life and the Transformation of the Panth
courses.summary: This course traces the life of the Sixth Nanak, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji (1595–1644), from his birth at Wadali through his long Guruship of thirty-eight years. Students examine how the Guru transformed the Panth from a devotional community into a sovereign people, responding to his father Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom with institutional, military, and spiritual innovations that continue to define Sikhi.
outcomes: Describe the major events of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's life from birth to Jyoti Jot
Explain the political context of the early seventeenth-century Mughal court and its impact on Sikh affairs
Analyze how the Guru's response to Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom reshaped Sikh identity
Identify the key figures surrounding the Sixth Guru, including Baba Budha Ji and Bhai Gurdas Ji
Evaluate primary sources such as Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin and Suraj Prakash as historical evidence
Trace the Guru's relocations — Amritsar, Kartarpur, Kiratpur — and their strategic significance
references: Bhagat Singh. Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin. Edited by Gurmukh Singh. Patiala: Punjabi University Publication Bureau, 1997.
Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1963.
Replace with a verified Ganda Singh work, e.g.: Singh, Ganda, and Teja Singh. A Short History of the Sikhs. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1950.
Khushwant Singh. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1: 1469–1839. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1963.
Harbans Singh. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Gopal Singh. A History of the Sikh People (1469–1988). New Delhi: World Book Centre, 1988.
Fauja Singh, ed. Historians and Historiography of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Oriental Publishers, 1978.

lessons.title: Birth, Lineage, and Early Years
lessons.summary: Introduces the birth of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji at Guru Ki Wadali, his family lineage, and the spiritual atmosphere of his early childhood under Guru Arjan Dev Ji.

lessons.title: The Martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Its Impact
lessons.summary: Examines the circumstances of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom in 1606 and how this event catalysed the Sixth Guru's transformation of Sikh identity.

lessons.title: Ascending the Throne: The Ceremony of 1606
lessons.summary: Details the investiture ceremony at Amritsar in 1606, including the symbolic donning of two swords and the formal declaration of a new Sikh identity.

lessons.title: The Miri-Piri Doctrine in Daily Life
lessons.summary: Explores how the two-sword doctrine manifested in the Guru's daily routine, governance style, and theological teachings.

lessons.title: Building a Sovereign Panth: Army, Horses, and Hawks
lessons.summary: Examines the institutional steps Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji took to build the Panth's military and administrative capacity.

lessons.title: Key Companions: Baba Budha Ji, Bhai Gurdas Ji, and Others
lessons.summary: Profiles the major figures who supported Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's ministry, including their roles and legacies.

lessons.title: Imprisonment in Gwalior Fort
lessons.summary: Examines the circumstances, duration, and significance of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's imprisonment at Gwalior Fort by Emperor Jahangir.

lessons.title: Release and Bandi Chhor Divas
lessons.summary: Covers the Guru's release from Gwalior Fort, the liberation of fifty-two imprisoned kings, and the significance of Bandi Chhor Divas.

lessons.title: The Four Battles Against Mughal Forces
lessons.summary: Surveys the four battles fought by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji against Mughal armies: Amritsar, Lahira, Kartarpur, and Phagwara.

lessons.title: Relocations: Kartarpur, Kiratpur, and the Shivalik Hills
lessons.summary: Examines the Guru's strategic relocations away from Amritsar and the founding of new Sikh settlements in the Shivalik foothills.

lessons.title: Family, Succession, and Handing the Guruship to Guru Har Rai Ji
lessons.summary: Covers Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's family life, the lives of his children, and the selection of his grandson as the Seventh Guru.

lessons.title: Legacy: Transforming the Panth for Generations to Come
lessons.summary: Synthesises the enduring institutional, theological, and cultural legacies of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's thirty-eight-year Guruship.

courses.title: Miri-Piri: The Two Swords and a New Sikh Identity
courses.summary: This course provides a deep theological and historical examination of the Miri-Piri doctrine introduced by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji in 1606. Students explore the conceptual foundations of this doctrine in earlier Gurbani, its institutional expression in the two swords and the Akal Takht, and its enduring significance for Sikh political theology and identity.
outcomes: Define the terms Miri and Piri and explain their theological relationship in Sikh thought
Trace the roots of the Miri-Piri concept in the Gurbani of earlier Gurus
Analyze how the doctrine was institutionalised through the Akal Takht and the two swords
Compare the Sikh understanding of temporal-spiritual integration with other religious traditions
Evaluate scholarly debates about whether the martial turn represented continuity or rupture with earlier Sikhi
Apply the Miri-Piri framework to contemporary questions about Sikh sovereignty and engagement with political life
references: Bhagat Singh. Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin. Edited by Gurmukh Singh. Patiala: Punjabi University Publication Bureau, 1997.
Harbans Singh. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Khushwant Singh. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1: 1469–1839. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1963.
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco, 1995.
W. H. McLeod. Sikhism. London: Penguin, 1997.
Pashaura Singh. Life and Work of Guru Arjan: History, Memory, and Biography in the Sikh Tradition. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2006.
Gurinder Singh Mann. The Making of Sikh Scripture. New York: Oxford University Press, 2001.

lessons.title: What Are Miri and Piri? Foundations of the Doctrine
lessons.summary: Introduces the terms Miri and Piri, their Persian-Arabic origins, and how Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji gave them new Sikh theological content.

lessons.title: Roots in Earlier Gurbani: Sovereignty in the Teachings of Guru Nanak Dev Ji
lessons.summary: Traces the theological precedents for Miri-Piri in the Gurbani of Guru Nanak Dev Ji and the subsequent Gurus, arguing that the doctrine has deep roots in the Sikh scriptural tradition.

lessons.title: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Martyrdom as Catalyst
lessons.summary: Examines how Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom functioned as the immediate catalyst for the explicit articulation of the Miri-Piri doctrine.

lessons.title: The Ceremony of 1606: Two Swords, One Guru
lessons.summary: Provides a detailed account of the 1606 investiture ceremony and the theological meanings encoded in each element of the ritual.

lessons.title: The Akal Takht as Institutional Expression of Miri
lessons.summary: Details the founding, design, and purpose of the Akal Takht as the physical and institutional embodiment of Miri within Sikh governance.

lessons.title: Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht: A Theological Dialogue in Stone
lessons.summary: Examines the architectural and theological relationship between Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht as complementary expressions of Piri and Miri.

lessons.title: The Sant-Sipahi Ideal
lessons.summary: Develops the theological concept of the sant-sipahi (saint-soldier) as the human embodiment of the Miri-Piri doctrine.

lessons.title: Deg and Teg: Two Forms of Divine Generosity
lessons.summary: Explores the complementary concepts of deg (the cauldron of food) and teg (the sword) as expressions of Miri-Piri in daily Sikh practice.

lessons.title: Miri-Piri and Dharam Yudh: When Is War Justified?
lessons.summary: Examines the Sikh doctrine of dharam yudh (righteous war) as the ethical framework that governs the exercise of the Miri sword.

lessons.title: Comparing Miri-Piri with Other Traditions of Spiritual-Temporal Integration
lessons.summary: Places the Miri-Piri doctrine in comparative religious perspective, examining parallels and contrasts with Christian, Islamic, and Hindu traditions of spiritual-temporal authority.

lessons.title: Scholarly Debates: Continuity or Rupture?
lessons.summary: Reviews major scholarly positions on whether the Miri-Piri doctrine represents a continuity with or a departure from the earlier Sikh tradition.

lessons.title: Miri-Piri in the Contemporary Panth
lessons.summary: Examines how the Miri-Piri doctrine functions in contemporary Sikh life, politics, and institutional structures.

courses.title: The Akal Takht: Origins, Purpose, and Enduring Significance
courses.summary: This course provides a comprehensive historical and theological examination of the Akal Takht, established by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji in 1606 CE. Students trace the structure's origins, its functions in the Guru period, its destruction and rebuilding, and its continuing role as the supreme temporal authority of the Sikh Panth.
outcomes: Explain the circumstances of the Akal Takht's founding in 1606 CE and the doctrine it embodies
Describe the original functions of the Akal Takht in Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's governance
Analyze the architectural relationship between the Akal Takht and Harmandir Sahib
Trace the history of the Akal Takht's destruction and rebuilding across different periods
Evaluate the contemporary functions and controversies surrounding the Akal Takht as a Sikh institution
Compare the Akal Takht's model of authority with other examples of spiritual-political institutions globally
references: Bhagat Singh. Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin. Edited by Gurmukh Singh. Patiala: Punjabi University Publication Bureau, 1997.
Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1963.
Harbans Singh. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Ganda Singh, ed. Early European Accounts of the Sikhs. Calcutta: Indian Studies Past & Present, 1962.
Khushwant Singh. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1: 1469–1839. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1963.
J. S. Grewal. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Fauja Singh, ed. Historians and Historiography of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Oriental Publishers, 1978.

lessons.title: The Founding of the Akal Takht: 1606 CE
lessons.summary: Examines the immediate circumstances of the Akal Takht's establishment, its design, and its initial meaning for the Sikh community.

lessons.title: The Name 'Akal Takht' and Its Theological Meaning
lessons.summary: Explores the theological significance of the name 'Throne of the Timeless' and its implications for Sikh understanding of sovereignty.

lessons.title: Architectural Relationship with Harmandir Sahib
lessons.summary: Analyses the spatial and architectural theology of the Akal Takht's relationship with Harmandir Sahib.

lessons.title: The Five Takhts: Akal Takht in Context
lessons.summary: Places the Akal Takht within the broader system of the Five Takhts and examines how this system functions as a distributed model of Sikh temporal authority.

lessons.title: Functions in the Guru Period: Court, Justice, and Military Command
lessons.summary: Describes the practical functions of the Akal Takht during the Guru period under Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji and subsequent Gurus.

lessons.title: The Jathedar: Origin and Role of the Office
lessons.summary: Traces the history of the Jathedar's office from its origins to its contemporary form and examines the responsibilities and limitations of the position.

lessons.title: The Hukamnameh Tradition
lessons.summary: Examines the tradition of the hukamnameh (authoritative edict) and its function in Sikh community governance.

lessons.title: Eighteenth-Century Challenges: Invasions and the Sarbat Khalsa
lessons.summary: Examines how the Sikh Panth used the Akal Takht as a centre of collective decision-making during the turbulent eighteenth century.

lessons.title: Destruction and Rebuilding: A History of Resilience
lessons.summary: Chronicles the multiple occasions on which the Akal Takht has been physically destroyed and subsequently rebuilt, and what this history reveals about the institution's meaning.

lessons.title: Operation Blue Star (1984) and Its Aftermath
lessons.summary: Examines the 1984 Indian Army operation at the Golden Temple complex, its impact on the Akal Takht, and the long-term consequences for Sikh-state relations.

lessons.title: Contemporary Functions and Controversies
lessons.summary: Examines the Akal Takht's current role in Sikh governance, recent controversies, and the ongoing challenges of maintaining institutional integrity.

lessons.title: The Akal Takht as Model: Sovereignty in Service
lessons.summary: Synthesises the historical and theological lessons of the Akal Takht and explores its significance as a model of religious-political governance.

courses.title: The Four Battles: Amritsar, Lahira, Kartarpur, and Phagwara
courses.summary: This course provides a detailed military and political history of the four battles fought by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji against Mughal imperial forces between 1629 and 1635 CE. Students examine the causes, conduct, and consequences of each engagement, the primary sources that record them, and their enduring significance for Sikh understanding of dharam yudh.
outcomes: Identify the causes and key participants in each of the four battles fought by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
Analyze primary source accounts of the battles in the Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin and Suraj Prakash Granth
Evaluate the dating controversies surrounding the four battles and their scholarly resolutions
Explain how each battle related to the broader political conflict between the Sikh Panth and the Mughal administration
Apply the concept of dharam yudh to assess the conduct of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji in these engagements
Assess the military and strategic significance of the battles for the long-term survival of the Panth
references: Bhagat Singh. Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin. Edited by Gurmukh Singh. Patiala: Punjabi University Publication Bureau, 1997.
Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1963.
Ganda Singh, ed. Early European Accounts of the Sikhs. Calcutta: Indian Studies Past & Present, 1962.
Khushwant Singh. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1: 1469-1839. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1963.
J. S. Grewal. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Fauja Singh, ed. Historians and Historiography of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Oriental Publishers, 1978.
Harbans Singh. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.

lessons.title: Introduction: Why Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji Went to War
lessons.summary: Establishes the political, theological, and historical context for the four battles, examining why Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji chose to engage the Mughal military.

lessons.title: Primary Sources for the Four Battles
lessons.summary: Critically examines the primary sources that record the four battles and evaluates their historical reliability.

lessons.title: Dating Controversies: Reconciling Gurbilas and Modern Scholarship
lessons.summary: Examines the chronological discrepancies in the Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin's dating of the four battles and how modern scholarship has addressed them.

lessons.title: The Hawk Dispute: Trigger of the Battle of Amritsar
lessons.summary: Examines the immediate cause of the Battle of Amritsar: the Mughal seizure of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's prized hawk.

lessons.title: The Battle of Amritsar (c. 1629 CE)
lessons.summary: Provides a detailed account of the first battle between Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji and Mughal forces at Amritsar.

lessons.title: The Battle of Lahira (c. 1631 CE)
lessons.summary: Examines the second of the four battles, fought at Lahira, and its significance in the ongoing conflict with Mughal forces.

lessons.title: The Battle of Kartarpur (c. 1634 CE)
lessons.summary: Examines the third battle, fought at the town of Kartarpur on the Beas River, and the political escalation it represented.

lessons.title: The Battle of Phagwara (c. 1635 CE)
lessons.summary: Covers the fourth and final battle of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's reign and its aftermath.

lessons.title: Weapons, Tactics, and the Art of War
lessons.summary: Examines the military technology, tactical approaches, and strategic thinking evident in the four battles as recorded in the Gurbilas.

lessons.title: Sikh Martyrs of the Four Battles
lessons.summary: Honours the Sikh warriors who gave their lives in the four battles and examines the tradition of martyrdom in Sikh theology.

lessons.title: Strategic Consequences: From Amritsar to Kiratpur
lessons.summary: Analyses the strategic consequences of the four battles and how they shaped the Panth's subsequent history.

lessons.title: Dharam Yudh: Theological Lessons of the Four Battles
lessons.summary: Synthesises the theological lessons of the four battles as an expression of the dharam yudh doctrine.

courses.title: Prisoner and Liberator: The Gwalior Fort and the Bandi Chhor
courses.summary: This course provides a detailed historical and theological study of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's imprisonment in Gwalior Fort by Emperor Jahangir and the celebrated Bandi Chhor episode in which the Guru secured the release of fifty-two imprisoned kings. Students examine the historical sources, the theological significance of collective liberation, and how Bandi Chhor Divas became one of the most important commemorations in the Sikh calendar.
outcomes: Explain the historical circumstances that led to Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's imprisonment in Gwalior Fort
Identify the key figures involved in the imprisonment and the eventual release, including Mian Mir
Describe the Bandi Chhor episode and analyze its theological significance within Sikh thought
Evaluate the different accounts of the imprisonment in Sikh and Mughal sources
Explain the origins and contemporary observance of Bandi Chhor Divas
Connect the Bandi Chhor episode to broader Sikh principles of solidarity and collective liberation
references: Bhagat Singh. Gurbilas Patshahi Chevin. Edited by Gurmukh Singh. Patiala: Punjabi University Publication Bureau, 1997.
Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Amritsar: Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1963.
Khushwant Singh. A History of the Sikhs, Volume 1: 1469-1839. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1963.
Ganda Singh, ed. Early European Accounts of the Sikhs. Calcutta: Indian Studies Past & Present, 1962.

lessons.summary: Examines the martyrdoms of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's three companions and their significance in the martyrdom narrative.

lessons.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's Final Meditation and Execution
lessons.summary: Examines the circumstances and spiritual character of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's execution at Chandni Chowk on November 24, 1675.

lessons.title: The Aftermath: Recovering the Guru's Body
lessons.summary: Examines the recovery of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's body and head after the martyrdom, and the devotion of those who risked their lives to perform this act.

lessons.title: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib
lessons.summary: Examines the two Delhi gurdwaras that mark the sites of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's martyrdom and cremation.

lessons.title: Hind di Chadar: Legacy and Significance
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the legacy of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's martyrdom and its enduring significance for Sikh identity and the history of religious freedom.

courses.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's Saloks: A Deep Study of Detachment and Courage
courses.summary: This course provides a rigorous theological and textual analysis of the fifty-seven Saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji in the Guru Granth Sahib. Drawing on Prof. Sahib Singh's exegetical method and Sikh theological scholarship, students engage deeply with the Guru's teachings on bairag (detachment), impermanence, the nature of the mind, and the fearless courage that flows from genuine surrender to Waheguru.
outcomes: Identify the structural place of the ninth Guru's Saloks within the Guru Granth Sahib
Analyze the major theological themes of bairag, impermanence, and fearlessness in the Saloks
Apply close reading techniques to specific Saloks with attention to poetic imagery and theological content
Evaluate the relationship between the Saloks' themes and the ninth Guru's biographical context
Distinguish the ninth Guru's distinctive theological voice from earlier Gurbani composers
Synthesize the Saloks' teachings on the nature of the mind and its transformation through Naam simran
references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1975.

Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind Mandair, eds. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.
Fenech, Louis E. Martyrdom in the Sikh Tradition: Playing the Game of Love. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

lessons.title: Introduction: The Saloks in Context
lessons.summary: Introduces Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's Saloks, their structural place in the Guru Granth Sahib, and their distinctive theological character.

lessons.title: The Salok Form in Gurbani
lessons.summary: Examines the salok as a literary and theological form in the Gurbani tradition and its particular use by Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji.

lessons.title: The Theme of Impermanence: Jagat Surat
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's theological treatment of the world's impermanence as expressed in his saloks.

lessons.title: Bairag: Detachment as Liberation, Not Negation
lessons.summary: Provides a careful theological analysis of bairag (detachment) in the ninth Guru's saloks, distinguishing it from world-denying asceticism.

lessons.title: Addressing the Mind: Man Tu Jot Saroop Hai
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's direct addresses to the mind in his saloks, focusing on the verse 'Man tu jot saroop hai'.

lessons.title: The Body's Mortality and the Soul's Endurance
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's theological treatment of the relationship between the mortal body and the enduring soul.

lessons.title: Maya and the Illusion of Permanence
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's treatment of maya as the force that creates the illusion of permanence and binds the mind to transient things.

lessons.title: Fear, Fearlessness, and the Divine Name
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's teaching on the relationship between fear, freedom from fear, and the practice of Naam simran.

lessons.title: Sorrow and Equanimity: Transcending Sukh-Dukh
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's teaching on equanimity in the face of pleasure and pain, joy and sorrow.

lessons.title: The Witness Self: Detachment in Relationship
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's concept of the 'witness self' — the inner awareness that observes without being captured by experience.

lessons.title: The Ninth Guru's Distinctive Voice in Gurbani
lessons.summary: Identifies the distinctive theological and poetic voice of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's saloks in relation to the broader Gurbani tradition.

lessons.title: Synthesis: From Bakala to Chandni Chowk — The Saloks as Prophetic Self-Description
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the major themes of the ninth Guru's saloks and their relationship to the arc of his life and martyrdom.

courses.title: The Travels of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji: Panjab, Bihar, Bengal, and Assam
courses.summary: This course examines the extensive travels of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji across the Indian subcontinent — from Punjab through Bihar, Bengal, and Assam — during the active years of his Guruship (1665-1675). Drawing on historical sources and hagiographical traditions, students trace the Guru's itinerary, the sangats (communities) he established or strengthened, the Gurbani he composed during these journeys, and the lasting institutional legacy of his travels for Sikh communities in eastern India.
outcomes: Trace the major routes and destinations of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's subcontintental travels
Identify the key sangats the Guru established or strengthened in Bihar, Bengal, and Assam
Explain the spiritual and institutional significance of the Guru's travels beyond Punjab
Analyze the relationship between the Guru's travel experiences and his Gurbani compositions
Evaluate the lasting institutional legacy of the ninth Guru's travels for Sikh communities in eastern India
Situate the travels within the broader context of the ninth Guru's ministry and the political environment
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1963.
Singh, Trilochan. Guru Tegh Bahadur: Prophet and Martyr. Delhi: Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee, 1967.
Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.

Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.

lessons.title: Introduction: The Traveling Guru
lessons.summary: Introduces the significance of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's travels as a dimension of his ministry and their importance for Sikh history.

lessons.title: The Punjab Base: Anandpur and the Early Ministry
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's establishment of Anandpur Sahib as his base and the early phase of his ministry in Punjab.

lessons.title: Motivations for the Eastern Travels
lessons.summary: Examines the spiritual, institutional, and political motivations behind Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's decision to travel east.

lessons.title: The Route East: Through the Gangetic Plain
lessons.summary: Traces the general route of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's eastward journey through the Gangetic plain.

lessons.title: Bihar: The Guru in the Land of the Ganges
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's ministry in Bihar and the communities he engaged with in this historically significant region.

lessons.title: Patna: The City That Would Witness a Guru's Birth
lessons.summary: Examines the ninth Guru's time at Patna, the birth of Gobind Rai there, and the city's enduring significance as Takht Sri Patna Sahib.

lessons.title: Bengal: Sikh Communities in the East
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's travels in Bengal and the communities established or strengthened there.

lessons.title: Dhaka and the Bengali Sangat
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's time in Dhaka (present Bangladesh) and his engagement with the Bengali Sikh community there.

lessons.title: Assam: The Furthest East
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's travels to Assam, the easternmost point of his journeys.

lessons.title: The Return Journey and Its Significance
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's return journey from the east and what he brought back to Punjab from his travels.

lessons.title: Gurbani Composed During the Travels
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurbani that Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji composed during his travels and how the travel experiences may have shaped his compositions.

lessons.title: The Lasting Legacy: Sikh Communities in Eastern India
lessons.summary: Assesses the lasting legacy of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's travels for Sikh communities in Bihar, Bengal, and Assam.

courses.title: Mughal India and the Context of the Ninth Guru's Ministry
courses.summary: This course examines the Mughal political and religious context within which Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's ministry unfolded, with particular attention to Aurangzeb's reign (1658-1707), the political economy of the empire, and the complex dynamics of Mughal-Sikh relations during the ninth Guru's decade of ministry. Students develop the historical and political literacy needed to understand the martyrdom's context and consequences.
outcomes: Describe the major features of Aurangzeb's religious and political agenda and its impact on non-Muslims
Explain the relationship between the Mughal state and the Sikh community across the Guru period
Analyze the specific political circumstances that led to the Kashmiri Pandits' appeal and the martyrdom
Evaluate different historical interpretations of Aurangzeb's religious policies
Identify the political consequences of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's martyrdom for the Sikh community
Connect the ninth Guru's ministry to the wider history of religious plurality in Mughal India
references: Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Sarkar, Jadunath. History of Aurangzib. Calcutta: M. C. Sarkar & Sons, 1924.
Singh, Trilochan. Guru Tegh Bahadur: Prophet and Martyr. Delhi: Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee, 1967.

Singh, Harbans. The Heritage of the Sikhs. New Delhi: Manohar, 1994.

lessons.title: Introduction: Why Historical Context Matters for Understanding the Martyrdom
lessons.summary: Establishes the importance of understanding Mughal political and religious history for comprehending the ninth Guru's martyrdom.

lessons.title: The Mughal Empire at Its Zenith and Turning Point
lessons.summary: Provides an overview of the Mughal Empire at the time of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's ministry, highlighting both its strength and the tensions that would eventually fragment it.

lessons.title: Aurangzeb: Character, Theology, and Political Vision
lessons.summary: Provides a nuanced portrait of Aurangzeb — his personal piety, his theological vision, and the political calculations that shaped his religious policies.

lessons.title: The Succession War and Its Religious Implications
lessons.summary: Examines the Mughal succession war of the 1650s and the religious significance of Dara Shikoh's defeat.

lessons.title: Aurangzeb's Religious Policies: Temple Destruction and Jizya
lessons.summary: Examines the specific religious policies Aurangzeb implemented, focusing on temple demolitions and the reintroduction of the jizya tax.

lessons.title: The Sikh Community Under Mughal Rule: From Guru Nanak to Guru Tegh Bahadur
lessons.summary: Traces the evolving relationship between the Sikh community and the Mughal state from Guru Nanak Dev Ji to the ninth Guru.

lessons.title: The Mughal-Sikh Conflict: From Guru Arjan Dev Ji to the Ninth Guru
lessons.summary: Traces the specific instances of Mughal-Sikh conflict from the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji to the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji.

lessons.title: Kashmir Under Mughal Rule and the Conversion Crisis
lessons.summary: Provides historical context for the forced conversion campaign in Kashmir that prompted the Kashmiri Pandits' appeal to Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji.

lessons.title: Political Economy and Religious Coercion
lessons.summary: Examines the political economy that made religious coercion financially and politically rational for the Mughal state.

lessons.title: The Political Consequences of the Martyrdom
lessons.summary: Examines the immediate and long-term political consequences of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's martyrdom for both the Sikh community and the Mughal state.

lessons.title: The Creation of the Khalsa as Political Response
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Gobind Singh Ji's creation of the Khalsa in 1699 as a political and spiritual response to his father's martyrdom.

lessons.title: Historical Debates About Aurangzeb and the Martyrdom
lessons.summary: Examines the major historiographical debates about Aurangzeb's religious policies and the martyrdom, presenting different scholarly perspectives.

courses.title: Historical Sources and the Memory of Hind di Chadar
courses.summary: This advanced course examines the historical sources — Sikh, Mughal, and later — through which memory of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's martyrdom has been preserved and transmitted. Students develop critical historical literacy by comparing accounts, assessing their reliability, understanding the genres and purposes of different source types, and engaging with historiographical debates about the martyrdom narrative.
outcomes: Identify and classify the major primary and secondary sources for the ninth Guru's martyrdom
Apply critical historiographical methods to Sikh hagiographical sources
Compare Sikh and Mughal accounts of the events of 1675
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of different source types for recovering historical events
Analyze how memory, community identity, and devotional purpose shape the transmission of historical accounts
Develop independent, evidence-based assessments of disputed historical questions about the martyrdom
references: Santokh Singh, Kavi. Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth. Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1963.
McLeod, W. H. The Evolution of the Sikh Community. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1976.

Singh, Trilochan. Guru Tegh Bahadur: Prophet and Martyr. Delhi: Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee, 1967.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind Mandair, eds. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.

lessons.title: Introduction: Why Source Criticism Matters
lessons.summary: Establishes the importance of source criticism for understanding the historical record of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's martyrdom.

lessons.title: The Genre of Sikh Hagiography: Understanding Janamsakhis and Granths
lessons.summary: Introduces the major genres of Sikh hagiographical writing and their characteristics as historical sources.

lessons.title: Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth: Kavi Santokh Singh's Major Work
lessons.summary: Provides a detailed assessment of the Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth as a historical source for Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's martyrdom.

lessons.title: Bichitra Natak: Guru Gobind Singh Ji's Testimony
lessons.summary: Examines the Bichitra Natak — Guru Gobind Singh Ji's autobiographical work — as a primary source for his father's martyrdom.

lessons.title: Mughal Court Sources: The Akhbarat and Persian Chronicles
lessons.summary: Examines Mughal court sources relevant to the ninth Guru's martyrdom and what they tell us from a non-Sikh perspective.

lessons.title: Early Sikh Sources: Gurbilases and Rahitnamas
lessons.summary: Examines earlier Sikh historical sources — the Gurbilases and Rahitnamas — and their evidence for the martyrdom narrative.

lessons.title: The Absence of Contemporary Documentation
lessons.summary: Examines the historiographical significance of the absence of contemporary documentation for the ninth Guru's martyrdom.

lessons.title: Oral Tradition and Its Role in Historical Memory
lessons.summary: Examines the role of oral tradition in preserving and transmitting memory of the ninth Guru's martyrdom.

lessons.title: How Devotional Purpose Shapes Historical Accounts
lessons.summary: Examines the ways in which devotional purposes shape hagiographical accounts of the martyrdom, and how to read such accounts critically.

lessons.title: Comparative Method: Reading Multiple Accounts Together
lessons.summary: Demonstrates the comparative method for historical source analysis through a case study of multiple accounts of a specific episode in the martyrdom narrative.

lessons.title: Major Disputed Questions About the Martyrdom
lessons.summary: Identifies and assesses the major historical questions about the martyrdom that remain genuinely disputed among scholars.

lessons.title: Toward a Critical Yet Respectful Historical Methodology
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the course's lessons about historical methodology and develops guidelines for critically examining Sikh sacred history with appropriate respect.

courses.title: Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar's Health Pothi: A Deep Study
courses.summary: This course offers a structured study of the Health Pothi compiled by Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar of village Daudhar, Moga, published under the spiritual lineage of Damdami Taksal. Students will examine its Ayurvedic and traditional remedies, its grounding in Gurmat principles, and its approach to preventive health, diet, exercise, and daily discipline as expressions of seva and simran.
outcomes: Identify the spiritual and institutional context from which the Health Pothi emerged
Analyze the text's dietary prescriptions in relation to Gurmat principles of moderation and purity
Evaluate traditional remedies presented in the Pothi using both historical and modern health frameworks
Explain the text's emphasis on exercise, langar preparation, and bodily discipline as spiritual practice
Distinguish between the Pothi's cultural-heritage value and evidence-based medical claims
Apply the Pothi's preventive health principles to contemporary Sikh lifestyle discussions

lessons.summary: An overview of the text's origins, its compiler Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar, and the spiritual lineage of Damdami Taksal within which it was produced.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The Text's Sources — Mahan Kosh and Ayurvedic Tradition
lessons.summary: Examining the primary sources the Pothi draws upon, with attention to Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh and the classical Ayurvedic texts referenced therein.
