lessons.summary: The Pothi's detailed guidance on food consumption, emphasizing moderation, timing, fresh preparation, and avoidance of harmful substances.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Roti, Dal, and the Art of Langar Preparation
lessons.summary: Analysis of the Pothi's detailed instructions on preparing roti and dal as spiritual practice, preventive medicine, and communal responsibility.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Water, Air, and Environmental Health
lessons.summary: The Pothi's chapters on clean water and fresh air as prerequisites for health, examined alongside traditional and contemporary environmental health principles.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Exercise, Walking, and the Active Body
lessons.summary: The Pothi's prescriptions for physical activity including walking, swimming, and vigorous exercise, understood as spiritual obligation and health maintenance.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Yoga, Massage, and Traditional Therapies
lessons.summary: Examination of the Pothi's chapters on yoga postures, massage, and various traditional therapies within Sikh and Ayurvedic contexts.

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Sarbloh, Purity, and the Khalsa Body
lessons.summary: The theological significance of Sarbloh (all-steel) in the Pothi and what it reveals about Khalsa conceptions of bodily purity and material discipline.

lessons.title: Lesson 10: Preventing Disease — The Pothi's Preventive Philosophy
lessons.summary: Analysis of the Health Pothi's preventive health orientation, which emphasizes lifestyle discipline over reactive treatment.

lessons.title: Lesson 11: Traditional Remedies — Reading with Historical and Critical Eyes
lessons.summary: A critically engaged examination of the Pothi's specific remedies, applying bibek budh to distinguish culturally grounded knowledge from claims requiring modern evidence evaluation.

lessons.title: Lesson 12: The Health Pothi as Living Sikh Heritage
lessons.summary: Situating the Health Pothi within the broader tradition of Sikh practical literature and reflecting on how communities can engage with it as living heritage.

courses.title: Medicine, Evidence, and Gurmat: Thinking Critically About Health
courses.summary: This course develops the critical reasoning skills Sikh thinkers need to evaluate competing health claims, medical systems, and traditional remedies through the lens of bibek budh (discerning intellect). Students examine the evidence bases — and their limitations — for Ayurveda, homeopathy, naturopathy, and allopathic medicine, understanding Waheguru as the ultimate healer and human medical knowledge as tools of divine grace.
outcomes: Define evidence-based medicine and explain how it differs from anecdote, tradition, and authority-based claims
Evaluate the scientific status of major medical systems including Ayurveda, homeopathy, naturopathy, and allopathic medicine
Explain the placebo effect and why it does not validate a treatment's specific mechanism
Apply the Sikh principle of bibek budh to health decisions without dismissing cultural and spiritual dimensions of healing
Distinguish between the cultural heritage value of traditional medicine texts and their clinical applicability
Articulate the Gurmat understanding of Waheguru as healer and human medicine as an instrument of grace

lessons.summary: A balanced examination of Ayurveda: its classical framework, which elements have empirical support, and where its traditional claims require modern scrutiny.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Homeopathy — Mechanism, Claims, and the Scientific Consensus
lessons.summary: An honest examination of homeopathy: its proposed mechanism, the scientific consensus on efficacy, and how Sikh critical thinking approaches extraordinary claims.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Naturopathy — What the Evidence Supports and What It Does Not
lessons.summary: An evidence-stratified examination of naturopathic medicine, distinguishing its well-evidenced components (diet, exercise, lifestyle) from practices that lack scientific support.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Allopathic Medicine — Strengths and Honest Limitations
lessons.summary: A balanced assessment of Western allopathic medicine: its evidence-based achievements, genuine limitations, and the Sikh approach to engaging it critically.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: The Placebo Effect — Real, Powerful, and Often Misunderstood
lessons.summary: A rigorous examination of the placebo effect: what it is, why it is genuinely significant, and why it does not validate the specific mechanism of an unproven treatment.

lessons.title: Lesson 8: Bibek Budh as Epistemological Framework
lessons.summary: A deeper examination of bibek budh as the Sikh epistemological foundation for evaluating health claims, situating it within the broader Gurmat understanding of discernment.

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Waheguru as the Ultimate Healer — Theological Grounding
lessons.summary: The Gurmat theological understanding of Waheguru as the true physician, and how this understanding contextualizes human medical knowledge.

lessons.title: Lesson 10: The Health Pothi and Traditional Sikh Medicine — Heritage and Critical Reading
lessons.summary: Applying the course's critical framework specifically to the Health Pothi of Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar, distinguishing its cultural-heritage value from its clinical claims.

lessons.title: Lesson 11: Making Health Decisions — A Sikh Framework
lessons.summary: A practical lesson integrating the course's intellectual content into a decision-making framework for health choices.

lessons.title: Lesson 12: Integrating Faith, Community, and Evidence in Health Practice
lessons.summary: A concluding synthesis examining how Sikh communities can build a health culture that honors tradition, embraces evidence, and centers human dignity.

courses.title: The Moving Body: Physical Exercise and the Khalsa Ethos

Drawing on the Shastar Vidya tradition, the Health Pothi, and Gurbani, students examine why the Khalsa body is understood as a site of both devotion and service, and how physical exercise functions within the broader Sikh framework of seva and simran.

lessons.summary: The theological and historical significance of Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji's integration of spiritual and temporal authority, and what it means for Sikh physical culture.

lessons.summary: The Nihang Singh order as the living embodiment of the Khalsa martial tradition, their distinctive practices, and their role in preserving shastar vidya.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Gatka — The Living Martial Art
lessons.summary: An examination of gatka as the accessible, living expression of the Sikh martial tradition, its ceremonial and competitive dimensions, and its contemporary revival.

lessons.summary: A close reading of the Health Pothi's specific prescriptions for exercise, drawing connections between its practical guidance and the Khalsa martial tradition.

lessons.summary: The Health Pothi's specific guidance on walking, swimming, and daily movement as foundational health practices.

lessons.summary: The Sikh principle of kirat karni (honest labor) as a foundation for understanding physical work and movement as intrinsically valuable.

Describe how the Health Pothi integrates Ayurvedic knowledge within a Gurmat framework
Evaluate the evidence base for selected Ayurvedic treatments referenced in Sikh traditional medicine

courses.title: Life, the Body, and Gurbani: Biology through a Sikh Lens
courses.summary: This course explores biological science through the lens of Gurbani's reverence for creation, adopting a non-concordist approach that neither claims Gurbani predicted modern biology nor reduces Gurbani to a science text. Students examine how themes of breath, interconnection, the body's complexity, and the web of life in Gurbani invite a posture of wonder (vismad) that enriches scientific inquiry without conflating two different modes of knowing.
outcomes: Explain the non-concordist approach to relating Gurbani and biological science
Identify key biological themes — breath, interdependence, the body, consciousness — that Gurbani addresses and biology illuminates from a different angle
Describe the major levels of biological organization from molecules to ecosystems
Analyze how Gurbani's concept of vismad (wonder) provides an appropriate spiritual posture toward biological complexity
Evaluate the limits of biological science in addressing questions of consciousness, meaning, and spiritual significance
Apply both scientific and Gurmat perspectives to biological topics without conflating them

courses.title: Quantum Mechanics, Consciousness, and Sikh Thought
courses.summary: This advanced course examines the genuine frontiers of quantum mechanics and consciousness science, while maintaining rigorous intellectual honesty about the speculative nature of quantum consciousness theories. Students learn what quantum mechanics actually claims, why popular 'quantum spirituality' claims often misrepresent the physics, and where genuine open questions about consciousness leave meaningful space for Sikh philosophical engagement.
outcomes: Explain the core principles of quantum mechanics including superposition, entanglement, and the measurement problem
Critically evaluate popular 'quantum consciousness' claims and distinguish them from legitimate scientific speculation
Describe the Penrose-Hameroff orchestrated objective reduction hypothesis and explain why it remains speculative
Identify genuine open questions in consciousness science where Sikh concepts of mann, atma, and jot speak to real philosophical problems
Apply the principle of bibek budh to extraordinary scientific and spiritual claims about consciousness
Articulate a mature Sikh intellectual posture toward frontier science that is neither concordist nor dismissive

courses.title: Guru Ram Das Ji: Life, Service, and the Path to Guruship

courses.title: The Lavan: Marriage, Love, and Union with Waheguru

This course provides a deep study of each of the four Lav, examining the textual meaning, spiritual symbolism, and practical significance of this composition. Students will explore how Guru Ram Das Ji uses the metaphor of marriage to describe stages of spiritual progression, and why the Lavan remain central to Sikh devotional and ceremonial life today.

courses.title: Founding Amritsar: The Sacred Tank and the City of Immortality
courses.summary: This course examines the founding of Ramdaspur — the city that became Amritsar — by Guru Ram Das Ji in the late sixteenth century. Beginning with the excavation of the Amrit Sarovar (Pool of Nectar) under Guru Amar Das Ji's direction, and culminating in the establishment of a thriving urban center during the time of Guru Arjan Dev Ji, this course traces the historical, theological, and architectural dimensions of one of the most significant sacred sites in the Sikh world. Students will engage with questions about how sacred space is created, maintained, and understood within Sikhism.
outcomes: Trace the historical sequence from initial excavation to the establishment of Ramdaspur as a city
Explain the theological significance of the Amrit Sarovar (Pool of Nectar) in Sikh tradition
Analyze how the founding of Amritsar reflects Guru Ram Das Ji's vision for a distinctly Sikh sacred center
Describe the social and economic dimensions of city-building in Mughal-era Punjab
Evaluate how the Harmandir Sahib completed Guru Ram Das Ji's foundational vision
Connect the concept of sacred space in Amritsar to broader Sikh theological principles

courses.title: Guru Ram Das Ji's Gurbani: Devotion, Longing, and Raag
courses.summary: This course undertakes a systematic study of the Gurbani composed by Guru Ram Das Ji across multiple raags in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Guru Ram Das Ji composed more than 600 hymns, making him one of the most prolific contributors to the scripture. His bani is marked by intense devotional longing (virha), radical humility, and a deep sense of the soul's dependence on the Guru's grace. Students will explore major compositions including the Lavan, the Chhant compositions, and select sabads across raags, developing an understanding of both the theological content and the musical context of Guru Ram Das Ji's spiritual poetry.
outcomes: Identify the major raags in which Guru Ram Das Ji's Gurbani appears in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji
Analyze the distinctive theological themes of virha (spiritual longing) and humility in Guru Ram Das Ji's compositions
Explain how Guru Ram Das Ji uses natural imagery to convey spiritual truths
Describe the role of the Guru in Guru Ram Das Ji's theology as expressed in his bani
Evaluate the relationship between the musical mode (raag) and the emotional/spiritual content in specific compositions
Connect Guru Ram Das Ji's Gurbani to broader themes in the devotional literature of the Punjab

courses.title: Hereditary Guruship: Succession, Controversy, and Resolution
courses.summary: The installation of Guru Ram Das Ji as the Fourth Sikh Guru marked a significant institutional shift: for the first time, the Guruship passed to a son-in-law rather than to an unrelated disciple. This course examines the circumstances, significance, and long-term consequences of this transition, including the controversies it generated within the Guru's family and the broader Sikh community. Students will engage with competing historical interpretations of hereditary succession and explore how the Sodhi lineage shaped the next six generations of Sikh Guruship.

Explain the theological basis for Sikh succession as presented in traditional sources

Evaluate competing scholarly interpretations of the significance of hereditary succession in Sikh history
Describe how the Sodhi lineage shaped the Guruship through the Tenth Guru

courses.title: Guru Ram Das Ji and the Elevation of Seva
courses.summary: Seva — selfless service — is one of the most central expressions of the three foundational pillars of Sikh spiritual practice: Naam Japo (naam simran — meditation on the divine name), Kirat Karo (honest work), and Vand Chhako (sharing one's earnings with others). Daswandh, the practice of contributing one-tenth of one's earnings, is the specific institutional form that Vand Chhako takes.

courses.title: Guru Arjan Dev Ji: Life, Ministry, and the First Sikh Martyrdom
courses.summary: Guru Arjan Dev Ji (1563–1606) was the Fifth Sikh Guru and one of the most consequential figures in the history of the Sikh faith. Born the youngest son of Guru Ram Das Ji, he served as Guru for twenty-five years, completing the Harmandir Sahib, compiling the Adi Granth, and — through his martyrdom in 1606 — transforming the entire character of the Sikh movement. This course traces his life and ministry with particular attention to the historical sources available for the period, and examines the multiple dimensions of his lasting legacy.

courses.title: Compiling the Adi Granth: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Vision, Method, and Universality
courses.summary: In 1604, Guru Arjan Dev Ji accomplished one of the most extraordinary acts in the history of world religion: the compilation of an interfaith sacred scripture that included the compositions of Sikh Gurus, Hindu bhagats, a Muslim saint, and others — all organized not by tradition or author but by musical mode (raag). This course studies the vision, methodology, and theological significance of the Adi Granth's compilation, examining its unique character as a universalist scripture, its editorial principles, the sources it drew on, and its subsequent elevation to the status of eternal Guru.

courses.title: Sukhmani Sahib: The Jewel of Peace — A Deep Study
courses.summary: Sukhmani Sahib — 'Jewel of Peace' — is one of the most beloved compositions in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Composed by Guru Arjan Dev Ji in Raag Gauri, it consists of 24 ashtapadis (eight-stanza units) each preceded by a slok, exploring the nature of Waheguru, the path to liberation, and the character of the ideal Sikh devotee (the Brahm-gyani). This course provides a structured, lesson-by-lesson exploration of the major themes and theological content of Sukhmani Sahib, drawing on Prof. Sahib Singh's Darpan commentary and examining the practical significance of this composition for daily Sikh devotional life.

courses.title: Harmandir Sahib: Architecture, Theology, and the Four Open Doors
courses.summary: The Harmandir Sahib — the 'Temple of God,' now known worldwide as the Golden Temple — stands at the center of the Amrit Sarovar in Amritsar as the holiest gurdwara in the Sikh world. Completed by Guru Arjan Dev Ji in 1604, its architecture embodies a sophisticated theological vision: the building is below ground level (symbolizing humility), connected by a causeway (the path of devotion), and has four doors open to all four directions (universal welcome). This course examines the architecture, theological symbolism, and historical context of the Harmandir Sahib, as well as its continuing significance for the global Sikh community.

Trace the historical development of the Harmandir Sahib from Guru Ram Das Ji's vision through Guru Arjan Dev Ji's completion
Explain the significance of the four open doors as a statement of Sikh universalism
Analyze the relationship between sacred architecture and theological vision in the Harmandir Sahib
Evaluate the historical significance of the installation of the Adi Granth in the Harmandir Sahib
Describe the role of the Harmandir Sahib in the life of the contemporary global Sikh community

lessons.summary: An overview of the Harmandir Sahib and its place at the center of Sikh spiritual geography.

lessons.title: From Vision to Reality: The Origins of Harmandir Sahib
lessons.summary: Tracing the origins of the Harmandir Sahib from Guru Ram Das Ji's vision through the early development of Amritsar.

lessons.title: Guru Arjan Dev Ji Takes the Project Forward
lessons.summary: How Guru Arjan Dev Ji provided the leadership and resources to bring the Harmandir Sahib to completion.

lessons.title: The Design Decision: Below Ground Level
lessons.summary: The theological significance of building the Harmandir Sahib below the level of the surrounding land.

lessons.title: The Four Open Doors
lessons.summary: The theological and social significance of the four open doors of the Harmandir Sahib.

lessons.title: The Causeway and the Parikrama
lessons.summary: The spiritual significance of the causeway connecting the Harmandir Sahib to the surrounding parikrama.

lessons.title: The Interior: Where the Guru Granth Sahib Ji Resides
lessons.summary: The interior of the Harmandir Sahib and the central role of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji within it.

lessons.title: The Foundation Stone: An Interfaith Gesture
lessons.summary: The tradition of Hazrat Mian Mir laying the foundation stone and what it expresses about Sikh universalism.

lessons.title: The Installation of the Adi Granth
lessons.summary: The ceremony of installing the Adi Granth in the Harmandir Sahib in 1604 and its significance.

lessons.title: Baba Buddha Ji: First Granthi
lessons.summary: The appointment of Baba Buddha Ji as the first Granthi of the Harmandir Sahib and its significance.

lessons.title: The Harmandir Sahib Through History
lessons.summary: Key historical events affecting the Harmandir Sahib from 1604 to the present.

lessons.title: The Living Sacred Center Today
lessons.summary: The Harmandir Sahib's role as a living sacred center for the global Sikh community today.

courses.title: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Gurbani: Themes, Rasas, and Message
courses.summary: Guru Arjan Dev Ji composed 2,218 hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji — the largest contribution of any single author. His bani spans multiple raags and poetic forms, ranging from the deep philosophical inquiry of Sukhmani Sahib to the joyful celebration of the divine presence, from intense virha (longing) to settled sehaj (equipoise). This course provides a thematic study of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Gurbani, examining its major theological ideas, its use of literary rasas (emotional registers), and its enduring message for Sikh devotional life.
outcomes: Identify the major theological themes in Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Gurbani
Explain the concept of 'rasa' in classical Indian literary theory and how it applies to Gurbani
Analyze specific compositions by Guru Arjan Dev Ji with attention to their theological content and literary form
Describe how Guru Arjan Dev Ji's bani expresses the experience of divine immanence
Evaluate the relationship between Guru Arjan Dev Ji's personal life and his theological vision as expressed in the bani
Connect the major themes of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Gurbani to the broader Sikh spiritual tradition
references: Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. 10 vols. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1962–1964.
Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind-pal Singh Mandair, eds. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperCollins, 1995.
Pashaura Singh. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Cole, W. Owen, and Piara Singh Sambhi. The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices. Brighton: Sussex Academic Press, 1978.
Singh, Teja. Sikhism: Its Ideals and Institutions. Bombay: Orient Longmans, 1951.

lessons.title: Introduction: The Most Prolific Composer of Gurbani
lessons.summary: An overview of Guru Arjan Dev Ji as the most prolific composer in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

lessons.title: Rasa Theory and Gurbani
lessons.summary: Classical Indian rasa theory and its application to understanding the emotional registers of Gurbani.

lessons.title: Shant Rasa: The Dominant Register
lessons.summary: The rasa of peace and tranquility as the characteristic emotional register of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's settled compositions.

lessons.title: The Theme of Divine Immanence
lessons.summary: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's distinctive emphasis on the divine presence as permeating all of creation.

lessons.title: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Vision of Waheguru
lessons.summary: The theological portrait of Waheguru that emerges from Guru Arjan Dev Ji's compositions.

lessons.title: The Soul's Journey in Mahala 5 Bani
lessons.summary: How Guru Arjan Dev Ji's compositions trace and guide the soul's journey from separation to union.

lessons.title: Grace (Nadar) and Liberation
lessons.summary: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's theology of divine grace as the ultimate ground of spiritual liberation.

lessons.title: Bani of Gratitude and Celebration
lessons.summary: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's compositions that express gratitude for divine grace and joy in the divine presence.

lessons.title: The Bani of Consolation and Courage
lessons.summary: Guru Arjan Dev Ji's compositions that offer consolation in times of difficulty and courage in the face of adversity.

lessons.title: Guru Arjan Dev Ji and the Bhagat Tradition
lessons.summary: How Guru Arjan Dev Ji's theology engages with and builds on the bhagat tradition he included in the Adi Granth.

lessons.title: Major Compositions Beyond Sukhmani Sahib
lessons.summary: An overview of major compositions by Guru Arjan Dev Ji beyond Sukhmani Sahib.

lessons.title: The Enduring Message
lessons.summary: The continuing relevance and spiritual significance of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's Gurbani for the global Sikh community today.

courses.title: The First Martyrdom: Mughal Politics, Historical Sources, and Legacy
courses.summary: The martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji in 1606 was a watershed event in Sikh history that transformed the trajectory of the Sikh movement. This advanced course examines the event through multiple historical lenses: the political context of the early Mughal empire under Jahangir, the primary sources (including Jahangir's own Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri), Sikh hagiographical accounts, and modern historical scholarship. Students will develop the skills to evaluate historical sources critically while understanding the theological and communal significance of the martyrdom.
outcomes: Critically evaluate the primary historical sources for Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom including the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri
Analyze the political context of the Mughal empire under Jahangir that contributed to the martyrdom
Compare the Mughal and Sikh accounts of the martyrdom and explain their different emphases
Explain the concept of shahidi (martyrdom) in Sikh theology and how Guru Arjan Dev Ji's death shaped it
Trace the immediate and long-term consequences of the martyrdom for the Sikh community
Evaluate competing scholarly interpretations of the causes and significance of the martyrdom
references: Jahangir. Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. Trans. Alexander Rogers. Ed. Henry Beveridge. London: Royal Asiatic Society, 1909.
Fenech, Louis E. Martyrdom in the Sikh Tradition: Playing the 'Game of Love.' Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Santokh Singh, Kavi. Suraj Parkash Granth (Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth). Patiala: Bhasha Vibhag Punjab, 1963.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Singh, Khushwant. A History of the Sikhs. Vol. 1. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1963.
Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

lessons.title: Introduction: A Watershed Event in Sikh History
lessons.summary: An overview of the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji as a turning point in the development of the Sikh faith.

lessons.title: The Mughal Empire Under Jahangir
lessons.summary: The political and religious character of Jahangir's rule and its implications for minority religious communities.

lessons.title: The Political Position of the Sikh Community in 1605–1606
lessons.summary: How the Sikh community's growth and organization appeared from the perspective of the Mughal state.

lessons.title: The Khusrau Rebellion: Immediate Trigger
lessons.summary: The rebellion of Prince Khusrau and its connection to the martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev Ji.

lessons.title: The Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri: What Jahangir Wrote
lessons.summary: A careful reading and analysis of Jahangir's own account of ordering Guru Arjan Dev Ji's execution.

lessons.title: Sikh Sources: The Suraj Parkash and Others
lessons.summary: The Sikh hagiographical sources for the martyrdom and how they compare to Mughal sources.

lessons.title: Chandu Shah: The Internal Factor
lessons.summary: The role of Chandu Shah in the martyrdom and what it reveals about the complex causation of the event.

lessons.title: The Events of the Martyrdom
lessons.summary: What the historical and traditional sources tell us about the actual events of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's death.

lessons.title: Tereya Kia Meetha Lagai: The Theology of the Martyrdom
lessons.summary: The compositions associated with Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom and the theology of acceptance they express.

lessons.title: Shahidi: Creating a Sikh Concept of Martyrdom
lessons.summary: How Guru Arjan Dev Ji's death created and defined the Sikh concept of shahidi (martyrdom).

lessons.title: Immediate Consequences: Guru Hargobind Ji and Piri-Miri
lessons.summary: How Guru Hargobind Ji's immediate response to the martyrdom transformed the institutional character of Sikhism.

lessons.title: Long-Term Legacy: Transformation of the Sikh Movement
lessons.summary: The long-term consequences of Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom for the development of the Sikh faith.

courses.title: The Sarbloh Granth: History, Attribution, and Manuscript Tradition
courses.summary: The Sarbloh Granth (Iron Scripture) is a voluminous text of approximately 1,344 pages attributed in Nihang Sikh tradition to Guru Gobind Singh Ji. This course examines its manuscript history, the circumstances of its publication, the nature of scholarly debates surrounding its attribution, and its place within living Khalsa praxis.
outcomes: Identify the principal manuscript traditions and published editions of the Sarbloh Granth
Summarize the arguments for and against Guru Gobind Singh Ji's authorship as presented by competing scholarly positions
Describe the role of Nihang Sikh traditions in preserving and transmitting the text
Analyze the structure and major sections of the Sarbloh Granth as a literary composition
Evaluate primary source evidence relating to the text's early history
Apply critical source analysis skills to contested scripture attribution questions
references: Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.
Singh, Kamalroop, and Gurinder Singh Mann. The Granth of the Tenth King. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 2015.
Loehlin, C. H. The Sikhs and Their Scriptures. Lucknow: Lucknow Publishing House, 1958.
Singh, Harbans. The Encyclopedia of Sikhism. 4 vols. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1992–1998.
Baba Santa Singh, ed. Sampooran Sri Sarbloh Granth Sahib Ji. Sri Anandpur Sahib: Panth Akali Buddha Dal, 1973.
Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.

lessons.title: Introduction: What Is the Sarbloh Granth?
lessons.summary: An orientation to the text, its canonical status among Nihang Sikhs, and why it remains one of the most discussed and least studied of the texts attributed to the Tenth Guru.

lessons.title: The Name Sarbloh: Iron as Theology
lessons.summary: An examination of the epithet Sarbloh — All-Iron — its theological meaning as a divine name, and its relationship to the Khalsa identity through the symbol of iron (sarbloh).

lessons.title: Structure and Major Sections
lessons.summary: A survey of the internal organization of the Sarbloh Granth, identifying its major compositional units from the Manglacharan through the mythological narratives.

lessons.title: The Nihang Tradition as Custodian
lessons.summary: An account of the Nihang Singh orders — particularly the Buddha Dal — as the primary custodians and practitioners of the Sarbloh Granth, and what their living tradition tells us about the text.

lessons.title: Publication History and Printed Editions
lessons.summary: A review of the known printed editions of the Sarbloh Granth, the circumstances of their publication, and what they reveal about the text's modern reception.

lessons.title: Manuscript Evidence and Early Sources
lessons.summary: An assessment of the manuscript evidence for the Sarbloh Granth and the significance of the absence of early independent references to the text.

lessons.title: The Attribution Debate: Arguments for Guru Gobind Singh Ji's Authorship
lessons.summary: A careful presentation of the theological, literary, and traditional arguments advanced in support of the Sarbloh Granth's attribution to Guru Gobind Singh Ji.

lessons.title: The Attribution Debate: Scholarly Concerns and Counter-Arguments
lessons.summary: A presentation of the historical and textual concerns raised by scholars who question or qualify the traditional attribution of the Sarbloh Granth.

lessons.title: Relationship to the Dasam Granth
lessons.summary: An examination of the literary and theological relationship between the Sarbloh Granth and the Dasam Granth, including shared metres, themes, and mythological frameworks.

lessons.title: Language, Metre, and Literary Style
lessons.summary: A study of the linguistic and literary features of the Sarbloh Granth, including its primary languages, poetic metres, and its place in the literary culture of the late Guru period.

lessons.title: The Sarbloh Granth in Living Sikh Practice
lessons.summary: An examination of how the Sarbloh Granth functions in the ceremonial, liturgical, and daily life of the Nihang Singh community.

lessons.title: Toward a Balanced Assessment: Faith, History, and Scholarship
lessons.summary: A concluding integration of the course's themes, modeling how a student can hold historical critical questions and devotional respect together with integrity.

courses.title: The Manglacharan and Opening Invocations of the Sarbloh Granth
courses.summary: The Manglacharan of the Sarbloh Granth is an extended opening invocation of extraordinary breadth, moving through praise of Waheguru manifested as Maja Lakshmi, Bhavani, Narayan, Kali, Sarasvati, and Ganpati before arriving at the foundational monotheistic declaration. This course provides close textual reading of the Manglacharan's structure, theology, and literary technique as preserved in the published edition of the Buddha Dal.
outcomes: Identify the major divine invocations present in the Manglacharan and their theological function
Explain how the Manglacharan frames Puranic mythology within a Gurmat monotheistic worldview
Analyze the literary technique of divine name-enumeration (namavali) as used in the opening sections
Compare the Manglacharan's theological structure to the opening invocations of the Dasam Granth
Interpret specific passages from the Manglacharan with reference to their theological meaning
Evaluate how the Manglacharan establishes the theological program of the entire Sarbloh Granth
references: Baba Santa Singh, ed. Sampooran Sri Sarbloh Granth Sahib Ji. Sri Anandpur Sahib: Panth Akali Buddha Dal, 1973.
Singh, Kamalroop, and Gurinder Singh Mann. The Granth of the Tenth King. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 2015.
Fenech, Louis E. The Darbar of the Sikh Gurus: The Court of God in the World of Men. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2008.
Hawley, John Stratton, and Mark Juergensmeyer. Songs of the Saints of India. New York: Oxford University Press, 1988.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus. San Francisco: HarperSanFrancisco, 1995.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.

lessons.title: What Is a Manglacharan?
lessons.summary: An introduction to the concept and function of the Manglacharan as the auspicious opening invocation of a sacred text, examining how this literary convention operates within Sikh scripture.

lessons.title: The Opening Verses: Ek Onkar and the Invocation of Maja Lakshmi
lessons.summary: A close reading of the very first lines of the Sarbloh Granth, from the foundational Ek Onkar declaration through the initial invocation of Maja Lakshmi.

lessons.title: Praise of Maja Lakshmi: Theological Meaning
lessons.summary: An extended examination of the theological significance of Maja Lakshmi as invoked in the Manglacharan, exploring her role as sustainer, giver of peace, and manifestation of divine grace.

lessons.title: The Dohra Form and Its Use in the Manglacharan
lessons.summary: A study of the Dohra couplet metre as it appears in the Manglacharan, examining its structural features and how it conveys theological meaning in compressed form.

lessons.title: Bhavani, Ishwari, and the Unity of Divine Names
lessons.summary: An examination of the Manglacharan's explicit declaration that Bhavani, Ishwari, and Maja are all names of the One, and what this reveals about the text's theological methodology.

lessons.title: Bisnupad Verses: The Cosmic Hymn
lessons.summary: A study of the Bisnupad metre as used in the Manglacharan, with close reading of the cosmic hymn that describes the divine as the lord of all creation.

lessons.title: The Creator as Master and the Creation as Spectacle
lessons.summary: An examination of the cosmogony presented in the Manglacharan, reading the Sarbloh Granth's account of how the divine creates and sustains the world.

lessons.title: Narayan, Kali, and the Warrior Divine
lessons.summary: An examination of the martial and warrior dimensions of the divine as invoked in the Manglacharan, including the Soratha verses praising Narayan, Kali, and the destroyer of demons.

lessons.title: Sarasvati and the Power of Sacred Speech
lessons.summary: An examination of the invocation of Sarasvati in the Manglacharan and its significance as a meditation on the divine as the power of sacred speech and wisdom.

lessons.title: The Technique of Divine Name Enumeration
lessons.summary: A study of the namavali technique — the garland of divine names — as employed throughout the Manglacharan, with attention to its spiritual and literary function.

lessons.title: The Manglacharan as Theological Program
lessons.summary: A synthetic reading of the Manglacharan as a whole, showing how its various sections together constitute a comprehensive theological program for the entire Sarbloh Granth.

lessons.title: Comparison with Other Sikh Opening Invocations
lessons.summary: A comparative examination placing the Sarbloh Granth Manglacharan alongside the Mool Mantar of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the opening of the Dasam Granth to illuminate similarities and distinctive features.

courses.title: Sarbloh Japji Sahib: A Deep Study
courses.summary: The Sarbloh Japji Sahib is a composition attributed to Guru Gobind Singh Ji that opens with an extended meditation on creation through the single Creator, drawing on cosmological frameworks similar to but distinct from the Japji Sahib of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. This course provides close textual reading of the Sarbloh Japji, examining its theology of creation, its devotional imperatives, and its place within the extended Nitnem of the Nihang Khalsa.
outcomes: Identify the structural parallels and theological differences between the Sarbloh Japji and Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib
Analyze the cosmological framework presented in the opening verses of the Sarbloh Japji
Explain the significance of the refrain 'Meditate on the One Name' as the devotional imperative of the composition
Interpret specific passages from the Sarbloh Japji with reference to Gurmat theology
Describe the role of the Sarbloh Japji within the Nihang daily liturgical practice
Evaluate how the Sarbloh Japji contributes to the broader theological vision of the Sarbloh Granth
references: Baba Santa Singh, ed. Sarbloh-Japji-Sahib-Sri-Sarbloh-Granth-Manglacharan. Sri Anandpur Sahib: Panth Akali Buddha Dal, 1973.
Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. 10 vols. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1972.
Singh, Kamalroop, and Gurinder Singh Mann. The Granth of the Tenth King. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 2015.

Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.
Cole, W. Owen, and Piara Singh Sambhi. The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices. 2nd ed. Brighton: Sussex Academic Press, 1995.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Sarbloh Japji
lessons.summary: An orientation to the Sarbloh Japji Sahib as a distinct composition, its place at the opening of the Sarbloh Granth's core text, and its relationship to the tradition of Japji recitation in Sikh practice.

lessons.title: The First Verse: Creation from the One
lessons.summary: A close reading of the first verse of the Sarbloh Japji, examining its account of creation proceeding from the single Creator and its theological implications.

lessons.title: The Devotional Imperative: Meditate on the Name
lessons.summary: An examination of the Rahao (pause) verse that forms the devotional heart of the first section: 'Meditate on the One Name, O mind, with your prayer beads.'

lessons.title: The Second Verse: Light, Earth, and the Cosmos
lessons.summary: A reading of the second verse of the Sarbloh Japji, which elaborates the cosmological vision by detailing how the Creator fashioned the physical universe.

lessons.title: Brahma and the Vedas: Cosmic Agents in the Sarbloh Japji
lessons.summary: An examination of the third verse's account of Brahma and the four Vedas, exploring how the Sarbloh Japji treats Puranic cosmic agents as instruments of the single Creator.

lessons.title: Vishnu's Incarnations and the Spectacle of Creation
lessons.summary: A deeper examination of the Sarbloh Japji's treatment of Vishnu's incarnations and the divine detachment that underlies the entire cosmic spectacle.

lessons.title: The Creation Continues: Gold, Mount Meru, and the Four Types of Life
lessons.summary: A reading of the extended cosmological inventory in the Sarbloh Japji covering the physical universe, the classification of living beings, and the cosmic timeframes.

lessons.title: The Cosmological Framework: Four Ages, Elements, and Social Order
lessons.summary: An examination of the Sarbloh Japji's account of how cosmic time, the elements, and even social hierarchy emerge from the single divine creative act.

lessons.title: Pain, Pleasure, and the Divine Decree
lessons.summary: An examination of the Sarbloh Japji's treatment of the dualities of human experience — pain and pleasure, virtue and sin — in relation to the divine will.

lessons.title: The Invisible Creator and the Pervasive Divine Presence
lessons.summary: A reading of the Sarbloh Japji passages that address the paradox of the divine as simultaneously invisible/unknowable and pervasively present in all creation.

lessons.title: The Name, the Abode, and the Light in All Things
lessons.summary: A reading of the Sarbloh Japji passage declaring that 'The Name and the Abode are present within every heart; the Light permeates all,' and its implications for Sikh spiritual practice.

lessons.title: Hari Maya, Lakshmi, and the Sustaining Grace
lessons.summary: A concluding reading of the Sarbloh Japji's return to the theme of Hari Maya as divine sustaining power, bringing together the cosmological and devotional threads of the composition.

courses.title: Mythology, Heroic Narrative, and the Warrior-Saint Ideal in the Sarbloh Granth
courses.summary: The Sarbloh Granth contains extensive mythological narratives — tales of divine combat, the slaying of demonic forces, and the triumph of righteousness — that serve a theological purpose: modeling and grounding the Khalsa warrior-saint ideal. This course examines the mythological content of the Sarbloh Granth, its sources in the Puranic tradition, and how the Gurmat lens transforms that tradition into a theology of sovereign service.
outcomes: Identify the principal mythological narratives in the Sarbloh Granth and their Puranic sources
Explain how the Sarbloh Granth transforms Puranic mythology through the Gurmat theological lens
Analyze the warrior-saint ideal as developed through the mythological content of the text
Compare the Sarbloh Granth's use of mythology with that of the Dasam Granth
Evaluate the theological claim that fighting oppression is a form of divine service
Interpret specific mythological passages as theological teachings relevant to Khalsa identity
references: Baba Santa Singh, ed. Sampooran Sri Sarbloh Granth Sahib Ji. Sri Anandpur Sahib: Panth Akali Buddha Dal, 1973.
Singh, Kamalroop, and Gurinder Singh Mann. The Granth of the Tenth King. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 2015.
Fenech, Louis E. The Darbar of the Sikh Gurus: The Court of God in the World of Men. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2008.

Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision of the Transcendent. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993.
Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.

lessons.title: Mythology as Theology: An Introduction
lessons.summary: An orientation to how the Sarbloh Granth uses mythological narrative as a vehicle for theological instruction, and why this approach is consistent with the broader Guru tradition.

lessons.title: The Devi Mahatmya and Its Influence
lessons.summary: An examination of the Sanskrit Devi Mahatmya — the primary Puranic source for the warrior goddess narratives — and how the Sarbloh Granth draws on and transforms this tradition.

lessons.title: Sumbhasura and Nisumbhasura: Tyranny as Theological Category
lessons.summary: A reading of the Sarbloh Granth's references to Sumbha and Nisumbha, interpreting these figures as theological symbols of tyranny and examining how their defeat illustrates divine sovereignty.

lessons.title: Chanda, Munda, and the Destruction of Ego
lessons.summary: An examination of the Sarbloh Granth's treatment of Chanda and Munda as symbolic figures, interpreting their defeat by the divine warrior as a teaching about the destruction of ego.

lessons.title: Raktabeej: The Self-Multiplying Demon and the Nature of Vice
lessons.summary: An analysis of the Raktabeej episode as used in the Sarbloh Granth tradition, exploring what this figure's ability to multiply from his own blood reveals about the nature of vice and ego.

lessons.title: Mahishasura: The Buffalo Demon and the Metaphysics of Arrogance
lessons.summary: An examination of Mahishasura's defeat as narrated in the Sarbloh Granth tradition, exploring the theological meaning of the buffalo demon as a symbol of brute, shape-shifting arrogance.

lessons.title: The Divine Warrior as Theological Model
lessons.summary: A synthetic examination of the divine warrior archetype as developed across the mythological sections of the Sarbloh Granth, articulating the theological attributes of this figure.

lessons.title: Heroic Narrative and the Khalsa Historical Imagination
lessons.summary: An examination of how the heroic mythological narrative of the Sarbloh Granth shaped the historical imagination and self-understanding of the Khalsa community.

lessons.title: The Saint-Soldier Ideal: Spiritual Foundation
lessons.summary: An examination of the spiritual dimension of the saint-soldier ideal as grounded in the theology of the Sarbloh Granth, focusing on the interior qualities of the Khalsa warrior.

lessons.title: The Saint-Soldier Ideal: Martial Expression
lessons.summary: An examination of the martial dimension of the saint-soldier ideal, exploring how the Sarbloh Granth grounds the Khalsa's readiness for physical defense in theological conviction.

lessons.title: Dharm Yudh: The Theology of Righteous War
lessons.summary: A focused examination of the concept of Dharm Yudh — righteous war — as developed through the Sarbloh Granth's theology, including its conditions, its limitations, and its spiritual dimensions.

lessons.title: Mythology, Memory, and the Living Khalsa
lessons.summary: A concluding reflection on how the mythological content of the Sarbloh Granth functions as living memory — shaping Khalsa identity, sustaining practice, and connecting the present community to its theological roots.

courses.title: The Philosophy of Sarbloh: Iron, Sovereignty, and the Eternal Form
courses.summary: This advanced course examines the philosophical core of the Sarbloh Granth: the identification of Waheguru with iron (sarbloh) as a theological and metaphysical statement about the nature of divine sovereignty, the incorruptibility of the divine form, and the Khalsa community as a living embodiment of that sovereignty. The course draws on the text's own language and the philosophical traditions it engages to develop a coherent account of Sarbloh philosophy.
outcomes: Articulate the philosophical claims embedded in the concept of Sarbloh as a divine attribute
Analyze the relationship between iron as material substance and iron as theological metaphor in the Sarbloh Granth
Compare the Sarbloh concept of divine form with the Gurmat concept of Nirankaar (formless divine)
Evaluate how the philosophy of Sarbloh grounds the Khalsa community's distinctive material practices
Examine the concept of divine sovereignty (Raj Karega Khalsa) in relation to the Sarbloh Granth's theology
Synthesize the Sarbloh Granth's philosophical contributions within the broader history of Sikh philosophical thought
references: Baba Santa Singh, ed. Sampooran Sri Sarbloh Granth Sahib Ji. Sri Anandpur Sahib: Panth Akali Buddha Dal, 1973.

lessons.title: Iron as Philosophy: Why Metal Matters
lessons.summary: An introduction to the philosophical question of why iron — a material substance — becomes a vehicle for theological meaning in the Sarbloh Granth, and why this is philosophically significant.

lessons.title: The Properties of Iron as Theological Symbols
lessons.summary: A systematic examination of iron's physical properties — strength, incorruptibility, magnetism, and capacity to be forged — and how each becomes a vehicle for theological meaning in the Sarbloh Granth.

lessons.title: Sarbloh and Nirankaar: Holding Form and Formlessness Together
lessons.summary: A philosophical examination of the apparent tension between the Sarbloh concept (divine with an iron form) and the Gurmat concept of Nirankaar (the formless divine), and how the Sarbloh Granth holds these in creative tension.

lessons.title: Iron in the Khalsa Kakars: The Philosophy of Embodied Theology
lessons.summary: An examination of how the philosophy of iron is embodied in the Khalsa identity markers (kakars), particularly the kara (iron bracelet) and kirpan (steel blade).

lessons.title: Amrit Sanchar and the Sarbloh Bowl
lessons.summary: An examination of the theological significance of preparing the Khalsa initiation water (amrit) in a sarbloh (iron) bowl, and how this connects iron philosophy to the central act of Khalsa identity.

lessons.title: Sarbloh Degh: The Iron Kitchen as Sacred Space
lessons.summary: An examination of the Nihang practice of Sarbloh Degh — cooking and eating only from iron vessels — and its philosophical foundations in the Sarbloh Granth's theology.

lessons.title: Divine Sovereignty: Raj Karega Khalsa
lessons.summary: An examination of the declaration 'Raj Karega Khalsa' (The Khalsa shall rule) in relation to the Sarbloh Granth's philosophy of divine sovereignty, exploring both the theological and political dimensions of this claim.

lessons.title: Weapons as Theology: Shastar Vidiya and the Philosophy of Iron
lessons.summary: An examination of the Nihang tradition of Shastar Vidiya (the science of weapons) and how the philosophy of iron elevates the use of weapons from martial technique to theological practice.

lessons.title: The Timeless Form: Sarbloh and Akal
lessons.summary: A philosophical examination of the relationship between the Sarbloh concept and Akal (the Timeless), exploring how iron's apparent temporal vulnerability is transcended in the theology of the eternal divine form.

lessons.title: Sarbloh and the Critique of Ego
lessons.summary: An examination of how the Sarbloh philosophy functions as a critique of the ego (haumai), with iron sovereignty as the philosophical contrast to the ego's corruptible, brittle pretensions to power.

lessons.title: Comparative Philosophy: Sarbloh and Other Traditions' Use of Metal
lessons.summary: A brief comparative examination of how other religious traditions have used metal — particularly iron and gold — as vehicles for theological meaning, placing the Sarbloh philosophy in broader context.

lessons.title: Synthesis: A Sarbloh Philosophy of Being and Action
lessons.summary: A concluding synthesis of the Sarbloh philosophy as a coherent account of being (what is real) and action (how to live in relation to that reality), articulating the philosophical vision as a whole.

courses.title: Authenticity, Scholarly Debates, and Khalsa Practice Today
courses.summary: This course examines the contemporary state of scholarly and community debates about the Sarbloh Granth's authenticity, considers what is at stake in these debates for the living Khalsa community, and offers students tools for engaging responsibly with contested sacred texts. It bridges historical-critical methodology with honest theological engagement, modeling the kind of integrative scholarship that Sikh studies needs.
outcomes: Summarize the current state of scholarly debate about the Sarbloh Granth's historical authenticity
Evaluate the different methodological approaches scholars bring to the question of Sikh scriptural attribution
Analyze the implications of the authenticity debate for Nihang Sikh identity and practice
Articulate the difference between historical authenticity questions and the question of a text's spiritual value
Apply lessons from the Sarbloh Granth debate to broader questions about contested sacred texts
Develop a personal scholarly and devotional posture toward the Sarbloh Granth grounded in intellectual honesty and spiritual respect
references: Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.
Singh, Kamalroop, and Gurinder Singh Mann. The Granth of the Tenth King. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 2015.

Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. New Delhi: Oxford University Press, 2000.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind Mandair, eds. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.

lessons.title: The Stakes of the Debate
lessons.summary: An orientation to why the authenticity debate about the Sarbloh Granth matters — for the Nihang community, for the broader Panth, and for the academic study of Sikhism.

lessons.title: Methodological Approaches to Sikh Scriptural Attribution
lessons.summary: A survey of the different methodological approaches scholars use when examining questions of scriptural attribution in Sikh studies, including their assumptions and their limitations.

lessons.title: The Historical-Critical School: McLeod and His Legacy
lessons.summary: An examination of the historical-critical approach to Sikh studies associated with W. H. McLeod, its contributions, its critics, and its relevance to the Sarbloh Granth debate.

lessons.title: Traditional and Devotional Responses to Historical Criticism
lessons.summary: An examination of how traditional Sikh scholars and the devotional community have responded to historical-critical approaches to the Sarbloh Granth.

lessons.title: The Nihang Community's Position
lessons.summary: A detailed examination of the Nihang community's position on the Sarbloh Granth's authenticity, their theological reasoning, and the evidence they present.

lessons.title: The SGPC and Mainstream Institutional Positions
lessons.summary: An examination of the position of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) and mainstream Sikh institutional bodies on the Sarbloh Granth, and the tensions this creates.

lessons.title: Kamalroop Singh and Recent Scholarship
lessons.summary: An examination of recent scholarship defending the Sarbloh Granth's traditional attribution, particularly the work of Dr. Kamalroop Singh, and its contribution to the debate.

lessons.title: What the Absence of 18th-Century Evidence Actually Proves (and Does Not Prove)
lessons.summary: A careful methodological examination of what the apparent absence of early independent references to the Sarbloh Granth can and cannot establish about its composition history.

lessons.title: The Question of Canonical Status
lessons.summary: An examination of what it means for a text to be canonical in the Sikh tradition, and how the Sarbloh Granth's uncertain canonical status is itself a theologically significant fact.

lessons.title: Authentic Praxis as Evidence
lessons.summary: An argument for treating the Nihang community's living praxis — their daily practice grounded in the Sarbloh Granth — as a form of evidence to be taken seriously alongside documentary historical evidence.

lessons.title: How to Hold Both Positions with Integrity
lessons.summary: A constructive discussion of how a student can hold historical critical questions and devotional respect together with genuine integrity, without collapsing into either uncritical acceptance or dismissive skepticism.

lessons.title: Looking Forward: What Future Scholarship Needs
lessons.summary: A concluding look at what the Sarbloh Granth debate needs in terms of future scholarship, primary source investigation, and community-academic dialogue to advance understanding.

courses.title: The Pran Sangli: Text, Breath, Attribution, and Sikh Thought
courses.summary: The Pran Sangli (Chain of Life) is a text attributed to Guru Gobind Singh Ji dealing with breath, creation, and spiritual liberation. This course examines the text carefully, explores its unique account of creation through divine breath, addresses the crucial Gurmat distinction between breath as a natural companion to Naam Simran and yogic pranayama as ego-driven breath control, and considers the scholarly questions surrounding its attribution and place in Sikh thought.
outcomes: Identify the major themes and compositional structure of the Pran Sangli text
Explain the Gurmat understanding of breath as a natural companion to Naam Simran, distinct from yogic pranayama
Analyze the Pran Sangli's cosmological account of creation through the divine Word and breath
Evaluate the attribution question for the Pran Sangli using evidence from the text itself and historical context
Compare the Pran Sangli's approach to breath with the approach of the Guru Granth Sahib Ji to the breath as divine gift
Articulate why the Gurmat approach to breath cannot be reduced to or conflated with yogic pranayama techniques
references: Sri-Pran-Sangli (attributed to Guru Gobind Singh Ji). Preserved in the SikhLibrary Digital Collection. Accessed via HuggingFace, jsdosanj/SikhLibrary, 2026.
Singh, Sahib. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Darpan. 10 vols. Jalandhar: Raj Publishers, 1972.
Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.
Singh, Harbans. The Encyclopedia of Sikhism. 4 vols. Patiala: Punjabi University, 1992–1998.
Whicher, Ian. The Integrity of the Yoga Darsana: A Reconsideration of Classical Yoga. Albany: SUNY Press, 1998.
Cole, W. Owen, and Piara Singh Sambhi. The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices. 2nd ed. Brighton: Sussex Academic Press, 1995.
Shackle, Christopher, and Arvind Mandair, eds. Teachings of the Sikh Gurus: Selections from the Sikh Scriptures. London: Routledge, 2005.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Pran Sangli
lessons.summary: An orientation to the Pran Sangli text — its name, its structure, its attributed authorship, and the distinctive questions it raises about breath, creation, and Sikh spirituality.

lessons.title: The Opening Verses: Creation from the One Creator
lessons.summary: A close reading of the Pran Sangli's opening verses, noting their similarities to the Sarbloh Japji and examining what the text's creation account contributes to the broader corpus.

lessons.title: The Title: What Does Pran Sangli Mean?
lessons.summary: An examination of the compound word Pran Sangli — Chain/Necklace of Life/Breath — and what the title reveals about the text's theological program.

lessons.title: The Four Types of Life and the Creator's Breath
lessons.summary: An examination of the Pran Sangli's account of the four types of living beings and how the creator's breath animates them all, developing the theological implications for understanding life.

lessons.title: Brahma, Vishnu, and the Spectacle of Creation
lessons.summary: An examination of how the Pran Sangli treats Brahma and Vishnu as instruments of the single Creator, paralleling the Sarbloh Japji's treatment of these figures.

lessons.title: The Gurmat Understanding of Breath as Divine Gift
lessons.summary: A focused examination of how the Guru Granth Sahib Ji understands breath as a divine gift, providing the theological framework within which the Pran Sangli is to be read.

lessons.title: Breath, Name, and Simran: The Gurmat Relationship
lessons.summary: A careful examination of the relationship between breath and the divine Name in Gurmat spiritual practice, drawing on both the Guru Granth Sahib Ji and the Pran Sangli.

lessons.title: Why Pranayama Is Not Gurmat Spirituality
lessons.summary: A direct and careful examination of why the Gurmat understanding of breath cannot be reduced to or conflated with yogic pranayama, and what distinguishes the two approaches at their root.

lessons.title: The Pran Sangli and Yogic Tradition: Similarities and Distinctions
lessons.summary: A nuanced examination of the Pran Sangli's relationship to the yogic tradition — acknowledging genuine similarities in vocabulary while identifying the crucial theological distinctions.

lessons.title: The Attribution Question: Evidence and Uncertainty
lessons.summary: A specific examination of the evidence for and against the Pran Sangli's attribution to Guru Gobind Singh Ji, drawing lessons from the course's broader discussion of Sikh scriptural attribution.

lessons.title: The Pran Sangli in Contemporary Sikh Practice
lessons.summary: An examination of how the Pran Sangli is (and is not) used in contemporary Sikh practice, and what its place in practice reveals about the diversity of the Sikh tradition.

lessons.title: Conclusion: Breath, Liberation, and the Natural Way
lessons.summary: A concluding synthesis of the Pran Sangli's theological contribution, bringing together its cosmological account of creation, its theology of breath, and the Gurmat understanding of the natural way of liberation.

courses.title: Sikh Apologetics: Advanced Methodology and Graduate Seminar
courses.source: Giani Ditt Singh, Ham Hindu Nahin (1897); Sikh Rahit Maryada
courses.summary: This graduate seminar surveys the methodological foundations of Sikh apologetics from the nineteenth-century Singh Sabha reform movement to contemporary interfaith discourse. Students engage primary sources — including Giani Ditt Singh's polemical writings and the Sikh Rahit Maryada — alongside secondary scholarship on religious identity and contested truth claims. The course trains scholars to deploy rigorous historical, philosophical, and textual methods when defending and clarifying Sikh theological distinctives.
outcomes: Critically analyze the historical development of Sikh apologetic methodology from the Singh Sabha period to the present.
Apply historical-critical, philosophical, and comparative-religious methods to primary Sikh apologetic texts.
Evaluate the theological and socio-political dimensions of major identity-formation disputes within Sikhism.
Construct graduate-level argumentative essays that engage both Sikh primary sources and contemporary academic scholarship.
Situate Sikh apologetics within broader global debates in philosophy of religion and postcolonial religious studies.
references: Ditt Singh, Giani. Ham Hindu Nahin. Lahore: Singh Sabha, 1897.
Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1994.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.
Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
Barrier, N. Gerald. The Sikhs and Their Literature. Delhi: Manohar, 1970.
Fox, Richard G. Lions of the Punjab: Culture in the Making. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1985.
McLeod, W. H. Who Is a Sikh? The Problem of Sikh Identity. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1989.

lessons.title: Foundations of Sikh Apologetics: History, Method, and Purpose
lessons.summary: Introduces the four primary methodological registers — historical-critical, philosophical, comparative-theological, and postcolonial — that structure the seminar's inquiry into Sikh apologetics.

lessons.title: The Singh Sabha Movement and the Construction of Sikh Orthodoxy
lessons.summary: Examines how the Singh Sabha movement (1873–c.1920) established the institutional and rhetorical parameters of modern Sikh apologetics in response to colonial pressures.

lessons.title: Giani Ditt Singh and the Polemical Tradition
lessons.summary: Analyzes Giani Ditt Singh's apologetic methodology through close reading of Ham Hindu Nahin and his journalism in the Khalsa Akhbar.

lessons.title: The Sikh Rahit Maryada as Apologetic Document
lessons.summary: Reads the Sikh Rahit Maryada as the culminating codification of Singh Sabha apologetics, analyzing both its theological content and its political dimensions.

lessons.title: Epistemology and the ਸ਼ਬਦ: Knowing and Defending Truth
lessons.summary: Develops the epistemological foundations of Sikh apologetics, centered on the concept of Shabad as both living Guru and epistemological criterion.

lessons.title: Colonial Encounters and the Discourse of Religious Distinctiveness
lessons.summary: Situates Sikh apologetics within the colonial context, analyzing how British administrative categories and missionary discourse shaped Sikh self-representation.

lessons.title: Philosophical Methods in Contemporary Sikh Apologetics
lessons.summary: Surveys analytical philosophy of religion, phenomenology, and comparative philosophy as resources for contemporary Sikh apologetic engagement.

lessons.title: Comparative Religion as Apologetic Strategy
lessons.summary: Evaluates the uses and limits of comparative religious analysis as an apologetic tool, advocating for honest comparativism over selective polemical use.

lessons.title: The Problem of ਹਉਮੈ in Apologetic Discourse
lessons.summary: Applies Gurmat's analysis of ego-centeredness as an internal critique of apologetic excess, developing standards of intellectual humility for the graduate scholar.

lessons.title: Identity, Boundary-Making, and the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ
lessons.summary: Analyzes the Khalsa as the paradigmatic Sikh boundary-making institution, engaging social-scientific and theological perspectives on identity construction.

lessons.title: Postcolonial Critiques and Sikh Self-Representation
lessons.summary: Engages Mandair's postcolonial critique of modern Sikh apologetics and evaluates proposals for authentic Sikh self-representation in diaspora contexts.

lessons.title: Graduate Seminar: Constructing a Sikh Apologetic Argument
lessons.summary: Capstone lesson guiding students through the construction of a complete, methodologically sophisticated Sikh apologetic argument with full scholarly apparatus.

courses.title: Advanced Sikh-Christian Theological Dialogue
courses.source: Giani Ditt Singh apologetics works; comparative theology
courses.summary: This graduate seminar conducts sustained, rigorous dialogue between Sikh and Christian theological traditions at the level of their foundational commitments: doctrines of God, revelation, soteriology, Christology, and eschatology. Students engage primary sources from both traditions alongside leading comparative theologians, developing the skills to conduct genuine interreligious dialogue that maintains Sikh distinctives without caricature of Christian thought. The course draws on Giani Ditt Singh's colonial-era Christian engagement as a historical baseline and advances beyond it.
outcomes: Articulate the foundational theological distinctives of Gurmat in relation to Christian doctrines of God, revelation, and salvation.
Critically read and evaluate colonial-era Sikh apologetic engagements with Christian missionary theology.
Conduct rigorous comparative theological analysis drawing on primary sources from both traditions.
Identify points of genuine theological convergence and irreducible difference between Sikh and Christian thought.
Construct a graduate-level Sikh-Christian comparative theological essay conforming to CMOS standards.
references: Ditt Singh, Giani. Ham Hindu Nahin. Lahore: Singh Sabha, 1897.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation. New York: Columbia University Press, 2009.
Singh, Pashaura, and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.
Clooney, Francis X. Comparative Theology: Deep Learning Across Religious Borders. Oxford: Wiley-Blackwell, 2010.
Knitter, Paul F. No Other Name? A Critical Survey of Christian Attitudes Toward the World Religions. Maryknoll, NY: Orbis, 1985.
Fenech, Louis E., and W. H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. 3rd ed. Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield, 2014.
Barrier, N. Gerald. The Sikhs and Their Literature. Delhi: Manohar, 1970.
Race, Alan. Christians and Religious Pluralism: Patterns in the Christian Theology of Religions. London: SCM Press, 1983.

lessons.title: Introduction: The History and Stakes of Sikh-Christian Dialogue
lessons.summary: Situates the Sikh-Christian dialogue in its colonial and contemporary contexts and establishes the comparative theological methodology for the seminar.

lessons.title: Doctrines of God: Monotheism, Trinity, and ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ
lessons.summary: Compares Sikh and Christian conceptions of divine unity, the Trinity, and the attributes of God.

lessons.title: Revelation and Scripture: Guru Granth Sahib and the Bible
lessons.summary: Analyzes the structure and authority of canonical scripture in each tradition and the hermeneutical principles governing its interpretation.

lessons.title: The Human Condition: ਹਉਮੈ and the Christian Doctrine of Sin
lessons.summary: Compares Gurmat's analysis of ego-centeredness with the Augustinian doctrine of original sin and concupiscence.

lessons.title: Soteriology I: ਨਾਮ, Grace, and Salvation
lessons.summary: Examines the role of the divine Name in Gurmat soteriology and compares it with Christian doctrines of grace and salvation.

lessons.title: Soteriology II: Atonement, Incarnation, and ਗੁਰਮਤਿ
lessons.summary: Engages the specifically Christian soteriological doctrines of atonement and incarnation from a Gurmat perspective.

lessons.title: Christology and Guruship: Divine Mediation in Two Traditions
lessons.summary: Compares the nature and function of Jesus Christ in Christian theology with the Sikh doctrine of Guruship.

lessons.title: Community and Ecclesiology: ਸੰਗਤ and the Church
lessons.summary: Compares Sikh and Christian theologies of communal religious life, leadership, and authority.

lessons.title: Ethics and Social Justice: ਸੇਵਾ and Christian Agape
lessons.summary: Compares the Sikh ethic of selfless service with Christian traditions of agape love and social gospel activism.

lessons.title: Political Theology: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ and Church-State Relations
lessons.summary: Compares the Sikh doctrine of dual sovereignty with Christian church-state theologies from Augustine to liberation theology.

lessons.title: Eschatology: Death, Judgment, and ਮੁਕਤੀ
lessons.summary: Compares Sikh and Christian accounts of individual and cosmic eschatology, liberation, and divine justice.

lessons.title: Capstone: Constructing a Sikh-Christian Comparative Theological Essay
lessons.summary: Guides students through the construction of a graduate-level Sikh-Christian comparative theological essay with full scholarly apparatus.

courses.title: Philosophy of Religion and Sikh Thought
courses.source: Academic philosophy of religion; Arvind-Pal Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (2009)
courses.summary: This seminar engages the classical and contemporary problems of philosophy of religion — the existence of God, the problem of evil, religious language, religious experience, and the rationality of faith — through the lens of Sikh thought. Students situate Gurmat within global debates in analytic and continental philosophy of religion, evaluating both the resources Gurmat brings to these debates and the ways engagement with philosophical analysis illuminates dimensions of Sikh theology. Mandair's postcolonial analysis of the category 'religion' provides a critical frame throughout.
outcomes: Articulate the major problems of philosophy of religion and evaluate Gurmat responses to each.
Situate Gurmat epistemology and theology within debates between analytic and continental philosophy of religion.
Apply Mandair's postcolonial critique of the category 'religion' to Sikh theological self-understanding.
Construct rigorous philosophical arguments engaging both Western philosophy and Gurmat primary sources.
Evaluate the adequacy of standard philosophy-of-religion categories (theism, mysticism, revelation) for Sikh thought.

Hick, John. An Interpretation of Religion: Human Responses to the Transcendent. 2nd ed. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2004.

lessons.title: Introduction: Philosophy of Religion and Sikh Thought
lessons.summary: Establishes the methodology of the seminar and the stakes of engaging Western philosophy of religion from a Gurmat perspective.

lessons.title: Arguments for the Existence of God and ਗੁਰਮਤਿ
lessons.summary: Evaluates the ontological, cosmological, and teleological arguments for divine existence and their relevance to Gurmat theology.

lessons.title: The Problem of Evil and ਧਰਮ
lessons.summary: Engages the logical and evidential problems of evil from a Gurmat perspective centered on haumai and karma.

lessons.title: Religious Language: Speaking of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ
lessons.summary: Analyzes the philosophical problem of religious language and evaluates Gurmat's distinctive use of apophatic and cataphatic discourse.

lessons.title: Religious Experience and ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ
lessons.summary: Develops philosophical arguments for the evidential value of Gurmat spiritual experience generated through Nam Simran.

lessons.title: Faith, Reason, and ਵਿਚਾਰ
lessons.summary: Articulates Gurmat's distinctive integration of faith and reason through the concept of vichar as disciplined inquiry.

lessons.title: Mysticism, Union, and ਮੁਕਤੀ
lessons.summary: Engages philosophical debates about mysticism and evaluates Gurmat descriptions of liberation against perennialist and constructivist accounts.

lessons.title: Religious Diversity and the Universalism of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ
lessons.summary: Articulates Gurmat's distinctive universalism as a philosophically superior alternative to both religious exclusivism and Hickean pluralism.

lessons.title: The Self, Personal Identity, and ਹਉਮੈ
lessons.summary: Develops a Gurmat philosophy of mind centered on the analysis of haumai and its overcoming in liberation.

lessons.title: Miracles, Divine Action, and ਸ਼ਬਦ
lessons.summary: Articulates a Gurmat account of divine action centered on Shabad as the primary vehicle of divine presence in the world.

lessons.title: Mandair's Postcolonial Critique: 'Religion' and ਗੁਰਮਤਿ
lessons.summary: Applies Mandair's critique of the category 'religion' to the seminar's use of philosophy of religion as an analytical framework.

lessons.title: Graduate Seminar: Philosophical Theology in a Sikh Key
lessons.summary: Capstone lesson constructing original philosophical-theological arguments developed from within Gurmat rather than in response to external frameworks.

courses.title: Dialectical Theology: Sikhi and Post-Modern Critique
courses.source: Postmodern theology; W.H. McLeod scholarly works
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the encounter between Sikh theology and postmodern philosophical critique, engaging thinkers from Derrida and Foucault to contemporary postcolonial and deconstructive theologians. Students develop resources for a dialectical response to postmodern challenges — neither capitulating to relativism nor retreating to pre-critical fundamentalism — grounded in the epistemological and theological resources of Gurmat. The work of W.H. McLeod provides a case study in the challenges and opportunities of critical historical scholarship applied to Sikh tradition.
outcomes: Articulate the major postmodern philosophical challenges to religious truth claims and evaluate their force.
Develop dialectical theological responses to deconstruction, genealogy, and postcolonial critique from within Gurmat.
Critically evaluate W.H. McLeod's historical-critical scholarship on Sikhism and the Sikh scholarly response to it.
Construct arguments for the coherence and integrity of Gurmat in the face of postmodern challenges to foundations.
Situate Gurmat within the global 'postmodern theology' conversation, identifying both resonances and irreducible differences.

lessons.title: Introduction: Postmodern Critique and the Challenge to Sikh Theology
lessons.summary: Establishes the dialectical methodology for engaging postmodern philosophical critique from a Gurmat perspective.

lessons.title: Deconstruction and the ਸ਼ਬਦ: Derrida and Gurmat Hermeneutics
lessons.summary: Engages Derrida's deconstructive reading strategy and develops a Gurmat hermeneutical response grounded in the ontological primacy of Shabad.

lessons.title: Genealogy, Power, and Sikh Institutional History
lessons.summary: Applies Foucauldian genealogical analysis to Sikh institutional history and evaluates its implications for Gurmat theological claims.

lessons.title: W.H. McLeod's Historical-Critical Method and Sikh Responses
lessons.summary: Analyzes McLeod's historical-critical scholarship on Sikhism and the range of Sikh scholarly responses it has generated.

lessons.title: The Postmodern Self and ਹਉਮੈ
lessons.summary: Compares postmodern critiques of the unified subject with Gurmat's analysis of haumai and its positive account of liberated selfhood.

lessons.title: Postmodern Ethics and ਧਰਮ
lessons.summary: Engages postmodern ethics of the Other and develops Gurmat's more robustly grounded ethics of dharma and seva.

lessons.title: Truth Claims After the Postmodern Turn: ਸੱਚ and Relativism
lessons.summary: Defends Gurmat's affirmation of Sach as ontological foundation against postmodern truth-relativism.

lessons.title: Postcolonial Theology and Gurmat Self-Understanding
lessons.summary: Develops resources from postcolonial theology for constructing a Gurmat theology that proceeds from indigenous categories.

lessons.title: Community, Narrative, and ਸੰਗਤ
lessons.summary: Evaluates communitarian and narrative theology as partial but inadequate models for Gurmat's theology of Sangat.

lessons.title: Political Theology After Postmodernism: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ and Power
lessons.summary: Applies Foucauldian power analysis to Sikh political theology and develops a self-critical account of Miri-Piri.

lessons.title: Postmodern Theology's Resources and Limits for Gurmat
lessons.summary: Provides a comprehensive dialectical assessment of what postmodern theology offers and what it cannot provide for Gurmat theological construction.

lessons.title: Capstone: Dialectical Response to a Postmodern Challenge
lessons.summary: Guides students through the construction of a complete dialectical Gurmat response to McLeod's historical-critical challenge to Sikh identity.

courses.title: Historical-Critical Methods in Sikh Scholarship
courses.summary: This graduate seminar provides rigorous training in the historical-critical methods applied to Sikh textual and historical scholarship, equipping students to read primary sources with methodological sophistication. The course examines source criticism, form criticism, redaction criticism, and social-historical analysis as they apply to the Guru Granth Sahib, the janam-sakhis, the Sikh Rahit Maryada, and major Sikh historical texts. Students develop the capacity to engage critically with both traditional and revisionist scholarship while maintaining rigorous scholarly standards.
outcomes: Apply source criticism, form criticism, and redaction criticism to major Sikh textual traditions.
Evaluate the historical evidence for key events and developments in Sikh history with methodological rigor.
Critically assess both traditional Sikh historiography and modern revisionist scholarship.
Situate Sikh textual traditions within their literary, social, and political contexts.
Construct graduate-level historical-critical analyses of Sikh primary sources conforming to CMOS standards.
