lessons.title: Introduction: Historical-Critical Method and Its Application to Sikh Studies
lessons.summary: Introduces the major tools of historical-critical analysis and establishes the critical-correlative relationship between historical scholarship and theological commitment.

lessons.title: Source Criticism and the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ Literature
lessons.summary: Applies source-critical analysis to the major janam-sakhi traditions, evaluating McLeod's pioneering conclusions and subsequent scholarly refinements.

lessons.title: Textual Transmission and the Guru Granth Sahib: ਬੀੜ Traditions
lessons.summary: Examines the manuscript traditions of the Guru Granth Sahib and the textual-critical methods for analyzing them.

lessons.title: Redaction Criticism: The Compilation of the Adi Granth

lessons.title: Form Criticism and Genres of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ
lessons.summary: Identifies and analyzes the major literary genres in the Guru Granth Sahib and their relationship to the social settings of Sikh worship.

lessons.title: Social-Historical Analysis of the Early Sikh Community
lessons.summary: Reconstructs the social composition and economic context of the early Sikh community and its implications for theological development.

lessons.title: The ਰਹਿਤ Literature: Tradition, Text, and Authority

lessons.title: Historical-Critical Analysis of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ Formation
lessons.summary: Reconstructs the historical evidence for the Khalsa's founding and early development using multi-method historical-critical analysis.

lessons.title: Colonial-Era Sikh Historiography and Its Assumptions

lessons.title: Postcolonial Revisions in Sikh Historical Scholarship
lessons.summary: Assesses the contributions and limitations of postcolonial approaches to Sikh historical scholarship, including Oberoi and Mandair.

lessons.title: The Relationship Between Historical Scholarship and Theological Commitment
lessons.summary: Defends critical correlation as the methodologically most adequate relationship between historical-critical scholarship and Sikh theological commitment.

lessons.title: Capstone: Historical-Critical Analysis of a Sikh Primary Source
lessons.summary: Guides students through an integrated multi-method historical-critical analysis of a Sikh Rahitnama text.

courses.title: Advanced Sikh Manuscript Illumination and Paleography
courses.source: Dr. Kamalroop Singh, The Guru's Word & Institutional Sikh Scripture (2017)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar provides advanced training in the paleographic analysis and art-historical interpretation of Sikh illuminated manuscripts, with particular attention to the decorated Guru Granth Sahib manuscripts of the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries. Students develop skills in Gurmukhi paleography, the identification of decorative programmes and their iconographic sources, and the art-historical contextualization of Sikh manuscript production within the broader traditions of South Asian illuminated manuscript culture. The seminar draws extensively on Kamalroop Singh's archival scholarship.
outcomes: Read and analyze Gurmukhi script in manuscripts from the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries using paleographic methods.
Identify and interpret the decorative programmes of illuminated Guru Granth Sahib manuscripts within their art-historical context.
Situate Sikh manuscript illumination within the broader traditions of Mughal, Rajput, and Persian manuscript culture.
Analyze the relationship between manuscript material culture and the theological status of scripture in Sikh tradition.
Construct graduate-level art-historical analyses of specific Sikh manuscripts conforming to CMOS standards.

lessons.title: Gurmukhi Paleography: Script Development from the Sixteenth to Nineteenth Century

lessons.title: Iconographic Sources: Mughal, Rajput, and Persian Influences
lessons.summary: Traces the iconographic sources of Sikh manuscript illumination within the broader traditions of South Asian visual culture.

lessons.title: The ਦਰਬਾਰੀ Manuscript: Patronage and Production at Sikh Courts
lessons.summary: Analyzes the production contexts of courtly Sikh manuscripts with focus on the Ranjit Singh Darbar period.

lessons.title: The ਪੋਥੀ Tradition: Proto-Canonical Manuscripts and Their Significance
lessons.summary: Examines the Goindval Pothis and other proto-canonical manuscript collections as evidence for the textual history of Sikh scripture.

lessons.title: Codicology: The Physical Structure of Sikh Manuscripts
lessons.summary: Provides systematic codicological training in the analysis of the physical structure of Sikh manuscript books.

lessons.title: Colophons, Scribal Notes, and Provenance

lessons.title: The Chaupai Sahib and Other Dasam Granth Manuscripts
lessons.summary: Analyzes the distinctive manuscript tradition of the Dasam Granth, including Kamalroop Singh's contributions to its textual history.

lessons.title: Digital Humanities and Sikh Manuscript Preservation
lessons.summary: Assesses the contributions of digital imaging, multispectral analysis, and digital corpus construction to Sikh manuscript scholarship.

lessons.title: Graduate Seminar: Producing a Manuscript Catalogue Entry
lessons.summary: Guides students through the production of a complete scholarly manuscript catalogue entry integrating all the analytical methods of the seminar.

courses.title: The Sikh Fresco Tradition: Advanced Critical Analysis
courses.source: B.N. Goswamy and Caron Smith, I am the Nabob: Love Poetry by a Sikh Ruler (2006)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar provides advanced critical analysis of the Sikh fresco tradition, focusing on the extensive mural programmes of gurdwaras, havelis, and palaces from the eighteenth through early twentieth centuries. Students develop skills in iconographic analysis, workshop attribution, the study of Punjabi fresco technique, and the theological interpretation of narrative and devotional image programmes. The seminar situates the Sikh fresco tradition within the broader context of South Asian wall painting and engages current debates in conservation and cultural heritage.
outcomes: Identify and analyze the major iconographic programmes of the Sikh fresco tradition using established art-historical methods.
Attribute fresco programmes to workshops and periods using stylistic, technical, and documentary evidence.
Interpret narrative and devotional fresco cycles in relation to Sikh theological and historical content.
Situate the Sikh fresco tradition within the broader history of South Asian mural painting.
Engage critically with conservation and heritage debates concerning threatened Sikh fresco sites.

lessons.title: Introduction: The Sikh Fresco Tradition — Scope, Significance, and Scholarship
lessons.summary: Introduces the geographic range, historical depth, and current scholarly frameworks for studying Sikh wall painting.

lessons.title: Punjabi Fresco Technique: Materials, Methods, and Conservation

lessons.title: The Gurdwara as Pictorial Space: Architecture and Image Programme
lessons.summary: Analyzes the relationship between gurdwara architectural design and fresco image programmes.

lessons.summary: Analyzes the iconographic conventions of Guru portraiture in Sikh fresco, tracing their development and theological significance.

lessons.title: Iconography II: Narrative Cycles from the ਜਨਮ-ਸਾਖੀ Literature
lessons.summary: Analyzes the narrative fresco cycles based on the janam-sakhi literature, focusing on their visual vocabulary and theological content.

lessons.title: Iconography III: The Battle Narratives and Martial Tradition
lessons.summary: Analyzes fresco programmes depicting Sikh battles and the martial tradition, focusing on their historical and theological dimensions.

lessons.title: Haveli and Palace Frescos: Secular and Sacred in Sikh Courtly Culture

lessons.title: Workshop Attribution and Regional Styles

lessons.title: B.N. Goswamy and the Critical Study of Sikh Art
lessons.summary: Examines Goswamy's methodological contributions to Sikh art history and evaluates their influence on the field.

lessons.title: Colonial Documentation and the Fresco Archive

lessons.title: Heritage, Threat, and Conservation Ethics
lessons.summary: Engages the conservation and heritage challenges facing the Sikh fresco tradition, analyzing both technical and ethical dimensions.

lessons.title: Graduate Seminar: Critical Analysis of a Sikh Fresco Programme
lessons.summary: Guides students through the construction of a complete critical analysis of a specific Sikh fresco programme integrating all the methods of the seminar.

courses.title: Modern Sikh Art: Theory, Identity, and Global Diaspora
courses.source: Pika Ghosh, Temple to Love: Architecture and Devotion in Seventeenth-Century Bengal (2005)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the development of modern and contemporary Sikh art, focusing on the intersection of artistic practice with questions of identity, diaspora, and postcolonial self-representation. Students analyze how Sikh artists in India and the global diaspora engage Sikh visual traditions, adapt them to new media and contexts, and negotiate between the demands of the contemporary art world and the theological and communal dimensions of Sikh visual culture. The seminar situates Sikh modern art within broader debates in postcolonial art history and diaspora aesthetics.
outcomes: Analyze the development of modern Sikh art from the late nineteenth century through the contemporary period.
Apply postcolonial art historical theory to the analysis of Sikh artistic production.
Evaluate how Sikh diaspora artists negotiate identity, heritage, and contemporary art world demands.
Situate modern Sikh art within global debates in postcolonial aesthetics and diaspora art theory.
Construct graduate-level art critical essays on modern and contemporary Sikh art conforming to CMOS standards.

lessons.title: Diaspora Aesthetics: Sikh Art in Britain, Canada, and the United States
lessons.summary: Analyzes the distinctive aesthetic strategies of Sikh diaspora artists in three major diaspora contexts.

lessons.title: Gender and Sikh Art: Women Artists and Feminist Critique
lessons.summary: Analyzes the work of Sikh women artists and applies feminist art historical critique to the Sikh visual tradition.

lessons.title: New Media and Digital Sikh Art
lessons.summary: Examines Sikh artistic production in digital and new media contexts, analyzing how new technologies transform Sikh visual tradition.

lessons.title: Gurbani Calligraphy and Text-Based Art
lessons.summary: Analyzes the tradition of Gurbani calligraphy and its development into a contemporary text-based art practice.

lessons.title: Postcolonial Theory and Sikh Art History
lessons.summary: Applies postcolonial theoretical frameworks to the analysis of Sikh art history, evaluating both their contributions and their limits.

lessons.title: Sacred and Secular: Sikh Art in Gallery and Gurdwara
lessons.summary: Analyzes the tensions and possibilities created by the display of Sikh art in gallery and museum contexts alongside its traditional gurdwara setting.

lessons.title: Graduate Seminar: Critical Essay on a Modern Sikh Artist
lessons.summary: Guides students through the construction of a graduate-level critical essay on a specific modern or contemporary Sikh artist.

courses.title: Sacred Space in the Sikh Tradition: Advanced Architecture and Theology
courses.source: Pashaura Singh and Louis E. Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (2014)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar analyzes the sacred architecture of the Sikh tradition — gurdwaras, takhts, and related sacred spaces — through integrated art-historical, architectural, and theological analysis. Students examine how Sikh sacred space embodies theological commitments, traces historical development from the Darbar Sahib to the global diaspora gurdwara, and engages current debates in sacred architecture theory. The seminar situates Sikh sacred architecture within comparative South Asian sacred architecture scholarship and analyzes the relationship between spatial design and the theology of the divine presence.
outcomes: Analyze the theological principles embodied in the design and spatial organization of gurdwara architecture.
Trace the historical development of Sikh sacred architecture from the sixteenth century to the present.
Apply architectural history methods to the analysis of specific gurdwara complexes.
Situate Sikh sacred architecture within comparative sacred architecture theory and South Asian architectural history.
Engage critically with contemporary debates about gurdwara architecture in the global diaspora.

lessons.title: Gurdwara Typology: Architectural Forms and Spatial Organization
lessons.summary: Develops a typology of gurdwara architectural forms and analyzes their relationship to liturgical and devotional functions.

lessons.title: Materials and Construction: The Technical Vocabulary of Sikh Architecture
lessons.summary: Develops familiarity with the materials and construction techniques characteristic of the Sikh architectural tradition.

lessons.title: The Langar Complex: Sacred Space and the Theology of ਸੇਵਾ
lessons.summary: Analyzes the langar complex as a distinctive sacred space that embodies the theology of seva within the gurdwara architectural programme.

lessons.title: Colonial-Era Gurdwara Construction and Its Legacy
lessons.summary: Examines the gurdwara construction activities of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and their architectural legacy.

lessons.title: Comparative Sacred Architecture: Sikh, Hindu, and Islamic Traditions

lessons.summary: Analyzes the gurdwara architecture of the global Sikh diaspora and its distinctive identity and contextual dimensions.

courses.title: Advanced Sikh-Sufi Dialogue: Mystical Poetry and Theology
courses.source: Pashaura Singh, The Bhagats of the Guru Granth Sahib (2003)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar conducts a rigorous comparative analysis of Sikh and Sufi mystical traditions, examining shared idioms of divine love, annihilation of ego, and the path of the devotee. Students engage primary texts from the Guru Granth Sahib and classical Sufi poetry alongside contemporary scholarship to trace historical encounters, theological convergences, and irreducible distinctions. The course cultivates critical fluency in both traditions at an advanced academic level.
outcomes: Critically analyze the theological structures of Sikh and Sufi mysticism using primary textual evidence.
Evaluate historical and sociological conditions that shaped Sikh-Sufi encounter in the Punjab.
Compare and contrast key concepts such as divine love, ego-annihilation, and the role of the spiritual guide in both traditions.
Apply contemporary comparative religion methodologies to Sikh and Sufi literary texts.
Synthesize original scholarly arguments about convergence and divergence in Sikh-Sufi thought.

lessons.summary: Establishes the methodological framework for Sikh-Sufi comparative study, surveys the field's historiography, and introduces the Punjab as a crucible of mystical encounter.

lessons.title: The Spiritual Guide: Guru and Murshid
lessons.summary: Compares the Sikh concept of the ਗੁਰੂ with the Sufi murshid, examining authority, transmission, and the pivotal Sikh theological move of vesting Guruship in scripture.

lessons.title: Poetic Form and Sacred Language
lessons.summary: Examines the literary vehicles of Sikh and Sufi mysticism, comparing poetic forms, musical structures, linguistic choices, and the use of bridal mysticism as a shared theological idiom.

lessons.title: Bhagat Farid in the Guru Granth Sahib: A Case Study
lessons.summary: Examines the inclusion of Sheikh Farid's compositions in the Guru Granth Sahib as a case study in Sikh-Sufi theological dialogue, analyzing the dialogical structure of Gurmat responses to Farid's verses.

lessons.title: Theological Divergences: Creation, Shariat, and Incarnation
lessons.summary: Examines the fundamental theological divergences between Sikh and Sufi thought, focusing on cosmology, the role of law, and concepts of divine embodiment.

lessons.title: Mystical States and Spiritual Stages
lessons.summary: Compares the Sufi systematic account of states and stations with the Gurmat phenomenology of the five ਖੰਡ, examining both convergences and the distinct theological frameworks embedding these experiences.

lessons.title: Gender, Body, and Mystical Metaphor
lessons.summary: Examines the gendered dimensions of Sikh and Sufi mystical language and the role of the body in both traditions, drawing on feminist religious scholarship.

lessons.title: Contemporary Sikh-Sufi Relations and Shared Shrines

courses.title: Sikh-Vedanta Comparative Metaphysics
courses.source: Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (2009)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar engages in rigorous comparative metaphysics between Sikh (Gurmat) theology and the major schools of Vedanta — Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita — with sustained attention to questions of ontology, cosmology, and the nature of liberation. Drawing on Mandair's post-colonial methodology and primary textual sources from the Guru Granth Sahib and the Vedantic canon, students develop the analytical tools to articulate both the deep engagement and the irreducible theological distinctiveness of Gurmat metaphysics. The course challenges reductive syncretic readings while illuminating the genuine philosophical complexity of both traditions.
outcomes: Articulate the metaphysical positions of Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita Vedanta with precision.
Analyze Gurmat theology's distinct metaphysical claims regarding the nature of the Divine, the soul, and creation.
Apply post-colonial methodological critiques to classical comparative religion approaches to Sikh-Hindu relations.
Evaluate the adequacy of 'non-dualism' as a category for understanding Gurmat metaphysics.
Construct original scholarly arguments about Gurmat's distinctive contribution to the history of South Asian metaphysics.

lessons.summary: Examines the Vedantic alternatives to Advaita — Ramanuja's qualified non-dualism and Madhva's dualism — providing the comparative base for analyzing Gurmat's distinct metaphysical position.

lessons.title: Gurmat Ontology: ਇੱਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ and the Nature of the Divine
lessons.summary: Analyzes the metaphysical content of the Mool Mantar and the Gurmat concept of the Divine, situating it in comparative relation to Vedantic ontology.

lessons.title: ਨਿਰਗੁਣ and ਸਰਗੁਣ: The Gurmat Dialectic of Transcendence and Immanence
lessons.summary: Analyzes the Gurmat dialectic of nirguna/nirguna and saguna/sarguna in comparison with Vedantic usage, arguing that Gurmat deploys these categories in a non-hierarchical dialectic that supports devotional theism.

lessons.title: ਮਾਇਆ in Gurmat vs. Maya in Advaita
lessons.summary: Demonstrates that despite lexical similarity, Gurmat's concept of ਮਾਇਆ as ethical attachment fundamentally differs from Advaita's ontological maya doctrine, with significant implications for the value of worldly life.

lessons.title: The Soul (ਜੀਵ / Jiva) in Comparative Perspective
lessons.summary: Compares Gurmat, Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, and Dvaita accounts of the individual soul's nature, its relationship to the Divine, and its ultimate destiny in liberation.

lessons.title: Liberation (ਮੁਕਤਿ / Moksha): Paths and Goals
lessons.summary: Compares the soteriological paths and liberation ideals of Gurmat and Vedantic schools, focusing on the distinctive Gurmat emphasis on grace, the ਨਾਮ, and the ਜੀਵਨ-ਮੁਕਤ ideal.

lessons.title: Creation and Cosmology Compared
lessons.summary: Examines the cosmological frameworks of Gurmat and Vedantic schools, focusing on the reality of creation and the theological implications of each tradition's cosmological commitments.

lessons.title: Post-Colonial Critique: Mandair and the Specter of Comparison
lessons.summary: Engages Mandair's post-colonial critique of comparative religion in relation to the Sikh-Vedanta comparison, examining the political stakes of comparison and the case for Gurmat intellectual autonomy.

lessons.title: The ਜੀਵਨ-ਮੁਕਤ Ideal: Engaged Embodied Liberation
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat ideal of liberation-while-living as a distinctive metaphysical commitment that reflects Gurmat's positive evaluation of embodied, worldly existence and spiritual equality.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Gurmat's Unique Metaphysical Contribution
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's comparative findings to articulate Gurmat theology's distinctive and irreducible metaphysical contribution, arguing against reductive syncretic readings.

courses.title: Sikh-Buddhist Comparative Ethics
courses.source: Comparative religious ethics; Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh scholarship
courses.summary: This graduate seminar conducts a rigorous comparative analysis of ethical frameworks in Sikh (Gurmat) theology and Buddhist thought, examining foundational questions of moral psychology, virtue, suffering, social ethics, and liberation. Drawing on primary texts from the Guru Granth Sahib and the Pali Canon alongside scholarship by Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh and comparative ethics theorists, students develop the analytical capacity to identify genuine structural parallels and irreducible differences between these two South Asian traditions. The course challenges students to think beyond surface-level convergences toward a nuanced understanding of each tradition's moral logic.
outcomes: Analyze the moral psychology of suffering and liberation in both Buddhist and Gurmat frameworks.
Compare the ethical roles of compassion (karuna / ਦਇਆ) and selfless service in both traditions.
Evaluate the social ethics of caste, gender, and community in Buddhist and Sikh thought.
Apply comparative religious ethics methodologies to primary textual evidence from both traditions.
Articulate the distinctive ethical contributions of Gurmat thought in relation to Buddhist ethics.
references: Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved (HarperSanFrancisco, 1995)
Damien Keown, The Nature of Buddhist Ethics (Palgrave Macmillan, 1992)
Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (Oxford University Press, 2000)
Mark Siderits, Personal Identity and Buddhist Philosophy (Ashgate, 2003)
Walpola Rahula, What the Buddha Taught (Grove Press, 1959)
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (I.B. Tauris, 2011)
Christopher Chapple, ed., Nonviolence to Animals, Earth, and Self in Asian Traditions (SUNY Press, 1993)
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge University Press, 1990)

lessons.title: Introduction: Methodological Foundations for Sikh-Buddhist Ethical Comparison
lessons.summary: Establishes the comparative religious ethics framework for the seminar and introduces the key methodological commitments and cautions governing the Sikh-Buddhist comparison.

lessons.title: The Structure of Suffering: Dukkha and ਹਉਮੈ
lessons.summary: Compares the Buddhist concept of dukkha and tanha with the Gurmat concept of ਹਉਮੈ, analyzing both structural parallels and the significant metaphysical differences in their accounts of the human problem.

lessons.title: The Moral Psychology of Desire and Attachment
lessons.summary: Analyzes Buddhist and Gurmat accounts of desire, comparing the Buddhist three poisons with the Gurmat five thieves and examining their different practical implications for the moral life.

lessons.title: Compassion: ਦਇਆ and Karuna
lessons.summary: Conducts a detailed comparison of Buddhist karuna and Gurmat ਦਇਆ, examining their metaphysical grounding, scope, and practical expression.

lessons.title: The Virtuous Life: Gurmat's Five Virtues and Buddhist Paramitas
lessons.summary: Compares the Gurmat catalogue of cardinal virtues with the Buddhist paramitas, examining the content and theoretical structure of each tradition's virtue framework.

lessons.title: Non-Violence (Ahimsa) in Buddhist and Sikh Ethics
lessons.summary: Compares Buddhist and Sikh approaches to non-violence, examining the Sikh concept of righteous force (ਧਰਮ ਯੁੱਧ) against Buddhist ahimsa and drawing out the political-ethical implications of each tradition's position.

lessons.title: Sangha and ਸੰਗਤ: Community as Ethical Formation
lessons.summary: Compares the Buddhist sangha and Sikh ਸੰਗਤ as institutions of ethical community, examining their structures, their anti-caste commitments, and the significance of their different relationships to monastic and householder life.

lessons.title: Caste, Equality, and Social Ethics
lessons.summary: Compares the anti-caste social ethics of Buddhist and Gurmat traditions, examining theoretical grounds, institutional embodiments, and the historical gap between egalitarian theology and social practice.

lessons.title: Gender, Embodiment, and Moral Agency
lessons.summary: Examines Buddhist and Gurmat positions on gender and embodiment, comparing their accounts of women's spiritual capacity and the implications of each tradition's moral anthropology for gender ethics.

lessons.title: Work, Wealth, and Economic Ethics
lessons.summary: Compares Buddhist and Gurmat economic ethics, examining the different roles of monasticism, honest labor (ਕਿਰਤ), generosity (ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ / dana), and the ਲੰਗਰ institution.

lessons.title: Liberation Ethics: Nirvana and ਮੁਕਤਿ as Ethical Goals
lessons.summary: Examines the relationship between the liberation ideal and ethics in both Buddhism and Gurmat, comparing nirvana and ਮੁਕਤਿ as ethical goals and analyzing the role of community in the liberated life.

lessons.title: Synthesis and Divergence: Assessing the Comparison
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's comparative ethical findings, identifying the most significant convergences and divergences between Buddhist and Gurmat ethics and drawing out their implications for comparative religious ethics.

courses.title: Interfaith Theology: A Graduate Seminar
courses.source: Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (2014)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines Sikh contributions to interfaith theology, situating the Guru Granth Sahib's pluralistic vision within the broader field of theology of religions. Moving beyond descriptive comparison, students engage normative questions: What theological claims about other traditions does Gurmat make? How does the Sikh tradition's historical encounter with Islam, Hinduism, and Christianity shape its interfaith theology? And how should Sikh scholars engage contemporary frameworks such as inclusivism, exclusivism, and pluralism? The course draws on the Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies and primary Sikh textual sources throughout.
outcomes: Analyze the major theological frameworks for understanding religious diversity: exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism.
Articulate the Gurmat theological position on religious diversity, drawing on primary textual evidence.
Evaluate Sikh historical encounters with Islam and Hinduism as shaped by theological commitments.
Apply contemporary interfaith theology scholarship to questions arising from Sikh pluralism.
Develop original scholarly arguments about the Sikh tradition's contribution to global interfaith discourse.
references: Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
John Hick, An Interpretation of Religion (Yale University Press, 1989)
Gavin D'Costa, The Meeting of Religions and the Trinity (Orbis, 2000)
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (I.B. Tauris, 2011)
Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (Columbia University Press, 2009)
W. Owen Cole and Piara Singh Sambhi, The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices (Sussex Academic Press, 1995)
Pashaura Singh, The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority (Oxford University Press, 2000)
Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries (University of Chicago Press, 1994)

lessons.title: Introduction: The Field of Interfaith Theology and the Sikh Contribution
lessons.summary: Introduces the academic field of interfaith theology, surveys the dominant frameworks (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), and argues for the Sikh tradition's distinctive and underrepresented contribution.

lessons.title: Exclusivism, Inclusivism, Pluralism: The Classical Framework
lessons.summary: Examines the classical threefold typology of theology of religions, analyzing the strengths and weaknesses of each position and beginning to locate Gurmat theology in relation to it.

lessons.title: Gurmat Theology of Religious Diversity: Primary Textual Evidence
lessons.summary: Conducts a close reading of primary textual evidence from the Guru Granth Sahib for Gurmat's theology of religious diversity, examining both its universalist affirmations and its specific theological commitments.

lessons.title: Sikh-Muslim Encounter: Theological Dimensions
lessons.summary: Examines the theological dimensions of the Sikh-Muslim historical encounter, from Guru Nanak's engagement with Islamic thought to the martyrdom traditions and their implications for Gurmat interfaith theology.

lessons.title: Sikh-Hindu Relations: Identity, Boundary, and Shared Heritage
lessons.summary: Examines the contested question of Sikh-Hindu theological relations, distinguishing historical interaction from theological identity and analyzing the Guru Granth Sahib's discriminating engagement with the Hindu tradition.

lessons.title: The Bhagats and the Theology of Inclusion
lessons.summary: Examines the theological significance of the Bhagat tradition in the Guru Granth Sahib, analyzing the criteria of inclusion and the model of engaged, discriminating interfaith appreciation it embodies.

lessons.title: Guru Gobind Singh and the Universal Vision
lessons.summary: Examines Guru Gobind Singh's contributions to Gurmat interfaith theology, focusing on the affirmation of ਮਾਨਸ ਕੀ ਜਾਤਿ, the universal dimension of the Khalsa institution, and the implications of the Guru Granth Sahib's finalization.

lessons.title: ਪਾਖੰਡ: The Gurmat Critique of Superficial Religion
lessons.summary: Analyzes the concept of ਪਾਖੰਡ as a cross-traditional critique in Gurmat theology, examining its implications for interfaith methodology and its positive corollary of a universal standard of genuine spirituality.

lessons.title: Sikh Engagement with Christianity: Colonial and Contemporary
lessons.summary: Examines the Sikh tradition's encounter with Christianity from the colonial period through the contemporary diaspora, analyzing both the power dynamics of the colonial encounter and the genuine theological grounds for contemporary dialogue.

lessons.title: The Sikh Diaspora and Interfaith Practice
lessons.summary: Examines how diaspora Sikh communities have navigated interfaith relations in practice, analyzing both the universal hospitality of the ਲੰਗਰ tradition and the tensions between theological universalism and communal identity.

lessons.title: ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ: The Universal Ethical Vision
lessons.summary: Examines the concept of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ (the welfare of all) as a theologically grounded universal ethical vision with significant implications for Gurmat's approach to interfaith engagement and global justice.

lessons.title: Sikh Interfaith Theology and Contemporary Pluralism
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's analysis into a coherent account of Gurmat's distinctive 'committed theological openness,' arguing for its significance in contemporary interfaith discourse.

courses.title: Gurmat Economic Philosophy: A Graduate Seminar
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh Rahit Maryada; contemporary Sikh economic ethics
courses.summary: This graduate seminar develops a systematic account of Gurmat economic philosophy, drawing on primary texts from the Guru Granth Sahib and the broader Sikh theological tradition alongside contemporary economic theory. The seminar examines the foundational Gurmat principles governing economic life — honest labor, sharing, the critique of exploitation, and the vision of an economy oriented toward universal welfare — and develops their implications for contemporary economic ethics. Students engage both classical Sikh textual sources and contemporary scholarly work in Sikh economics and religious ethics.
outcomes: Articulate the foundational Gurmat principles governing economic life, drawing on primary textual evidence.
Analyze the ethical critique of economic exploitation and inequality in the Guru Granth Sahib.
Evaluate the institutional economic expressions of Gurmat values — ਲੰਗਰ, ਦਸਵੰਧ, and ਸੇਵਾ — as models for economic ethics.
Apply Gurmat economic philosophy to contemporary questions of economic justice and development.
Compare Gurmat economic ethics with other religious economic ethics frameworks.
references: W. H. McLeod, Sikhism (Penguin, 1997)
Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (I.B. Tauris, 2011)
Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905, tr. Talcott Parsons, 1930)
Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom (Anchor Books, 1999)
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge University Press, 1990)
Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (Oxford University Press, 2001)
W. Owen Cole and Piara Singh Sambhi, The Sikhs: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices (Sussex Academic Press, 1995)

lessons.title: Introduction: Toward a Gurmat Economic Philosophy
lessons.summary: Establishes the methodological framework for developing a Gurmat economic philosophy, introduces the foundational triad of ਨਾਮ ਜਪਣਾ, ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ, and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ, and surveys the relevant scholarly literature.

lessons.title: ਕਿਰਤ: The Theology of Honest Labor
lessons.summary: Examines the concept of ਕਿਰਤ (honest labor) as the foundational economic principle of Gurmat ethics, analyzing its theological grounding and institutional implications.

lessons.title: ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ: Sharing as Economic Ethics
lessons.summary: Examines the principle of ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ as a normative economic ethic, analyzing its theological grounding in divine stewardship and its implications for redistribution and property rights.

lessons.title: ਮਾਇਆ and the Moral Limits of Wealth
lessons.summary: Examines the concept of ਮਾਇਆ as an economic-ethical category in Gurmat thought, distinguishing legitimate wealth from destructive attachment and articulating the Gurmat alternative to both asceticism and materialism.

lessons.title: ਲੋਭ: Greed as the Central Economic Vice
lessons.summary: Analyzes the Gurmat concept of ਲੋਭ (greed) as the central economic vice, examining its institutional expressions and the Gurmat alternative grounded in ਨਾਮ-centered economic motivation.

lessons.title: The ਲੰਗਰ Institution as Economic Model
lessons.summary: Analyzes the ਲੰਗਰ as a distinctive economic institution, examining its theological rationale, its structural features, and its implications for contemporary thinking about gift economies and food security.

lessons.title: ਦਸਵੰਧ: Tithing and Communal Finance
lessons.summary: Examines ਦਸਵੰਧ as a Gurmat economic institution, analyzing its theological grounding, historical development, and implications for communal welfare financing.

lessons.title: Exploitation, Caste, and Economic Justice
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat critique of caste-based economic exploitation, analyzing both the primary textual evidence and the structural economic justice implications of Gurmat economic ethics.

lessons.title: The Gurmat Critique of Economic Inequality
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat normative position on economic inequality, engaging contemporary philosophical frameworks (Rawls, Sen) alongside Gurmat textual sources.

lessons.title: Gurmat Economic Philosophy and Modern Capitalism
lessons.summary: Develops a nuanced Gurmat assessment of modern capitalism, distinguishing what Gurmat ethics affirms, critiques, and would transform in contemporary economic structures.

lessons.title: ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ and Global Development Economics
lessons.summary: Develops the implications of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ for global development economics, engaging Sen's capability approach and examining the Sikh tradition's institutional contributions to development.

lessons.title: Synthesis: A Gurmat Economic Ethics for the Twenty-First Century
lessons.summary: Synthesizes Gurmat economic principles into a coherent ethical framework and develops their implications for contemporary economic challenges.

courses.title: Halemi Raj: The Economics of a Just Sikh Society
courses.summary: This graduate seminar investigates the concept of Halemi Raj — the 'reign of the humble,' the Sikh vision of a just society governed by divine ethics — as a comprehensive political-economic framework. Drawing on Kapur Singh's foundational Parasaraprasna, the Guru Granth Sahib, and contemporary political philosophy, students examine how Gurmat political theology generates a distinctive vision of just governance, equitable economic relations, and collective welfare. The seminar traces the concept from its scriptural roots through historical expressions and develops its implications for contemporary political economy.
outcomes: Analyze the concept of Halemi Raj as a Sikh political-economic framework drawing on primary textual sources.
Evaluate Kapur Singh's theological account of Sikh political philosophy in Parasaraprasna.
Compare Halemi Raj with Western theories of just governance and political economy.
Assess the historical expressions of Sikh political economy in the Khalsa polity.
Develop original scholarly arguments about Halemi Raj's relevance to contemporary political economy.
references: Kapur Singh, Parasaraprasna (Guru Nanak Dev University, 1989)
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge University Press, 1990)
Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Arvind-Pal Singh Mandair, Religion and the Specter of the West (Columbia University Press, 2009)
John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Harvard University Press, 1971)
W. H. McLeod, Sikhism (Penguin, 1997)
Louis E. Fenech and W. H. McLeod, Historical Dictionary of Sikhism (Scarecrow Press, 2014)
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (I.B. Tauris, 2011)

lessons.title: Introduction: Halemi Raj and the Sikh Political Imagination
lessons.summary: Introduces the concept of ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ as the Sikh political ideal, situates Kapur Singh's Parasaraprasna as the primary secondary text, and establishes the political theology framework for the seminar.

lessons.title: Kapur Singh's Parasaraprasna: A Critical Overview
lessons.summary: Provides a critical overview of Kapur Singh's Parasaraprasna, analyzing its scholarly contributions and its political context.

lessons.title: Theological Foundations: Divine Sovereignty and Human Government
lessons.summary: Examines the theological foundations of Gurmat political thought, focusing on the concept of divine sovereignty and its implications for human governance.

lessons.title: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ: Integrating Spiritual and Political Authority
lessons.summary: Examines the doctrine of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ as the Sikh theological integration of political and spiritual authority, tracing its historical and institutional expressions.

lessons.title: The ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ as Political Community
lessons.summary: Examines the Khalsa as a political community in Gurmat theology, analyzing its constitution, authority, and role in the Halemi Raj vision.

lessons.title: Justice (ਨਿਆਉ) in Gurmat Political Ethics
lessons.summary: Examines the concept of ਨਿਆਉ (justice) in Gurmat political thought, analyzing its content, its institutional expressions, and its relationship to contemporary theories of justice.

lessons.title: The Guru Granth Sahib's Critique of Unjust Rule
lessons.summary: Examines the explicit political critique of unjust governance in the Guru Granth Sahib, analyzing the tradition's prophetic political voice.

lessons.title: Sarbat Khalsa: Democratic Deliberation in Sikh Polity
lessons.summary: Examines the Sarbat Khalsa tradition as a form of democratic deliberation within a theologically constituted community, analyzing its historical practice and contemporary relevance.

lessons.title: Historical Expressions: The Misl System and the Sikh Kingdom
lessons.summary: Examines historical expressions of Gurmat political economy in the Misl confederacy system and the Kingdom of Lahore, assessing how closely they embodied the Halemi Raj ideal.

lessons.title: Halemi Raj and Social Contract Theory
lessons.summary: Compares Gurmat Halemi Raj political philosophy with Western social contract theory, examining both convergences and the fundamental theological distinction.

lessons.title: Economic Dimensions of Halemi Raj
lessons.summary: Develops the economic policy implications of the Halemi Raj vision, drawing on the analyses of earlier lessons to construct a coherent Gurmat political economy.

lessons.title: Halemi Raj in the Twenty-First Century
lessons.summary: Develops the implications of Halemi Raj for twenty-first century political realities, examining how the diaspora Sikh community can express ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ in pluralist democratic contexts.

courses.title: Langar as Economic System: Theory, Practice, and Global Impact
courses.source: Sikh institutional economics; contemporary food systems research
courses.summary: This graduate seminar conducts a rigorous analysis of the Sikh ਲੰਗਰ institution as an economic system, examining its theoretical foundations in Gurmat ethics, its historical development, its contemporary global expressions, and its implications for food systems research, institutional economics, and political economy. Students engage primary Sikh textual sources alongside contemporary economic analysis to develop both a deep understanding of the ਲੰਗਰ's theological grounding and a rigorous account of its economic logic and global relevance.
outcomes: Analyze the theological and ethical foundations of the ਲੰਗਰ institution in Gurmat thought.
Evaluate the ਲੰਗਫਰ as a distinct economic model combining gift economy, voluntary labor, and universal access.
Assess the historical development of the ਲੰਗਰ from its founding through contemporary global expressions.
Apply contemporary food systems and institutional economics frameworks to the ਲੰਗਰ model.
Develop original scholarly arguments about the ਲੰਗਰ's contribution to global food security discourse.
references: Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge University Press, 1990)
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (I.B. Tauris, 2011)
Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom (Anchor Books, 1999)
Marcel Mauss, The Gift (1925, tr. W. D. Halls, Norton, 1990)
Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons (Cambridge University Press, 1990)
W. H. McLeod, Sikhism (Penguin, 1997)
Gurinder Singh Mann, The Making of Sikh Scripture (Oxford University Press, 2001)

lessons.title: Introduction: The ਲੰਗਰ as Economic Institution
lessons.summary: Introduces the ਲੰਗਰ as an economic institution of remarkable scale and efficiency, establishes the methodological framework for its analysis, and surveys the relevant economic and theological scholarly literature.

lessons.title: Theological Foundations: Why Free Food?
lessons.summary: Examines the theological rationale for the ਲੰਗਰ institution, tracing its roots in Gurmat principles of equality, sharing, and the divine presence in all.

lessons.title: Historical Origins: Mata Khivi and the Early ਲੰਗਰ
lessons.summary: Examines the historical origins of the ਲੰਗਰ institution, focusing on Mata Khivi's credited role in its development and the institution's evolution through the Guru period.

lessons.title: ਪੰਗਤ: The Economics of Equal Seating
lessons.summary: Analyzes the ਪੰਗਤ practice as an economic institution, examining how equal seating challenges the caste-based organization of economic life and enacts a different economic logic.

lessons.title: The Gift Economy: Mauss and the ਲੰਗਰ
lessons.summary: Applies Marcel Mauss's gift economy theory to the ਲੰਗਰ institution, analyzing how the ਲੰਗਰ operates as a gift economy and what this reveals about the institution's economic logic.

lessons.title: Voluntary Labor (ਸੇਵਾ) as Economic Input
lessons.summary: Analyzes voluntary labor (ਸੇਵਾ) as the primary economic input of the ਲੰਗਰ model, examining its institutional management, its motivational structure, and its economic significance.

lessons.title: Financing the ਲੰਗਰ: ਦਸਵੰਧ and Community Contribution
lessons.summary: Examines the financing mechanisms of the ਲੰਗਰ institution, analyzing how ਦਸਵੰਧ and voluntary contribution create a sustainable community financing model.

lessons.title: Scale and Efficiency: The Golden Temple Model
lessons.summary: Examines the large-scale ਲੰਗਰ operation at the Harmandir Sahib as a case study in economic efficiency, organizational science, and sustainable community provision.

lessons.title: Disaster Response: ਲੰਗਰ as Emergency Economics
lessons.summary: Examines the ਲੰਗਰ's remarkable track record of rapid disaster response as a case study in emergency economic provision and community resilience.

lessons.title: The ਲੰਗਰ and Global Food Security
lessons.summary: Examines the ਲੰਗਰ's contribution to global food security discourse, analyzing how the institution addresses food insecurity and what lessons it offers for global food policy.

lessons.title: Ostrom's Commons and the ਲੰਗਰ
lessons.summary: Applies Ostrom's institutional analysis of the commons to the ਲੰਗਰ institution, examining how it solves common-pool resource problems through community governance.

lessons.title: The ਲੰਗਰ Model for the Twenty-First Century
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's analyses into a comprehensive account of the ਲੰਗਰ model's economic logic and its relevance to twenty-first century food security and institutional economics.

courses.title: Sarbat da Bhala and Global Development Economics
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh political philosophy; global development theory
courses.summary: This graduate seminar develops the concept of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ (the welfare of all) as a Sikh contribution to global development economics, examining its theological foundations, institutional expressions, and implications for contemporary development theory and practice. Students engage primary Sikh textual sources alongside major frameworks in global development economics — including Sen's capability approach, the Human Development Index, and post-development critiques — to develop a rigorous account of how the Sikh universal welfare vision contributes to and challenges contemporary development discourse.
outcomes: Articulate the theological foundations of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ in the Guru Granth Sahib and the Sikh Ardas.
Evaluate the convergences and divergences between Gurmat universal welfare and Sen's capability approach.
Analyze Sikh institutional expressions of universal welfare — ਲੰਗਰ, ਸੇਵਾ organizations, and disaster response.
Apply post-development critiques to assess the limitations of mainstream development frameworks from a Gurmat perspective.
Develop original scholarly arguments about the Sikh tradition's contribution to global development ethics.
references: Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom (Anchor Books, 1999)
Mahbub ul Haq, Reflections on Human Development (Oxford University Press, 1995)
Martha Nussbaum, Creating Capabilities (Harvard University Press, 2011)
Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (I.B. Tauris, 2011)
Arturo Escobar, Encountering Development (Princeton University Press, 1995)
Jeffrey Sachs, The End of Poverty (Penguin, 2005)
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge University Press, 1990)

lessons.title: Introduction: ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ as a Development Framework
lessons.summary: Introduces ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ as a Sikh contribution to global development economics, surveys the relevant development theory literature, and establishes the seminar's methodological framework.

lessons.title: Theological Foundations: Divine Creation and Universal Obligation
lessons.summary: Examines the theological grounding of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ in the Gurmat conviction of the Divine's equal presence in all creation.

lessons.title: The Sikh Ardas: Institutionalizing Universal Welfare
lessons.summary: Examines the Sikh Ardas as the institutional mechanism through which ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ is regularly recited and renewed as a communal commitment.

lessons.title: Sen's Capability Approach and Gurmat Welfare Ethics
lessons.summary: Examines the convergences and divergences between Sen's capability approach and Gurmat ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ as frameworks for understanding universal human welfare.

lessons.title: The Human Development Index and Gurmat Values
lessons.summary: Evaluates the Human Development Index as a measure of human welfare from a Gurmat perspective, identifying its strengths, limitations, and the dimensions it misses from a ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ standpoint.

lessons.title: Post-Development Critiques and the Gurmat Alternative
lessons.summary: Engages post-development critiques of mainstream development discourse from a Gurmat perspective, examining how ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ offers an alternative to Western development hegemony.

lessons.title: ਸੇਵਾ Organizations and Development Practice
lessons.summary: Examines Sikh ਸੇਵਾ organizations engaged in development and humanitarian work, analyzing their institutional models, motivational structures, and development approaches.

lessons.title: Gender and Development: Gurmat Contributions
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat tradition's contributions to gender and development discourse, analyzing both the theological resources for gender equality and the gap between theological ideal and institutional practice.

lessons.title: Environmental Welfare: Creation Care in Gurmat Ethics
lessons.summary: Examines Gurmat theological resources for environmental ethics and their implications for sustainable development discourse.

lessons.title: Economic Rights and ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ
lessons.summary: Examines the concept of economic rights from a Gurmat perspective, analyzing how ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ generates economic rights claims and their implications for development policy.

lessons.title: Sikh Diaspora Philanthropy and Global Development
lessons.summary: Examines the remarkable philanthropic record of the Sikh diaspora as an expression of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ, analyzing both its scale and its motivational structure.

lessons.title: Synthesis: ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ for the Twenty-First Century
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's analysis to develop a comprehensive account of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ's contributions to and challenges within twenty-first century development discourse.

courses.title: Gurmat and Distributive Justice
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh ethics; John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the concept of distributive justice — the fair distribution of resources, opportunities, and welfare across society — from the perspective of Gurmat theology and in dialogue with major Western theories of justice, particularly John Rawls's theory of justice as fairness. Drawing on primary texts from the Guru Granth Sahib and contemporary political philosophy, students develop a rigorous account of the Gurmat vision of just distribution and its implications for contemporary economic policy. The seminar explores both the convergences and the significant differences between Rawlsian and Gurmat approaches to economic justice.
outcomes: Articulate the major contemporary theories of distributive justice — Rawls, libertarianism, utilitarianism, capabilities — with precision.
Analyze the Gurmat theological foundations of distributive justice, drawing on primary textual evidence.
Compare Rawlsian justice as fairness with Gurmat principles of just distribution.
Evaluate the institutional implications of Gurmat distributive justice for economic policy.
Develop original scholarly arguments about Gurmat's distinctive contribution to distributive justice theory.
references: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Harvard University Press, 1971)
John Rawls, Political Liberalism (Columbia University Press, 1993)
Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (Basic Books, 1974)
Amartya Sen, The Idea of Justice (Harvard University Press, 2009)
Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, eds., The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (Oxford University Press, 2014)
Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, Sikhism: An Introduction (I.B. Tauris, 2011)
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (Cambridge University Press, 1990)
Martha Nussbaum, Creating Capabilities (Harvard University Press, 2011)

lessons.title: Introduction: Distributive Justice and the Gurmat Tradition
lessons.summary: Introduces distributive justice as a field and establishes the Gurmat tradition's engagement with it, situating the seminar within the broader academic discourse.

lessons.title: Major Theories of Distributive Justice: A Critical Survey
lessons.summary: Surveys the major contemporary theories of distributive justice — utilitarianism, libertarianism, Rawlsian liberalism, and the capabilities approach — to provide the comparative framework for the seminar.

lessons.title: Rawls's Theory of Justice as Fairness
lessons.summary: Provides a detailed analysis of Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971), focusing on the original position, the veil of ignorance, and the two principles of justice.

lessons.title: Libertarian Critiques: Nozick and the Entitlement Theory
lessons.summary: Examines Robert Nozick's libertarian critique of Rawls and its relevance to the Gurmat distributive ethics discussion.

lessons.title: Gurmat Theological Foundations of Just Distribution
lessons.summary: Develops the theological foundations of Gurmat distributive justice, analyzing how the recognition of divine ownership and universal divine presence generates obligations of just sharing.

lessons.title: ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ as a Distributive Justice Principle
lessons.summary: Develops ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ as a systematically articulated principle of distributive justice, comparing it with Rawls's difference principle and examining its institutional implications.

lessons.title: Rawls and Gurmat Compared: Veil of Ignorance vs. Divine Vision
lessons.summary: Conducts a systematic comparison of Rawls's veil of ignorance methodology with the Gurmat theological vision of the Divine's equal presence in all, examining what each reveals about the other.

lessons.title: Caste, Structural Injustice, and Gurmat Redistribution
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat approach to structural injustice — particularly caste-based economic inequality — as a case study in how Gurmat distributive ethics addresses systematic economic disadvantage.

lessons.title: Gurmat Critique of Inherited Wealth and Privilege
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat critique of inherited wealth and structural privilege as sources of unjust distribution, analyzing the tradition's account of legitimate vs. illegitimate sources of economic advantage.

lessons.title: Institutional Expressions: ਲੰਗਰ and ਦਸਵੰਧ as Justice Mechanisms
lessons.summary: Analyzes the ਲੰਗਰ and ਦਸਵੰਧ as institutional justice mechanisms, examining how they implement the Gurmat principles of just distribution at community scale.

lessons.title: Global Distributive Justice and ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ
lessons.summary: Examines the global dimensions of distributive justice from a Gurmat perspective, analyzing how ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ generates obligations of global redistribution.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Gurmat's Contribution to Distributive Justice Theory
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's comparative analysis to articulate Gurmat theology's distinctive contributions to distributive justice theory and assess the strengths and limitations of the Gurmat approach.

courses.title: Gurmat and Virtue Ethics: An Advanced Inquiry
courses.source: SGGS; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics; Sikh moral philosophy
courses.summary: This graduate seminar investigates the convergences and divergences between classical virtue ethics (Aristotelian and Stoic) and the Sikh moral framework rooted in Gurbani. Students engage primary sources from the Sri Guru Granth Sahib alongside Aristotle, MacIntyre, and contemporary Sikh philosophers to construct a rigorous comparative account of virtuous personhood. The course culminates in an original analysis of how Gurmat reconfigures the virtuous life through the concept of the Gurmukh.
outcomes: Critically compare Aristotelian eudaimonia with the Gurmat concept of spiritual flourishing expressed through ਨਾਮ and ਸੇਵਾ
Analyze primary Gurbani passages to identify and systematize a Sikh virtue taxonomy
Evaluate Alasdair MacIntyre's tradition-constituted rationality against the Gurmat tradition
Construct original arguments about how ਹਉਮੈ functions as the root vice within Sikh moral psychology
Assess contemporary applications of Sikh virtue ethics to professional, civic, and ecological domains
references: Aristotle. Nicomachean Ethics, trans. Terence Irwin (Hackett, 1999)
MacIntyre, Alasdair. After Virtue: A Study in Moral Theory (University of Notre Dame Press, 1981)
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Name of My Beloved: Verses of the Sikh Gurus (HarperCollins, 1995)
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation (Columbia University Press, 2009)

lessons.title: Introduction: Virtue Ethics and Gurmat — Framing the Inquiry
lessons.summary: This opening lesson frames the comparative inquiry between classical virtue ethics and Gurmat, establishing methodological principles and identifying key structural parallels and divergences.

lessons.title: Aristotelian Eudaimonia and the Gurmat Vision of Flourishing
lessons.summary: A detailed comparison of Aristotle's account of eudaimonia with the Gurmat vision of spiritual flourishing, examining shared teleological structures and the role of grace.

lessons.title: The Gurmukh as Moral Ideal: A Structural Analysis
lessons.summary: Systematic analysis of the Gurmukh as Gurmat's moral ideal, comparing it with Aristotle's spoudaios and the Stoic sage, with attention to the role of grace and theocentric grounding.

lessons.title: Haumai as Root Vice: Sikh Moral Psychology
lessons.summary: A philosophical analysis of haumai as the foundational moral disorder in Gurmat, examining the five vices and comparing this account with Aristotelian and Augustinian treatments of vice.

lessons.title: The Virtue of Sach: Truth as Ontology and Ethics
lessons.summary: Investigation of Sach as simultaneously a metaphysical attribute of the Divine and the highest human virtue, examining its multidimensional significance in Gurmat moral philosophy.

lessons.title: Seva, Simran, and the Habitual Structure of Virtue
lessons.summary: Analysis of seva and simran as the twin disciplines of virtuous formation in Gurmat, comparing their function with Aristotelian habituation and MacIntyre's concept of practices.

lessons.title: Stoic Virtue and Gurmat: Points of Convergence
lessons.summary: Examination of Stoic virtue ethics as a comparative framework for Gurmat, identifying important convergences around the supremacy of virtue, cosmopolitanism, and equanimity.

lessons.title: MacIntyre's Tradition-Constituted Rationality and the Sikh Tradition
lessons.summary: Application of MacIntyre's framework of tradition-constituted rationality to Gurmat, examining its explanatory power and its limits in the context of post-colonial critique.

lessons.title: Gender, Virtue, and Gurmat: Critical Perspectives
lessons.summary: Critical examination of gender and virtue in Gurmat, engaging feminist virtue ethics and attending to both the egalitarian theology of the SGGS and the institutional failures of the tradition.

lessons.title: Virtue Ethics in the Sangat: Community as Moral School
lessons.summary: Analysis of the Sangat as the primary institution of Gurmat virtue formation, examining Langar and Sangat as MacIntyrean practices that constitute the Sikh moral community.

lessons.title: Contemporary Applications: Professional and Civic Virtue in Gurmat
lessons.summary: Examination of Gurmat virtue ethics in contemporary professional and civic contexts, including professional integrity, economic ethics, civic courage, and environmental responsibility.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Toward a Gurmat Virtue Ethics — Works Cited
lessons.summary: Synthetic lesson constructing a rigorous account of Gurmat virtue ethics that honors its theological distinctiveness while engaging contemporary philosophical scholarship.

courses.title: Sikh Bioethics: Life, Death, and Medical Decision-Making
courses.source: Sikh Rahit Maryada; SGGS; contemporary bioethics literature
courses.summary: This graduate seminar applies Sikh theological and ethical principles to the major questions of contemporary bioethics, including beginning-of-life issues, end-of-life care, organ donation, genetic technology, and healthcare justice. Students engage primary Sikh sources alongside leading bioethics scholarship to construct rigorously argued positions on contested medical-ethical questions. The course insists on fidelity to Gurmat principles while engaging the full complexity of contemporary biomedical contexts.
outcomes: Apply Gurmat principles from the SGGS and Sikh Rahit Maryada to specific contemporary bioethical dilemmas
Critically analyze dominant secular bioethics frameworks (principlist, utilitarian, deontological) from a Sikh perspective
Construct original Sikh bioethical arguments regarding end-of-life care, organ donation, and genetic technology
Evaluate the institutional bioethics of Sikh healthcare organizations using Gurmat criteria
Assess the compatibility of Sikh bioethical principles with pluralistic secular healthcare systems

lessons.summary: Framing the field of Sikh bioethics, establishing methodological principles, and introducing the core Gurmat theological framework for bioethical reasoning.

lessons.summary: Examination of the theological grounding of life's sanctity in Gurmat, with attention to the concepts of aatma, deh, and bhaana.

lessons.title: Beginning-of-Life Issues: Conception, Abortion, and Reproductive Technology
lessons.summary: Sikh ethical analysis of abortion, IVF, female feticide, and surrogacy using Gurmat principles.

lessons.title: Genetic Technology and the Sikh Ethical Framework
lessons.summary: Application of Gurmat ethics to gene editing, genetic enhancement, prenatal testing, and heritable germline modification.

lessons.title: Organ Donation and Transplantation in Sikh Perspective
lessons.summary: Analysis of the Sikh position on organ donation, grounded in seva and the theology of death as transition.

lessons.title: Pain, Suffering, and the Virtue of Acceptance
lessons.summary: Gurmat theology of suffering and its implications for pain management, chronic illness, and disability ethics.

lessons.title: End-of-Life Care: Sikh Perspectives on Palliative Medicine
lessons.summary: Sikh principles for palliative care, truth-telling at end of life, and the spiritual dimensions of the dying process.

lessons.title: Euthanasia and Assisted Dying: A Sikh Ethical Analysis
lessons.summary: Rigorous Sikh analysis of active euthanasia and assisted dying, distinguishing between killing and allowing to die.

lessons.title: Mental Health, Stigma, and the Sikh Community
lessons.summary: Critical engagement with mental health stigma in Sikh communities and construction of a Gurmat framework for mental health ethics.

lessons.title: Healthcare Justice and the Sikh Ethics of Access
lessons.summary: Sikh theological foundations for healthcare justice and universal access, grounded in seva and the equal dignity of all persons.

lessons.title: Sikh Healthcare Institutions: Historical and Contemporary
lessons.summary: Historical and contemporary analysis of Sikh healthcare institutions as expressions of Gurmat bioethical principles.

lessons.title: Synthesis: A Sikh Bioethical Framework — Works Cited
lessons.summary: Synthetic account of the four-pillar Sikh bioethical framework and future research agenda.

courses.title: Environmental Ethics in Sikh Thought: An Advanced Study
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh ecology; contemporary environmental philosophy
courses.summary: This graduate seminar investigates the ecological dimensions of Sikh theology and ethics, situating Gurmat within the global conversation on environmental philosophy and religion and ecology. Drawing on primary texts from the SGGS, the seminar constructs a Sikh environmental ethics capable of engaging contemporary ecological crises including climate change, biodiversity loss, and resource depletion. The course examines both the theoretical foundations and practical expressions of Sikh ecological commitment.
outcomes: Identify and analyze the ecological theology embedded in the SGGS, including the doctrine of divine immanence in creation
Critically compare Sikh ecological thought with deep ecology, ecofeminism, and indigenous environmental philosophies
Evaluate the concept of stewardship versus dominion as competing theological framings of human responsibility for creation
Construct original Sikh arguments on climate ethics, biodiversity conservation, and environmental justice
Assess the practical expressions of Sikh environmental ethics in historical and contemporary community practices
references: Chapple, Christopher Key, and Mary Evelyn Tucker, eds. Hinduism and Ecology (Harvard University Press, 2000)
Gottlieb, Roger S., ed. The Oxford Handbook of Religion and Ecology (Oxford University Press, 2006)

lessons.title: Introduction: Religion, Ecology, and Gurmat — Framing the Inquiry
lessons.summary: Framing the inquiry into Sikh environmental ethics, establishing methodological principles and situating Gurmat within the religion-and-ecology conversation.

lessons.title: The Ecological Theology of the SGGS: Divine Immanence in Creation
lessons.summary: Examination of the SGGS's doctrine of divine immanence in creation and its ecological implications.

lessons.title: Pavan, Pani, Vasudha: The Sacred Elements in Gurmat
lessons.summary: Analysis of the SGGS's honoring of air, water, and earth as sacred, and the ecological ethics this grounds.

lessons.title: Haumai and the Roots of Environmental Destruction
lessons.summary: Gurmat psychological analysis of the ego-roots of environmental destruction, including greed, attachment, and the logic of domination.

lessons.title: Santokh as Ecological Virtue: The Ethics of Sufficiency
lessons.summary: Analysis of contentment as the cardinal ecological virtue opposing the consumerism driving ecological crisis.

lessons.title: Gurmat and Deep Ecology: Convergences and Divergences
lessons.summary: Comparative analysis of Gurmat ecological theology and Naess's deep ecology, identifying substantive convergences and important divergences.

lessons.title: Ecofeminism and Gurmat: Nature, Gender, and the Divine
lessons.summary: Engagement with ecofeminist environmental philosophy from a Gurmat perspective, connecting the critique of domination with Sikh egalitarian theology.

lessons.title: Stewardship vs. Dominion: Framing Human Responsibility
lessons.summary: Analysis of the stewardship vs. dominion debate and Gurmat's participatory alternative to both frames.

lessons.title: Climate Ethics and the Sikh Framework
lessons.summary: Application of Gurmat principles to climate change ethics, including intergenerational justice and global climate justice.

lessons.title: Biodiversity, Species, and the Value of Natural Diversity
lessons.summary: Sikh theological grounding for biodiversity conservation and the moral urgency of the current extinction crisis.

lessons.title: Environmental Justice and the Sikh Community
lessons.summary: Analysis of environmental justice from a Gurmat perspective, with attention to Punjab's ecological crisis and structural dimensions of environmental harm.

lessons.title: Synthesis: A Gurmat Environmental Ethics — Works Cited
lessons.summary: Synthetic account of the Gurmat environmental ethics developed in the seminar and its distinctive contributions to global environmental philosophy.

courses.title: Sikh Military Ethics: Dharam Yudh and Just War Theory
courses.source: SGGS; Zafarnama; Michael Walzer, Just and Unjust Wars (1977)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the Sikh tradition's sophisticated doctrine of righteous warfare (Dharam Yudh) and situates it within the global conversation on just war theory. Drawing on the SGGS, Guru Gobind Singh Ji's Zafarnama, and the Dasam Granth, alongside Walzer, Grotius, and contemporary military ethics, the seminar constructs a rigorous account of when and how violence may be morally justified in Sikh thought. The course engages historical cases from Sikh military history and contemporary applications to terrorism, humanitarian intervention, and civil disobedience.
outcomes: Analyze the theological foundations of Dharam Yudh in the Sikh tradition, distinguishing it from both pacifism and realism
Compare the Sikh criteria for justified warfare with the classical just war criteria of jus ad bellum and jus in bello
Critically evaluate the Zafarnama as a primary source for Sikh military ethics
Assess contemporary applications of Sikh military ethics to terrorism, humanitarian intervention, and asymmetric warfare
Construct original arguments about the relationship between the Khalsa martial identity and Gurmat ethical principles

lessons.title: Jus ad Bellum in Sikh Thought: Criteria for Just Resort to War

lessons.title: Martyrdom (Shaheedi) in Sikh Thought: Theology and Ethics
lessons.summary: Theological and ethical analysis of Sikh martyrdom and its role in sustaining Dharam Yudh principles.

lessons.title: Sikh Military History as Ethical Laboratory
lessons.summary: Application of Dharam Yudh principles to historical cases from Sikh military history.

lessons.title: Terrorism, Asymmetric Warfare, and Sikh Criteria
lessons.summary: Application of Dharam Yudh principles to contemporary asymmetric warfare and terrorism.

lessons.title: Humanitarian Intervention and the Khalsa Obligation
lessons.summary: Analysis of humanitarian intervention through the lens of Dharam Yudh and comparison with R2P doctrine.

courses.title: Dasvandh as Spiritual-Financial Practice: A Graduate Study
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh Rahit Maryada; contemporary philanthropy theory
courses.summary: This graduate seminar investigates the Sikh practice of Dasvandh — the commitment of one-tenth of one's income to the community — as a theological, ethical, and economic institution. The course situates Dasvandh within the broader history of religious tithing, the economics of voluntary giving, and contemporary philanthropy theory, while examining its distinctive Gurmat grounding. Students engage primary Sikh sources, the Sikh Rahit Maryada, and leading scholarship in religious economics and philanthropy.
outcomes: Analyze the theological grounding of Dasvandh in Gurmat theology, distinguishing it from mere charitable giving
Compare Dasvandh with analogous institutions (Christian tithing, Islamic Zakat, Jewish tzedakah) in comparative religious economics
Evaluate the economic and institutional dimensions of Dasvandh in historical and contemporary Sikh communities
Construct original arguments about Dasvandh's relevance to contemporary philanthropy theory and practice
Assess the challenges of Dasvandh observance in diaspora contexts and propose frameworks for institutional renewal

lessons.title: Institutional Design for Dasvandh: Gurdwara Finance
lessons.summary: Analysis of Gurdwara financial governance principles for sustaining Dasvandh practice in diaspora contexts.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Dasvandh as Spiritual-Financial Practice — Works Cited

courses.title: Sikh Philanthropic Finance and Institutional Giving
courses.source: Sikh institutional history; SGPC archives; philanthropy scholarship
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines Sikh philanthropic finance as a multi-layered phenomenon: theologically grounded in Gurmat values, historically institutionalized through the Gurdwara system and the SGPC, and practically expressed through the activities of diaspora communities and humanitarian organizations. Students analyze primary Sikh sources, historical institutional data, and contemporary philanthropy scholarship to construct a rigorous account of Sikh institutional giving.

courses.title: Wealth, Stewardship, and Sikh Values: An Advanced Seminar
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh economic ethics; stewardship theory
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the Sikh theological and ethical framework for wealth stewardship, integrating Gurmat principles with contemporary economic theory, behavioral economics, and applied finance ethics. Drawing on the SGGS and the three-pillar framework of Sikh ethical life, students construct a rigorous account of how wealth should be earned, managed, deployed, and shared according to Gurmat values. The course addresses wealth inequality, investment ethics, and estate planning as contemporary applications.
outcomes: Articulate the Gurmat theological anthropology of stewardship and its implications for wealth management
Apply the three pillars (Naam Japna, Kirat Karni, Vand Chhakna) to contemporary household financial decisions
Evaluate the compatibility of specific financial practices with Gurmat stewardship principles
Construct original arguments about the relationship between spiritual practice and financial behavior in Gurmat
Assess the Gurmat response to wealth inequality, investment ethics, and intergenerational wealth transfer

Apply the Gurmat concepts of Kirat Karni, Sach, Santokh, and Sarbat da Bhala to specific contemporary market practices

Construct original arguments about the relationship between consumer culture and the Gurmat critique of Maya
Develop a distinctively Sikh economic ethics that goes beyond both capitalism and socialism

courses.title: Punjab Agricultural Traditions: History, Practice, and Ecology
courses.source: Historical and ecological scholarship on Punjab agriculture; SGGS
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the deep history of Punjab's agricultural traditions from antiquity through the present, tracing the interplay between indigenous ecological knowledge, Sikh religious values, colonial land policy, and the Green Revolution. Students engage primary texts, oral traditions, and scholarly literature to develop a nuanced understanding of agricultural systems as living cultures shaped by cosmology, community, and political economy.
outcomes: Analyze Punjab's agricultural history from pre-colonial ecological practices through the contemporary crisis of soil degradation and farmer debt
Articulate the Sikh Gurus' theological and practical contributions to agricultural ethics and land stewardship
Evaluate the colonial land settlement policies that transformed Punjab's agrarian social structure
Critically assess the Green Revolution's technological and socio-ecological legacy in Punjab
Develop evidence-based proposals for ecologically sustainable agricultural futures grounded in Gurmat values

courses.title: Food Systems, Langar, and Sustainable Agriculture
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh studies; food systems scholarship
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the Sikh institution of ਲੰਗਰ — the free community kitchen — as a model for reimagining food systems from the ground up. Drawing on Sikh theology, food systems theory, agroecology, and food justice scholarship, students analyze ਲੰਗਰ as a living counter-system that embodies the values of dignity, equality, and ecological responsibility that contemporary food justice movements are struggling to articulate. The course develops practical frameworks for applying ਲੰਗਰ principles to food system transformation at scales from the household to the global.

Apply food systems theory to the analysis of ਲੰਗਰ as an alternative food institution
Evaluate the potential of ਲੰਗਰ principles for addressing food insecurity, inequality, and ecological degradation in contemporary food systems
Critically assess the ecological dimensions of ਲੰਗਰ practice and identify pathways to greater ecological sustainability
Develop evidence-based food system transformation proposals grounded in Gurmat values and food systems science

courses.title: Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar's Health Pothi: A Graduate Deep Study
courses.source: Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar, Health Pothi (complete text study)
courses.summary: This graduate seminar conducts a systematic, in-depth scholarly study of Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar's Health Pothi, examining its textual structure, therapeutic content, historical context, and relationship to the Sikh tradition's understanding of bodily health as the foundation for spiritual practice. Students engage the text critically, applying pharmacological, ethnobotanical, and theological analytical frameworks to its content. The course develops students' capacity for rigorous engagement with traditional Sikh health literature.

courses.title: Evidence-Based Medicine and Gurmat: An Advanced Critical Seminar
courses.source: Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar, Health Pothi; RCT methodology; SGGS
courses.summary: This advanced seminar examines the epistemological foundations and methodological principles of evidence-based medicine (EBM) in dialogue with the Sikh tradition's approach to knowledge, health, and healing. Students critically evaluate the hierarchy of evidence, randomized controlled trial methodology, and systematic review frameworks while engaging the Health Pothi of Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar as a case study in traditional health knowledge evaluation. The course develops rigorous capacity for integrating traditional health knowledge with contemporary evidence standards.

Apply systematic review and meta-analysis methodologies to the evaluation of traditional health claims
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of RCT methodology for studying complex traditional medicine interventions

Produce original scholarly work evaluating specific Health Pothi recommendations against contemporary evidence

Students analyze Sikh positions on bodily integrity, end-of-life care, reproductive ethics, organ donation, and healthcare justice, developing the capacity to articulate coherent Sikh ethical positions on contested medical questions.

courses.title: Chronic Disease, Healing, and Gurmat Frameworks

courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines integrative health — the whole-person approach that combines the best of conventional medicine with evidence-based traditional and complementary approaches — through the lens of the Sikh mind-body framework. Drawing on the Health Pothi of Bhagat Jaswant Singh Daudar and the Guru Granth Sahib's understanding of the relationship between mind, body, and spirit, students develop a sophisticated framework for integrative wellness that is both scientifically rigorous and theologically grounded. The course addresses stress, sleep, nutrition, movement, contemplative practice, and social connection as the pillars of integrative Sikh wellness.
