Wittgenstein, Ludwig. Philosophical Investigations. Translated by G. E. M. Anscombe. Oxford: Blackwell, 1953.

lessons.title: Introduction: Why Dialogue? Gurmat in the Contemporary Philosophical Arena
lessons.summary: Establishes the rationale, risks, and method of engaging Gurmat philosophy in critical dialogue with contemporary Western philosophy.

lessons.title: Mandair's Postcolonial Framework: Critique and Evaluation
lessons.summary: Provides a systematic evaluation of Mandair's postcolonial reading of Sikh philosophy, assessing both its contributions and its limitations for Gurmat self-understanding.

lessons.title: Gurmat and Phenomenology: Experiencing the Divine
lessons.summary: Applies phenomenological methods to the analysis of Sikh religious experience, examining how ਨਾਮ practice, ਕੀਰਤਨ, and ਸੰਗਤ constitute distinctive modes of divine-human encounter.

lessons.title: Analytic Philosophy of Religion: Gurmat Epistemology in Dialogue
lessons.summary: Engages analytic philosophy of religion—including Plantinga's reformed epistemology and Alston's religious experience—with Gurmat's epistemological commitments.

lessons.title: Gurmat and Existentialism: ਹਉਮੈ, Authenticity, and Freedom
lessons.summary: Conducts a systematic engagement between Gurmat's account of ਹਉਮੈ and the existentialist tradition's analyses of authenticity, freedom, and bad faith.

lessons.title: Feminist Philosophy and Gurmat: Gender, Power, and Liberation
lessons.summary: Engages Gurmat theology and practice with feminist philosophy, examining both the tradition's egalitarian resources and the persistent gender inequities in Sikh community life.

lessons.title: Gurmat Ethics in Contemporary Moral Philosophy
lessons.summary: Engages Gurmat's ethical framework with contemporary moral philosophy, analyzing how Gurmat's account of ਸੇਵਾ, ਸੱਚ, and ਧਰਮ relates to virtue ethics, deontology, and care ethics.

lessons.title: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ and Political Philosophy
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat concept of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ (temporal-spiritual sovereignty) in dialogue with contemporary political philosophy, analyzing its implications for understanding religion and political authority.

lessons.title: ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and Political Theory: Sovereignty and Community
lessons.summary: Examines the concept of ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ as a political-theological community in dialogue with contemporary theories of sovereignty, community, and political identity.

lessons.title: Gurmat and Environmental Philosophy
lessons.summary: Examines Gurmat's theological resources for environmental philosophy, analyzing how the tradition's account of creation, ਹੁਕਮ, and ਸੇਵਾ can ground an environmental ethics.

lessons.title: Gurmat and Philosophy of Mind
lessons.summary: Examines Gurmat's account of consciousness, the mind-body relationship, and spiritual experience in dialogue with contemporary philosophy of mind.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Gurmat's Contribution to Contemporary Philosophy
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's comparative analyses into a comprehensive account of Gurmat's distinctive and important contributions to contemporary philosophical debate.

courses.title: Advanced Sikh Constitutional Theory and Governance
courses.source: Kapur Singh, Parasaraprasna (1989); Sikh political thought
courses.summary: This graduate seminar conducts a rigorous investigation of Sikh constitutional theory and the principles of governance embedded in Gurmat political philosophy. Drawing on Kapur Singh's Parasaraprasna, the concept of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ, and classical constitutional theory, students analyze the Sikh tradition's distinctive account of authority, law, and political community.
outcomes: Critically analyze Kapur Singh's constitutional theory in Parasaraprasna as a foundational text of Sikh political philosophy
Examine the philosophical foundations of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ as a constitutional principle integrating spiritual and temporal authority
Evaluate the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ Panth's governance structures—ਗੁਰਮਤਾ, ਸਰਬਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ—as constitutional mechanisms
Assess the relationship between Gurmat political philosophy and modern democratic constitutional theory
Develop original analysis of Sikh constitutional principles applicable to contemporary Sikh institutional governance

lessons.title: Introduction: Constitutional Theory and Gurmat Political Philosophy
lessons.summary: Establishes the theoretical foundations of the seminar, introducing Sikh constitutional theory as a distinctive tradition worthy of systematic philosophical analysis.

lessons.title: Kapur Singh's Parasaraprasna: A Critical Analysis
lessons.summary: Provides a systematic critical analysis of Kapur Singh's Parasaraprasna as the foundational text of modern Sikh constitutional theory.

lessons.title: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ as Constitutional Principle
lessons.summary: Provides a detailed philosophical analysis of ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ as the central constitutional principle of Sikh political theory.

lessons.title: The ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ Panth: Sovereignty and Political Community
lessons.summary: Examines the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ Panth as a distinctive form of political community, analyzing the grounds of its sovereignty and its constitutional character.

lessons.title: ਗੁਰਮਤਾ and ਸਰਬਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ: Constitutional Mechanisms
lessons.summary: Examines the ਗੁਰਮਤਾ and ਸਰਬਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ as the primary constitutional mechanisms through which the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ exercises collective sovereignty.

lessons.title: ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਿਆਦਾ as Constitutional Law
lessons.summary: Examines the Sikh Rehat Maryada as a constitutional document, analyzing its scope, authority, and development.

lessons.title: SGPC: Institution, Authority, and Legitimacy
lessons.summary: Critically examines the SGPC as a Sikh constitutional institution, analyzing the grounds of its authority and the critiques of its legitimacy.

lessons.title: Gurmat Constitutional Theory and Liberal Democratic Theory
lessons.summary: Conducts a systematic comparison between Sikh constitutional theory and Rawlsian liberal democratic theory, identifying convergences and fundamental divergences.

lessons.title: Sikh Constitutionalism and Human Rights
lessons.summary: Examines the relationship between Sikh constitutional principles and the international human rights framework, analyzing areas of convergence and tension.

lessons.title: The Question of Sikh Sovereignty: Theoretical Dimensions
lessons.summary: Examines the theoretical dimensions of Sikh sovereignty claims, analyzing the philosophical foundations of ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ sovereignty in relation to modern state sovereignty.

lessons.title: Governance of Diaspora Sikh Institutions
lessons.summary: Examines the governance challenges of diaspora Sikh institutions—Gurdwara committees, charitable organizations, educational institutions—through the lens of Sikh constitutional principles.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Principles of Sikh Constitutional Governance
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's analyses into a coherent statement of the principles of Sikh constitutional governance applicable to contemporary Sikh institutional life.

courses.title: Sikh Nationalism, Sovereignty, and the Modern State
courses.source: Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries (1994); Sikh political history
courses.summary: This graduate seminar critically analyzes the historical development and contemporary dimensions of Sikh nationalism, examining the tension between the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ Panth's sovereignty claims and the modern nation-state system. Drawing on Oberoi, Tatla, and political theory, students investigate how Sikh political identity has been constructed, contested, and mobilized.
outcomes: Critically analyze Harjot Oberoi's constructivist account of Sikh religious boundaries and its implications for understanding Sikh political identity
Evaluate competing theories of Sikh nationalism—primordialist, constructivist, and instrumentalist—using historical evidence
Examine the 1984 crisis as a pivotal moment in the development of contemporary Sikh political consciousness
Assess the theoretical relationship between ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ sovereignty and modern nation-state sovereignty
Analyze diaspora Sikh political mobilization and its implications for the concept of transnational religious nationalism

lessons.title: Oberoi's Constructivist Account: Critical Analysis
lessons.summary: Provides a systematic critical analysis of Harjot Oberoi's The Construction of Religious Boundaries, evaluating both its scholarly contributions and its contested implications.

lessons.title: The Formation of Sikh Political Identity: 19th–20th Century
lessons.summary: Examines the political dimensions of the Singh Sabha movement and the early 20th century Akali movement as formative moments in modern Sikh political identity.

lessons.title: Partition 1947: Loss, Displacement, and Political Consciousness
lessons.summary: Examines the 1947 Partition's impact on Sikh political consciousness, analyzing how the trauma of displacement shaped subsequent Sikh political demands.

lessons.title: Punjab Politics, 1947–1966: Autonomy and Reorganization
lessons.summary: Examines the complex politics of Punjab's reorganization on linguistic lines and the Akali Dal's campaigns for greater Sikh political autonomy in independent India.

lessons.title: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution: Aspirations and Interpretations
lessons.summary: Examines the Anandpur Sahib Resolution of 1973 as a pivotal document in modern Sikh political history, analyzing its demands and its contested interpretations.

lessons.title: 1984: Operation Bluestar, Genocide, and Political Transformation
lessons.summary: Examines the 1984 events as a pivotal moment in Sikh political history, analyzing Operation Bluestar, the November pogroms, and their lasting impact on Sikh political consciousness.

lessons.title: The Khalistan Movement: History, Analysis, and Legacy
lessons.summary: Provides a historically accurate and analytically rigorous examination of the Khalistan movement, assessing its origins, its trajectory, and its contemporary legacy.

lessons.title: Theories of Sikh Nationalism: Primordialism, Constructivism, Instrumentalism
lessons.summary: Systematically evaluates the major theoretical frameworks for analyzing Sikh nationalism, assessing their explanatory adequacy against the historical evidence.

lessons.title: Diaspora Sikh Political Mobilization
lessons.summary: Examines the political mobilization of Sikh diaspora communities in the UK, Canada, and the USA, analyzing its forms, its impact, and its relationship to Punjab politics.

lessons.title: Contemporary Sikh Political Landscape: Punjab and Global ਪੰਥ
lessons.summary: Examines the contemporary Sikh political landscape in Punjab and the diaspora, analyzing current dynamics and future trajectories.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Sikh Nationalism and the Future of Sikh Sovereignty
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the seminar's historical and theoretical analyses into an assessment of the future prospects and challenges of Sikh sovereignty in the contemporary world.

courses.title: Comparative Political Theory: Sikh and Global Perspectives
courses.source: SGGS; comparative political theory; Sikh political philosophy
courses.summary: This graduate seminar uses comparative political theory methodology to situate Gurmat political philosophy in dialogue with major traditions of global political thought—Islamic, Buddhist, Confucian, and Western liberal. Students develop analytical frameworks for identifying genuine commonalities and important differences, and argue for Gurmat's distinctive contributions to global political theory.
outcomes: Apply comparative political theory methodology to analyze Gurmat political philosophy in its global context
Conduct rigorous comparative analyses between Gurmat and Islamic, Buddhist, Confucian, and Western liberal political traditions
Identify the distinctive features of Gurmat political philosophy that constitute original contributions to global political theory
Critically evaluate the methodological challenges of comparative political theory across non-Western traditions
Develop original comparative arguments that illuminate both Gurmat political philosophy and the traditions with which it is compared

lessons.title: Introduction: Comparative Political Theory — Method and Stakes

lessons.title: Gurmat Political Philosophy: Core Concepts for Comparison
lessons.summary: Provides a systematic overview of Gurmat's core political concepts, preparing them for comparative analysis in subsequent lessons.

lessons.title: Gurmat and Islamic Political Theory: Authority, Sovereignty, and ਧਰਮ/Shari'a
lessons.summary: Conducts a systematic comparative analysis between Gurmat and Islamic political theory, examining both significant convergences and important divergences.

courses.title: Guru Gobind Singh's Political Vision and Legacy
courses.source: Kavi Santokh Singh, Suraj Prakash; Gurbilas Patshahi 10; Zafarnama
courses.summary: This course examines the political theology of Guru Gobind Singh, situating his thought within seventeenth-century Mughal imperial crisis and the emergent Sikh sovereign imaginary. Drawing on the Zafarnama, Gurbilas Patshahi 10, and the Suraj Prakash, students analyze how sovereignty, justice, and sacred war were theorized in Guru Gobind Singh's court. The course concludes with long-run assessments of his legacy in Sikh constitutionalism and diaspora political thought.
outcomes: Critically analyze the political theology embedded in the Zafarnama and situate it within Mughal political discourse.
Evaluate competing historiographical interpretations of Guru Gobind Singh's sovereignty claims.
Apply concepts of sacred kingship, martyrdom, and dharmic war to the events of 1699–1708.
Trace the genealogy of Khalsa sovereignty from Guru Gobind Singh's vision to modern Sikh political thought.
Construct original arguments about the relationship between spiritual authority and temporal power in Sikh tradition.

courses.title: Advanced Lexicography: Mahan Kosh and Sikh Dictionary Traditions

Students examine the methodological, theological, and political dimensions of Sikh dictionary-making from early manuscript glossaries through the Singh Sabha reform era. Situate Sikh ethics within comparative frameworks of contemporary ethical theory.

courses.title: Sikh Diaspora Social Theory: Identity, Community, and Belonging
courses.source: Sikh diaspora scholarship; Stuart Hall, Cultural Identity and Diaspora; SGGS
courses.summary: This graduate seminar develops a rigorous social theory of the Sikh diaspora, engaging transnationalism, cultural identity theory, and ethnoreligious sociology through case studies of British, North American, East African, and Australasian Sikh communities. Students develop tools for analyzing identity formation, institutional development, and normative negotiation in diaspora contexts.
outcomes: Apply Stuart Hall's cultural identity theory and transnationalism frameworks to specific Sikh diaspora communities
Analyze the sociology of the gurdwara as a multifunctional social institution across diaspora contexts
Engage feminist, race-critical, and generational dimensions of Sikh diaspora experience with scholarly depth
Evaluate the role of digital media in transforming diaspora community formation and normative authority
Contribute to Sikh diaspora social theory with original analysis of primary and secondary sources
references: Brah, Avtar. Cartographies of Diaspora. Routledge (1996)
Dusenbery, Verne A. A Sikh Diaspora? In Nation and Migration, University of Pennsylvania Press (1995)

lessons.title: Second and Third Generation Identity Negotiations

lessons.title: Gender and Diaspora: Sikh Women's Lives Across Borders

lessons.title: Religion and Diaspora: The Gurdwara as Social Institution

lessons.title: Kirpan, Turban, and the Politics of Sikh Visibility
lessons.summary: Examines the politics of Sikh visible identity — particularly the kirpan and dastar — in diaspora legal and political contexts.

lessons.title: Digital Diasporas: Online Sikh Community and Identity

courses.title: Sikh Institutions and Power: SGPC, Takhts, and Governance
courses.source: SGPC institutional history; Harjot Oberoi; Sikh political sociology
courses.summary: This graduate seminar analyzes the sociology of Sikh institutional power, examining the historical development and contemporary functioning of the SGPC, the five Takhts, and the complex relationships among religious authority, political power, and community governance. Students engage critically with institutional structure, caste and gender inequalities, diaspora governance, and reform possibilities grounded in Gurmat principles.
outcomes: Apply Weber, Bourdieu, and sociology of religion frameworks to the analysis of Sikh institutional power
Analyze the historical formation, constitutional structure, and normative authority of the SGPC and Akal Takht
Critically evaluate the relationship between the Akali Dal and SGPC and its implications for Sikh religious governance
Assess caste and gender dimensions of institutional power within the Panth with scholarly rigor
Develop reform proposals grounded in both sociological analysis and Gurmat theological principles
references: Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries. University of Chicago Press (1994)

lessons.title: Singh Sabha Movement and Institutional Reform

lessons.title: Gurdwara Act 1925 and the Institutionalization of Sikh Authority

lessons.title: Caste, Class, and Institutional Power within the Panth

lessons.title: Gender and Institutional Power: Women in Sikh Governance
lessons.summary: Examines the gendered dimensions of Sikh institutional power, analyzing women's exclusion from and engagement with Sikh governance structures.

lessons.title: Diaspora Institutions and the Governance Gap
lessons.summary: Examines the institutional development of diaspora Sikh communities and the governance gap between diaspora practice and Punjab institutional authority.

lessons.title: Synthesis: Reforming Sikh Institutions for the Twenty-First Century
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the course's analysis of Sikh institutional power and articulates a framework for institution reform grounded in Gurmat principles.

courses.title: Community Building Theory and Gurmat: An Advanced Study
courses.source: SGGS; community development theory; Sikh sangat tradition
courses.summary: This graduate seminar applies sociological theories of community formation — social capital, Tönnies, Durkheim, Weber — to the Sikh concept of ਸੰਗਤ, analyzing how Gurmat principles both intersect with and exceed the categories of secular community theory. Students examine Sikh institutional forms including ਲੰਗਰ, ਸੇਵਾ, and ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ governance through multiple sociological lenses. The course culminates in the development of a preliminary Gurmat community development theory.
outcomes: Critically apply major sociological theories of community (Tönnies, Durkheim, Putnam) to Sikh ਸੰਗਤ
Analyze the theological foundations and institutional expressions of ਲੰਗਰ and ਸੇਵਾ
Examine gender, power, and caste dynamics within Sikh community institutions
Evaluate inter-generational transmission of Sikh community norms in diaspora contexts
Articulate the outlines of a Gurmat community development theory grounded in both sociological and theological analysis

lessons.summary: Analyzes gender dynamics in Sikh community institutions, examining the gap between theological equality and institutional practice.

lessons.title: Inter-generational Transmission of Community Norms
lessons.summary: Examines how Sikh community values and practices are transmitted across generations in diaspora contexts.

lessons.title: Conflict Resolution within ਪੰਥ: Historical and Contemporary Models

lessons.title: Digital Communities and ਸੰਗਤ in the Twenty-First Century
lessons.summary: Examines how digital technologies are reshaping Sikh community formation and the theological questions raised by virtual ਸੰਗਤ.

lessons.title: Community Development Praxis: Applying ਗੁਰਮਤਿ Principles
lessons.summary: Examines the practical application of Gurmat principles to community development initiatives in Sikh contexts.

lessons.title: Toward a Gurmat Community Development Theory: Synthesis and Critique

courses.title: Gender Theory and Sikh Studies: Advanced Critical Analysis
courses.source: Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Feminine Principle in the Sikh Vision (1993); gender theory
courses.summary: This graduate seminar applies feminist and gender theory — including Butler's performativity, Crenshaw's intersectionality, and postcolonial critique — to the analysis of Sikh gender dynamics, from the feminist theology of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ to the colonial construction of Sikh femininity in the Singh Sabha movement. Students engage critically with foundational scholarship by Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh and Doris Jakobsh and develop the outlines of a feminist Gurmat critique. The course addresses contemporary debates about women's religious authority, same-sex marriage, and LGBTQ+ inclusion in Sikh communities.
outcomes: Apply feminist and gender theoretical frameworks to the analysis of Sikh texts and institutions
Critically evaluate the contributions of Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh and Doris Jakobsh to Sikh gender studies
Analyze how colonial encounter shaped Sikh gender norms in the Singh Sabha period
Apply intersectionality theory to examine compound effects of caste and gender in Sikh community life
Articulate the elements of a feminist Gurmat critique grounded in the tradition's own theological resources

lessons.summary: Analyzes the theological egalitarianism of the Anand Karaj marriage ceremony and debates about its contemporary application.

lessons.summary: Applies intersectionality theory to analyze the compounding effects of caste and gender in Sikh community life.

lessons.title: Queer Theory and Sikh Studies: Emerging Conversations

lessons.summary: Advanced analysis of the theological language of SGGS for feminist and gender-theoretical implications.

lessons.title: Gender, Diaspora, and the Negotiation of Sikh Womanhood

courses.title: Advanced Naam Simran: Theory, Practice, and Mystical States
courses.source: SGGS; Prof. Sahib Singh exegesis; contemplative theology
courses.summary: This advanced graduate seminar examines ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ — the contemplative practice of remembering the Divine Name — from multiple scholarly angles: theological metaphysics, classical exegesis (Prof. Sahib Singh), phenomenology of mystical states, comparative contemplative studies, and contemporary psychology of meditation. Students develop a rigorous, academically grounded understanding of the theory, practice, and experiential dimensions of the Sikh contemplative path. The course culminates in an examination of the integration of ਸਿਮਰਨ into the totality of Sikh life and its relationship to the goal of ਮੁਕਤੀ.
outcomes: Articulate the metaphysical status of ਨਾਮ in Gurmat theology with precision
Critically engage Prof. Sahib Singh's exegetical approach to ਸਿਮਰਨ passages in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ
Analyze the stages of ਸਿਮਰਨ and the phenomenological features of advanced contemplative states
Evaluate the relationship between ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ (grace) and human effort in the practice of ਸਿਮਰਨ
Apply comparative contemplative studies frameworks to the Sikh contemplative tradition
references: Benson, Herbert. The Relaxation Response. William Morrow, 1975.

lessons.summary: Maps the stages of ਸਿਮਰਨ practice as described in Gurbani and the contemplative tradition.

lessons.summary: Examines the bodily dimensions of ਸਿਮਰਨ practice and its relationship to breath and physiological processes.

courses.title: Mystical Experience in the Sikh Tradition: A Graduate Study
courses.source: SGGS; William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902); Sikh mysticism
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines mystical experience in the Sikh tradition through the frameworks of William James, Rudolf Otto, and comparative mysticism scholarship, while attending to the specific character of Sikh mystical literature in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ. Students engage the perennialist/constructivist debate, analyze the theology of union and distinction in Gurmat, and examine the bhagat poetry as mystical literature. The course culminates in a synthetic account of Sikh mysticism's distinctive contribution to the global history of religious experience.
outcomes: Apply James's four marks of mystical experience to specific passages of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ
Critically evaluate the perennialist/constructivist debate and its implications for Sikh mystical studies
Analyze the Gurmat theology of mystical union and its distinction from both monism and theistic dualism
Examine the bhagat poetry in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ as a resource for comparative mystical literature
Articulate the distinctive contribution of Sikh mysticism to global comparative religion
references: James, William. The Varieties of Religious Experience. Longmans, Green and Co., 1902.

courses.title: The Sikh Theology of Liberation: Mukti, Naam, and Union
courses.source: SGGS; Prof. Sahib Singh, Shabadarth SGGS; Sikh liberation theology
courses.summary: This graduate seminar develops a systematic account of Sikh liberation theology, examining the theological meaning of ਮੁਕਤੀ, the role of ਨਾਮ as the vehicle of liberation, the function of the Guru's grace, and the ideal of the ਜੀਵਨਮੁਕਤ — the one liberated while alive. Drawing on Prof. Sahib Singh's exegesis and comparative liberation theologies, students articulate the distinctive contribution of Gurmat to the global conversation about ultimate liberation. The course addresses ontological, soteriological, ethical, communal, and eschatological dimensions.
outcomes: Articulate the semantic range and theological precision of ਮੁਕਤੀ in SGGS
Analyze ਹਉਮੈ as the theological diagnosis of the human predicament
Examine the roles of ਨਾਮ and ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ in the liberation process
Describe the ideal of ਜੀਵਨਮੁਕਤ and its social-ethical implications
Compare Sikh liberation theology with Hindu, Buddhist, and Latin American liberation theologies

courses.title: Contemplative Practice in Sikhi: Graduate Seminar
courses.source: SGGS; contemplative studies; Thomas Merton; Sikh nitnem
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines Sikh contemplative practice — including ਨਿਤਨੇਮ, ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਵੇਲਾ, ਕੀਰਤਨ, ਅਖੰਡ ਪਾਠ, and ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ — through the frameworks of comparative contemplative studies, neuroscience, and Gurmat theology. Drawing on Thomas Merton's comparative contemplative theology and the tradition's own exegetical resources, students develop a comprehensive understanding of how Sikh contemplative practice is structured, practiced, and integrated with active life. The course addresses bodily dimensions, community context, contemporary adaptations, and the integration imperative.

Apply comparative contemplative frameworks (Merton, James, neuroscience) to Sikh practice
Examine the communal dimensions of Sikh contemplative practice through the concept of ਸੰਗਤ
Critically evaluate contemporary adaptations of Sikh contemplative practice
Articulate the integration of contemplative practice and active worldly engagement in the Sikh householder ideal

courses.title: Spiritual Direction in the Sikh Tradition: Theory and Practice
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh pastoral tradition; spiritual direction literature
courses.summary: This graduate seminar develops a systematic Sikh theology of spiritual direction, examining the Guru-ਸਿੱਖ relationship as paradigm, the role of ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ as living director, the ਸੰਤ tradition, and the ਸੰਗਤ as collective accompaniment. Drawing on contemporary spiritual direction literature (Barry, Connolly, Schneiders) and the resources of ਗੁਰਮਤਿ, students develop both a theological framework and practical competencies for Sikh pastoral care. The course addresses discernment, suffering, mental health boundaries, and cross-cultural direction.

Identify the core competencies for formation as a Sikh spiritual director

courses.title: Historical Development of Sikh Theological Thought
courses.source: Kavi Santokh Singh, Suraj Prakash; Sikh theological history
courses.summary: This graduate seminar traces the historical development of Sikh theological thought from Guru Nanak's foundational theology through the major doctrinal developments of the ten Gurus, the eighteenth-century contestation, the Suraj Prakash tradition of Kavi Santokh Singh, the Singh Sabha modernization, and contemporary theological engagements. Students analyze how core theological commitments — ਨਾਮ, ਗੁਰੂ, ਸੰਗਤ, ਮੁਕਤੀ — have been progressively elaborated in response to historical challenges while maintaining coherent theological continuity.

courses.title: Sikh Eschatology: Death, Afterlife, and Liberation
courses.source: SGGS; Prof. Sahib Singh exegesis; Sikh afterlife theology
courses.summary: This graduate seminar develops a systematic account of Sikh eschatological theology, examining the doctrines of ਆਵਾਗਉਣ (rebirth), ਕਰਮ, ਸੱਚ ਖੰਡ (the realm of truth), ਜੀਵਨਮੁਕਤ (liberation while living), and the theology of death and dying. Drawing on Prof. Sahib Singh's exegesis and comparative eschatological frameworks, students analyze how the tradition's account of ultimate human destiny shapes ethics, contemplative practice, and community life. The course addresses contemporary challenges to Sikh eschatological theology from secular and scientific perspectives.
outcomes: Articulate the structure of Sikh eschatological theology including ਆਵਾਗਉਣ, ਕਰਮ, and ਮੁਕਤੀ
Analyze the theological significance of ਸੱਚ ਖੰਡ as the ultimate eschatological destination
Examine the paradox of the ਜੀਵਨਮੁਕਤ as realized eschatology
Apply Prof. Sahib Singh's exegetical method to key eschatological passages
Compare Sikh eschatological theology with Hindu, Islamic, and Christian counterparts

courses.source: Prof. Sahib Singh, Shabadarth Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (1962-1964); hermeneutics theory
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the theory and practice of interpreting the Sikh sacred scripture, situating classical Sikh exegetical methods within broader comparative hermeneutics. Students engage with Prof. Sahib Singh's grammatical-contextual method, the Fareedkot Tika tradition, Nihang oral commentary, and contemporary critical approaches. The course develops skills for independent scholarly commentary on Gurbani.

courses.title: Sikh Historiography: Methods, Sources, and Critical Analysis
courses.source: Kavi Santokh Singh, Suraj Prakash Granth (1843); Sikh historiography
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the production, methods, and critical analysis of Sikh historical writing from the earliest Janam Sakhis through the colonial encounter to the debates of postcolonial Sikh historiography. Students engage with primary historical sources — including the Suraj Prakash Granth, Sikh Rahitnamas, and colonial administrative records — while developing critical tools for evaluating historical claims in the Sikh tradition.
outcomes: Evaluate the historiographical methods and limitations of major Sikh historical genres including Janam Sakhis, Gurbilas literature, and Rahitnamas.
Apply modern historical-critical methods to primary Sikh historical sources.
Analyze the impact of colonial encounter on the construction of Sikh historical narratives.
Engage critically with the debates between W. H. McLeod and Sikh traditionalist historians.
Produce original historical research using primary Sikh sources with appropriate critical methodology.
references: Santokh Singh, Sri Gur Pratap Suraj Granth, ed. Vir Singh (Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1927–1935)
W. H. McLeod, Early Sikh Tradition: A Study of the Janam-Sakhis (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1980)

lessons.title: Bhai Gurdas and the Vars: Poetry as Historical Testimony
lessons.summary: Analyzes Bhai Gurdas's Vars as historically valuable eyewitness testimony in balladic form.

lessons.title: Colonial Historiography and the Sikh Past
lessons.summary: Examines the colonial archive and its role in shaping historical knowledge about the Sikh tradition.

lessons.title: The Singh Sabha and the Invention of Tradition

lessons.title: Postcolonial Sikh Historiography: Debates and Directions

lessons.title: Martyrdom and Historical Memory: Shahidi in Sikh Tradition

lessons.title: Toward a Critical Sikh Historical Method

courses.title: Sikh Political Philosophy: Sovereignty, Justice, and the Halemi Raj
courses.source: SGGS; Kapur Singh, Parasaraprasna; Sikh political thought
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the foundations of Sikh political philosophy through rigorous engagement with Gurbani, the doctrine of Miri-Piri, Kapur Singh's political theology, and contemporary debates about Sikh sovereignty. Students analyze the Gurmat vision of just governance, the theological grounding of political resistance, and the concept of the Halemi Raj as a model for a just social order.
outcomes: Analyze the theological foundations of Sikh political thought in Gurbani and the Miri-Piri doctrine.
Evaluate Kapur Singh's political philosophy in Parasaraprasna against Western political theory.
Critically examine the concept of Sikh sovereignty and its relationship to the Khalsa polity.
Apply Gurmat political philosophy to contemporary debates about justice, rights, and governance.
Produce original political-theological analysis connecting Sikh doctrines to political theory.

lessons.title: Contemporary Sikh Political Philosophy: Sovereignty, Diaspora, and Rights

lessons.title: Toward a Gurmat Political Philosophy for the Twenty-First Century
lessons.summary: Synthesizes course materials toward a Gurmat political philosophy addressing pluralism, institutional design, economic justice, and ecological ethics.

courses.title: Bani and Body: A Sikh Phenomenology of Embodied Practice
courses.source: SGGS; Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Phenomenology of Perception (1945); Sikh philosophy
courses.summary: This graduate seminar brings the methodology of phenomenological philosophy — particularly Merleau-Ponty's analysis of embodied perception — into dialogue with the Sikh theology of the body, Gurbani recitation, Amrit Sanchar, and the practices of kirtan and seva. Students develop philosophical tools for analyzing embodied religious practice and apply them to the Sikh tradition's distinctive understanding of the body as a vehicle for spiritual transformation.
outcomes: Apply Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the lived body to the analysis of Sikh embodied practices.
Analyze the Gurmat theology of the body and its relationship to spiritual transformation.
Conduct phenomenological analysis of specific Sikh practices including kirtan, Amrit Sanchar, and seva.
Evaluate feminist phenomenological perspectives on Sikh embodied practice.
Produce original phenomenological analysis of a selected Sikh practice.

courses.title: The Guru Granth Sahib as Literature: Poetics, Raag, and Aesthetics
courses.source: SGGS; Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh, The Name of My Beloved (1995); literary theory
courses.summary: This graduate seminar analyzes the Sri Guru Granth Sahib as a literary work of extraordinary complexity and beauty, examining its poetic forms, multilingual registers, raag organization, imagery, and aesthetic dimensions. Students engage with classical Indian literary theory (rasa, alamkara), modern literary criticism, and the scholarship of Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh to develop sophisticated tools for literary-critical engagement with Gurbani.
outcomes: Apply classical Indian poetic theory (rasa shastra, alamkara) to the analysis of Gurbani compositions.
Analyze the literary forms and structures of the SGGS, including the raag organization and compositional genres.
Evaluate Nikky-Guninder Kaur Singh's literary-critical approach to Gurbani aesthetics.
Conduct close reading of selected Gurbani passages using literary-critical methodology.
Situate Gurbani's literary aesthetics within the broader context of early modern South Asian literature.

courses.title: Sikhi and Modernity: Colonial Encounter, Reform, and Postcolonial Thought
courses.source: Harjot Oberoi, The Construction of Religious Boundaries (1994); Singh Sabha movement
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the transformative encounter between the Sikh tradition and colonial modernity, analyzing how British colonialism, the Singh Sabha reform movement, print culture, and postcolonial political developments reshaped Sikh identity, institutions, and self-understanding. Students engage critically with postcolonial theory and Sikh historical scholarship to analyze the construction of modern Sikh identity.

courses.title: Gurmat Epistemology: Knowledge, Truth, and the Nature of Mind
courses.source: SGGS; epistemology literature; Arvind-Pal Mandair scholarship
courses.summary: This graduate seminar examines the epistemological foundations of Gurmat — the teaching of the Gurus — exploring how knowledge, truth, and mind are theorized within the Sikh scriptural tradition. Drawing on the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhai Gurdas, and contemporary Sikh philosophy, students interrogate how ਨਾਮ, ਸ਼ਬਦ, and ਸੱਚ function as epistemic categories. The course is comparative, situating Gurmat epistemology alongside Western and South Asian philosophical traditions.
outcomes: Critically analyze the epistemological claims embedded in key SGGS compositions
Compare Gurmat theories of knowledge with Western empiricist, rationalist, and phenomenological traditions
Articulate the role of ਹਉਮੈ as an epistemic obstruction and the conditions for its transcendence
Evaluate scholarly debates in Sikh studies regarding the nature of divine revelation and human cognition
Produce original graduate-level research situating Gurmat epistemology within contemporary philosophy of mind

lessons.summary: Examines ਸੱਚ as both ontological and epistemological category in the SGGS, engaging Gurmat truth-theory with Western metaphysics and South Asian philosophy of language.

lessons.title: ਹਉਮੈ as Epistemic Distortion: The Anatomy of Ignorance
lessons.summary: A close analysis of ਹਉਮੈ as the central cognitive and soteriological obstacle in Gurmat, examined through philosophy of mind, comparative mysticism, and SGGS textual analysis.

lessons.title: ਸ਼ਬਦ as Epistemic Medium: The Word and the Mind
lessons.summary: Examines ਸ਼ਬਦ as the primary epistemic vehicle in Gurmat, analyzing its ontological status, its relation to language and sound, and its function in cognitive transformation.

lessons.title: ਨਾਮ: Toward a Gurmat Philosophy of Naming
lessons.summary: Analyzes ਨਾਮ as a philosophical category in Gurmat, engaging theories of naming, reference, and religious language in Western and South Asian traditions.

lessons.title: Revelation, Reason, and ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ: Grace as Epistemic Condition
lessons.summary: Examines the relationship between divine grace (ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ), rational inquiry, and revelation in Gurmat epistemology, comparing with Western theological and rationalist traditions.

lessons.title: The Role of ਸੰਗਤ in the Construction of Knowledge
lessons.summary: Analyzes the holy congregation (ਸੰਗਤ) as an epistemological institution in Gurmat, drawing on social epistemology, feminist standpoint theory, and Sikh historical sociology.

lessons.title: Mind (ਮਨ), Body, and Knowing: Gurmat Philosophy of Cognition
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat account of ਮਨ (mind) as cognitive faculty, situating it within South Asian psychologies and contemporary philosophy of mind.

lessons.title: ਮਾਇਆ and the Phenomenology of Ordinary Consciousness
lessons.summary: A phenomenological analysis of ਮਾਇਆ as the condition of ordinary distorted consciousness in Gurmat, with comparisons to Husserl, Heidegger, and South Asian philosophical traditions.

lessons.title: ਅਨਭਉ: Direct Experience and the Limits of Language
lessons.summary: Analyzes ਅਨਭਉ — direct experiential knowing — in Gurmat epistemology, addressing the paradox of ineffability and the relationship between experience and expression.

lessons.title: ਬਿਬੇਕ: Discernment, Ethics, and Epistemic Virtue
lessons.summary: Examines ਬਿਬੇਕ as a cultivated faculty of discernment in Gurmat, comparing with Aristotelian phronesis and the virtue epistemology tradition.

lessons.title: Gurmat Epistemology in Contemporary Philosophical Dialogue
lessons.summary: A synthetic examination of Gurmat epistemology's contributions to contemporary philosophy of mind, religion, and social epistemology, and a Works Cited section for the seminar.

courses.title: Advanced Gurmukhi: Grammar, Prosody, and Poetic Structure
courses.source: Prof. Sahib Singh, Gurbani Vyakaran; SGGS prosody
courses.summary: This graduate seminar undertakes an advanced analysis of Gurmukhi as both a script and a literary language, examining the grammatical structures, prosodic systems, and poetic conventions of Gurbani with scholarly rigor. Drawing on Prof. Sahib Singh's Gurbani Vyakaran and the prosodic diversity of the SGGS, students engage the full range of classical Indian metrical forms deployed by the Gurus alongside the unique linguistic features of the Gurbani idiom. The course is essential for scholars seeking to read and interpret Gurbani in the original.
outcomes: Analyze complex grammatical constructions in Gurbani with reference to Prof. Sahib Singh's Vyakaran
Identify and scan the major metrical forms (ਛੰਦ) used in the SGGS
Distinguish the linguistic layers (Punjabi, Braj Bhasha, Sanskrit, Persian/Arabic) in Gurbani compositions
Produce scholarly commentary on selected Gurbani texts at the grammatical and prosodic level
Situate Gurbani's literary language within the broader tradition of medieval Indian devotional poetry
references: Singh, Sahib. Gurbani Vyakaran (Punjabi Grammar of Gurbani). Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1939 (repr. 2003).
Shackle, Christopher. A Guru Nanak Glossary. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, 1981.

lessons.title: The Gurmukhi Script: History, Structure, and Scholarly Conventions
lessons.summary: An advanced introduction to the Gurmukhi script's historical development, phonological organization, and scholarly conventions for reading and transcribing Gurbani.

lessons.title: The Grammar of Gurbani: Prof. Sahib Singh's Vyakaran Framework
lessons.summary: A detailed examination of Prof. Sahib Singh's grammatical framework for Gurbani, situating it within the tradition of Punjabi linguistics and evaluating its contemporary relevance.

lessons.title: Case System and Postpositions in Gurbani Syntax
lessons.summary: A technical analysis of the Gurbani case system, postpositions, and their syntactic functions, with worked examples from the SGGS.

lessons.title: Verbal Morphology in Gurbani: Tense, Aspect, and Mood
lessons.summary: A systematic analysis of verb forms in Gurbani, covering tense, aspect, mood, and the theological implications of verbal choices in key SGGS compositions.

lessons.title: The Multilingual Texture of Gurbani: Sanskrit, Braj, Persian, and Arabic Strata
lessons.summary: Analyzes the multiple linguistic layers in Gurbani, examining how Sanskrit, Braj Bhasha, Persian, and Arabic elements function grammatically, theologically, and poetically.

lessons.title: Classical Indian Metrics in the SGGS: ਛੰਦ and Prosodic Forms
lessons.summary: A systematic introduction to the classical Indian metrical tradition (ਛੰਦ) as deployed in the SGGS, with practical guidance for scansion.

lessons.title: ਸਲੋਕ and ਪਦ: The Primary Compositional Units
lessons.summary: A detailed analysis of the ਸਲੋਕ and ਪਦ as the primary poetic units of the SGGS, with attention to their structural features and theological deployment.

lessons.title: ਵਾਰ Form: Structure, Genre, and Theological Function
lessons.summary: A detailed study of the ਵਾਰ as a literary-theological form in the SGGS and Bhai Gurdas, examining its historical roots and its transformation in the Gurmat tradition.

lessons.title: The Organization of the SGGS: ਰਾਗ, ਮਹਲਾ, and Compositional Sequence
lessons.summary: Examines the editorial and organizational principles of the SGGS, analyzing the significance of the ਰਾਗ framework, ਮਹਲਾ designations, and compositional sequencing.

lessons.title: Poetic Devices in Gurbani: Metaphor, Simile, and Allusion
lessons.summary: Analyzes the major poetic devices deployed in Gurbani — metaphor, simile, allusion, apostrophe, and paradox — with close reading of representative compositions.

lessons.title: Reading Gurbani: Philological Method and Interpretive Principles
lessons.summary: Establishes the methodological principles of advanced Gurbani philology, integrating grammatical, prosodic, contextual, and theological dimensions of interpretation.

lessons.title: Advanced Commentary: Close Reading of Selected Compositions
lessons.summary: An applied exercise in advanced Gurbani philology, demonstrating close grammatical, prosodic, and theological reading of selected SGGS compositions, with a Works Cited section.

courses.title: Sikh Ethics: A Graduate Seminar in Gurmat Moral Philosophy
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh ethics scholarship; contemporary moral philosophy
courses.summary: This graduate seminar undertakes a systematic analysis of Gurmat moral philosophy, examining the ethical dimensions of the Sikh scriptural tradition through the frameworks of Western normative ethics, virtue ethics, and South Asian moral thought. Students interrogate key Gurmat ethical categories — ਸੇਵਾ, ਧਰਮ, ਸੱਚ, ਦਇਆ, and ਸੰਤੋਖ — as well as the ethical implications of the Khalsa tradition, caste critique, and contemporary Sikh ethical challenges. The seminar produces graduates capable of original research in Sikh moral philosophy.
outcomes: Articulate the foundational ethical categories of Gurmat and their grounding in SGGS theology
Compare Gurmat moral philosophy with Kantian deontology, consequentialism, and Aristotelian virtue ethics
Analyze the ethical dimensions of Khalsa identity and the ਰਹਿਤ tradition
Evaluate Gurmat resources for addressing contemporary ethical challenges including environmental ethics, bioethics, and social justice
Produce original graduate-level research in Sikh ethics that contributes to the scholarly literature
references: Mandair, Arvind-Pal S. Religion and the Specter of the West: Sikhism, India, Postcoloniality, and the Politics of Translation. Columbia University Press, 2009.

Singh, Gurharpal and Giorgio Shani. Sikh Nationalism. Cambridge University Press, 2020.

lessons.title: Foundations of Gurmat Moral Philosophy
lessons.summary: Establishes the foundational ethical framework of Gurmat, situating it within the SGGS and in relation to Western and South Asian moral traditions.

lessons.title: The Five Virtues: ਸੱਚ, ਦਇਆ, ਸੰਤੋਖ, ਨਿਮਰਤਾ, ਪਿਆਰ
lessons.summary: A systematic philosophical analysis of the five cardinal virtues of Gurmat ethics, examining their content, their relationships, and their grounding in Gurmat ontology.

lessons.title: ਸੇਵਾ: The Ethics of Selfless Service
lessons.summary: A philosophical analysis of ਸੇਵਾ as the central ethical practice of Gurmat, examining its theological grounding, institutional forms, and comparative significance.

lessons.title: ਧਰਮ and the Moral Order: Gurmat vs. Hindu Dharma
lessons.summary: Analyzes Gurmat's distinctive concept of ਧਰਮ as moral order, examining its difference from the caste-based Hindu dharma and its role in Gurmat ethics.

lessons.title: The Ethics of ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat ethics of honest labor and equitable sharing as foundational social-economic norms, situating them in contemporary debates about distributive justice.

lessons.title: Caste, Equality, and the Gurmat Social Ethic
lessons.summary: Analyzes the Gurmat critique of caste hierarchy and its positive vision of social equality, situating it within both the Indian social reform tradition and contemporary debates about structural justice.

lessons.title: Gender Ethics in Gurmat Thought
lessons.summary: A critical examination of Gurmat's resources for gender equality, analyzing both the scriptural affirmation of women's dignity and the historical tensions in Sikh gender practice.

lessons.title: The ਰਹਿਤ Tradition: Khalsa Ethics and Disciplinary Code
lessons.summary: Examines the ਰਹਿਤ (Khalsa code of conduct) as a normative ethical-liturgical framework, analyzing its historical development and its relationship to Gurmat moral philosophy.

lessons.title: ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ: The Ethics of Temporal and Spiritual Authority
lessons.summary: Analyzes the ਮੀਰੀ-ਪੀਰੀ doctrine as a distinctive Gurmat ethical-political philosophy, examining its theological grounding and its implications for Sikh political thought.

lessons.title: Violence, Nonviolence, and Just War in Gurmat Ethics
lessons.summary: Examines the Gurmat ethical framework for thinking about violence and the use of force, analyzing the tradition's distinctive synthesis of nonviolence (ਅਹਿੰਸਾ) and righteous force (ਧਰਮ ਯੁੱਧ).

lessons.title: Environmental Ethics in Gurmat Perspective
lessons.summary: Examines Gurmat's resources for environmental ethics, analyzing the tradition's understanding of creation (ਕੁਦਰਤਿ) and its implications for ecological responsibility.

lessons.title: Contemporary Sikh Ethical Challenges: Bioethics, Global Justice, and Interfaith Ethics
lessons.summary: Applies the Gurmat ethical framework to contemporary challenges, including bioethical questions, global distributive justice, and the ethics of interfaith engagement, with a Works Cited section.

courses.title: Sikh Community, Power, and Society: Advanced Sociological Analysis
courses.source: SGGS; Sikh sociological studies; Harjot Oberoi
courses.summary: This graduate seminar applies advanced sociological theory to the study of the Sikh community, examining questions of identity construction, religious boundaries, gender, diaspora, nationalism, and institutional power. Drawing on Harjot Oberoi's landmark sociological work, classical sociological theory, and contemporary Sikh studies scholarship, students analyze the Sikh community as a complex social formation shaped by theology, history, and the demands of modernity. The seminar prepares students to conduct original sociological research on Sikh communities globally.
outcomes: Apply classical and contemporary sociological theory to the analysis of Sikh community formation and transformation
Critically engage Harjot Oberoi's constructivist approach to Sikh identity and evaluate the scholarly responses it generated
Analyze the Sikh diaspora as a sociological formation, examining questions of identity, integration, and transnationalism
Examine the sociological dimensions of Sikh institutional life, including the SGPC, Gurdwara governance, and political organization
Produce original graduate-level sociological research on a specific dimension of Sikh community life
references: Oberoi, Harjot. The Construction of Religious Boundaries: Culture, Identity, and Diversity in the Sikh Tradition. University of Chicago Press, 1994.

lessons.title: Sociology of Religion and the Sikh Tradition
lessons.summary: Introduces the major theoretical frameworks of the sociology of religion and examines their applicability to the analysis of the Sikh community.

lessons.title: Harjot Oberoi and the Construction of Sikh Religious Boundaries
lessons.summary: A critical examination of Harjot Oberoi's landmark sociological study, evaluating his constructivist argument and the scholarly debate it generated.

lessons.title: The ਸੰਗਤ as Social Institution: Community, Practice, and Power
lessons.summary: Analyzes ਸੰਗਤ as a social institution, examining its historical development, internal power dynamics, and role in community formation.

lessons.title: The ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and Identity Formation in 1699
lessons.summary: Examines the sociological significance of Guru Gobind Singh's establishment of the ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ in 1699, analyzing it as an event of collective identity formation.

lessons.title: Colonialism and the Transformation of Sikh Identity
lessons.summary: Analyzes the impact of British colonial governance on Sikh community identity, examining how colonial enumeration, military recruitment, and institutional reform shaped modern Sikh self-understanding.

lessons.title: The SGPC and Institutional Consolidation of Sikh Authority
lessons.summary: Examines the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) as an institutional expression of Sikh community authority, analyzing its formation, functions, and contemporary challenges.

lessons.title: Gender and Power in Sikh Institutional Life
lessons.summary: Applies feminist sociological analysis to Sikh institutional life, examining the patterns of gender inclusion and exclusion in Gurdwara governance, clergy roles, and community leadership.

lessons.title: The Sikh Diaspora: Community, Identity, and Transnationalism
lessons.summary: Analyzes the Sikh diaspora as a sociological formation, examining identity construction, integration patterns, transnational connections, and diaspora politics.

lessons.title: Sikh Nationalism and Political Mobilization
lessons.summary: Examines the sociology of Sikh nationalism and political mobilization, analyzing the development of Khalistan movements, Akali politics, and diaspora political activism.

lessons.title: Caste and Social Stratification in Sikh Communities
lessons.summary: Examines the persistent sociological reality of caste stratification in Sikh communities, analyzing the tension between the Gurmat theological critique of caste and its social persistence.

lessons.title: Conversion, Apostasy, and Boundary Maintenance
lessons.summary: Examines the sociological dynamics of religious conversion, apostasy, and boundary maintenance in the Sikh tradition, analyzing both historical patterns and contemporary challenges.

lessons.title: Contemporary Sikh Sociology: Globalization, Youth Identity, and Digital Community
lessons.summary: Examines contemporary challenges to Sikh community sociology, including the effects of globalization, the distinctive identity challenges of second-generation diaspora youth, and the emergence of digital Sikh community spaces, with Works Cited.

courses.title: The Punjabi Intellectual Tradition: Bhai Gurdas to Modern Scholarship
courses.source: Bhai Vir Singh complete works; Bhai Gurdas, Vaaran; Punjabi literary history
courses.summary: This graduate seminar traces the arc of Punjabi intellectual and literary tradition from the compositions of Bhai Gurdas in the early seventeenth century through the literary renaissance of Bhai Vir Singh in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to contemporary Punjabi scholarship. Students engage the major figures, texts, and themes of the Punjabi intellectual tradition in their historical and theological contexts, analyzing the relationship between literary form, religious thought, and community identity. The seminar is essential for scholars of Punjabi literature, Sikh theology, and South Asian intellectual history.
outcomes: Analyze the major works of Bhai Gurdas within their theological, historical, and literary contexts
Trace the development of Punjabi literary tradition from the Guru period through colonial modernity
Critically evaluate Bhai Vir Singh's literary and intellectual project within the context of the Singh Sabha movement
Situate the Punjabi intellectual tradition within the broader history of South Asian literary and intellectual life
Produce original graduate-level research on a figure, text, or theme in the Punjabi intellectual tradition
references: Vir Singh, Bhai. Sundari. Khalsa Samachar, 1898.
Gurdas, Bhai. Vaaran Bhai Gurdas. Ed. Hazara Singh and Vir Singh. Amritsar: Khalsa Samachar, 1911.

lessons.title: Introduction: The Punjabi Intellectual Tradition and Its Scope
lessons.summary: An introduction to the scope, character, and significance of the Punjabi intellectual tradition, situating it within South Asian literary and intellectual history.

lessons.title: Bhai Gurdas: Life, Context, and Corpus
lessons.summary: Examines the life and historical context of Bhai Gurdas, establishing the biographical and intellectual framework for the study of his compositions.

lessons.title: The ਵਾਰਾਂ of Bhai Gurdas: Form, Theology, and History
lessons.summary: A detailed literary and theological analysis of the ਵਾਰਾਂ of Bhai Gurdas, examining their formal structure, major themes, and historical significance.

lessons.title: Bhai Gurdas as Theologian: Key Themes in the ਵਾਰਾਂ
lessons.summary: Analyzes the major theological themes of Bhai Gurdas's ਵਾਰਾਂ, examining his contributions to Gurmat theological elaboration.

lessons.title: The ਕਬਿੱਤ ਸਵੱਯੇ of Bhai Gurdas: The Secondary Corpus
lessons.summary: Analyzes the secondary corpus of Bhai Gurdas — the ਕਬਿੱਤ ਸਵੱਯੇ — examining their formal features, theological content, and literary significance.

lessons.title: Punjabi Prose in the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ Tradition
lessons.summary: Examines the ਜਨਮਸਾਖੀ literature — the hagiographic biographical narratives of Guru Nanak — as the founding genre of Punjabi prose.

lessons.title: The ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ Literature: Hagiography and History
lessons.summary: Examines the ਗੁਰਬਿਲਾਸ literary tradition — celebratory Guru biographies — analyzing its genre characteristics, theological purposes, and historiographical complexity.

lessons.title: Punjabi Literature of the Eighteenth Century: Crisis and Creativity
lessons.summary: Examines the Punjabi literary tradition of the tumultuous eighteenth century, analyzing how literary production responded to political crisis and community transformation.

lessons.title: Bhai Vir Singh: Life, Context, and the Literary Renaissance
lessons.summary: Examines Bhai Vir Singh's life and the historical context of the Punjabi literary renaissance he led, analyzing his position within the Singh Sabha movement and colonial Punjabi culture.

lessons.title: Bhai Vir Singh's Fiction: ਸੁੰਦਰੀ and the Punjabi Novel
lessons.summary: A literary analysis of Bhai Vir Singh's fiction, focusing on ਸੁੰਦਰੀ as the founding text of the modern Punjabi novel and its place in South Asian literary history.

lessons.title: Bhai Vir Singh as Poet and Scholar: ਕਲਮ in Service of Community
lessons.summary: Examines Bhai Vir Singh's poetry and scholarly work, analyzing his contribution to Punjabi literary aesthetics and to the recovery of the classical Sikh textual heritage.

lessons.title: From Vir Singh to Contemporary Scholarship: The Modern Punjabi Intellectual Tradition
lessons.summary: Traces the development of the Punjabi intellectual tradition from Bhai Vir Singh through the twentieth century to contemporary scholarship, with a Works Cited section.

courses.title: The Theology of Liberation in Sikh Thought: Mukti, Naam, and Waheguru
courses.source: SGGS; Prof. Sahib Singh, Shabadarth SGGS; Sikh liberation theology
courses.summary: This graduate seminar undertakes a systematic theological analysis of liberation (ਮੁਕਤਿ) in the Sikh tradition, examining how the SGGS theorizes the human condition, the goal of liberation, and the path by which liberation is achieved through ਨਾਮ and the grace of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ. Drawing on Prof. Sahib Singh's authoritative Shabadarth commentary, the Gurmat theological tradition, and comparative liberation theology, students engage the full depth of the Sikh soteriological vision. The seminar situates Gurmat liberation theology within global comparative theology and contemporary spiritual discourse.
outcomes: Articulate the systematic structure of Gurmat liberation theology as expressed in the SGGS
Analyze the relationship between ਨਾਮ, ਸ਼ਬਦ, and ਮੁਕਤਿ in Gurmat soteriology
Compare Gurmat liberation theology with Hindu Advaita, Buddhist Nirvana, Christian salvation, and liberation theology
Evaluate Prof. Sahib Singh's interpretive framework for understanding key SGGS passages on liberation
Produce original graduate-level theological research on Gurmat soteriology contributing to comparative theology
references: Singh, Sahib. Shabadarth Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. 4 vols. Amritsar: Singh Brothers, 1959–1962.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. Oxford University Press, 2000.

Fenech, Louis E. and W.H. McLeod. Historical Dictionary of Sikhism. Scarecrow Press, 2014.

lessons.title: The Problem of Liberation: Gurmat Soteriology in Context
lessons.summary: Introduces the theological question of liberation in Gurmat thought, situating it within South Asian and global soteriological traditions.

lessons.title: ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ: The Theological Ground of Gurmat Liberation
lessons.summary: Examines the nature of ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ as the theological ground of Gurmat liberation theology, analyzing the divine attributes and their soteriological significance.

lessons.title: The Human Condition: ਜਨਮ ਮਰਨ, ਹਉਮੈ, and the Need for Liberation
lessons.summary: Analyzes the Gurmat account of the human predicament — the cycle of birth and death and the ego-distortion of ਹਉਮੈ — that constitutes the soteriological problem.

lessons.title: ਨਾਮ and ਸ਼ਬਦ: The Soteriological Path
lessons.summary: Analyzes ਨਾਮ and ਸ਼ਬਦ as the primary soteriological vehicles in Gurmat, examining their nature, their relationship, and their role in the liberation process.

lessons.title: ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ: The Practice of Liberation
lessons.summary: A detailed analysis of ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ as the primary liberative practice in Gurmat, examining its forms, stages, and transformative effects.

lessons.title: ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ: Grace as the Ground of Liberation
lessons.summary: Analyzes the role of divine grace (ਗੁਰਪ੍ਰਸਾਦਿ) in Gurmat soteriology, examining its relationship to human effort and comparing it with grace in other theological traditions.

lessons.title: ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ: Liberation Within Embodied Life
lessons.summary: Examines the distinctive Gurmat concept of ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤਿ — liberation while living — analyzing its theological basis and its implications for Gurmat ethics and spirituality.

lessons.title: The Cosmology of ਜਪੁ: Spiritual Realms and the Path to ਸਚਖੰਡ
lessons.summary: Analyzes the cosmological-soteriological framework of the ਜਪੁ (the SGGS's opening composition), examining the five spiritual realms and their significance for Gurmat liberation theology.

lessons.title: ਮਿਲਾਪ: The Theology of Union with the Divine
lessons.summary: Analyzes the Gurmat theology of divine-soul union (ਮਿਲਾਪ), examining the nature of union, the role of love, and the relationship between union and individual identity.

lessons.title: Liberation and Ethics: The Social Dimension of ਮੁਕਤਿ
lessons.summary: Examines the relationship between liberation (ਮੁਕਤਿ) and ethical action in Gurmat theology, analyzing how the liberated state grounds and energizes moral and social engagement.

lessons.title: Prof. Sahib Singh's Interpretive Framework: Shabadarth and Soteriology
lessons.summary: Examines Prof. Sahib Singh's hermeneutical approach in the Shabadarth commentary, analyzing the interpretive principles he applies to soteriological passages and evaluating his contribution to Gurmat theology.

lessons.title: Gurmat Liberation Theology in Comparative Perspective
lessons.summary: A synthetic comparative examination of Gurmat liberation theology alongside Buddhist, Hindu, Christian, and Islamic soteriological traditions, with a Works Cited section.

courses.title: Sikhi and Cosmology: What Gurbani Reveals About the Universe
courses.source: SGGS; Pashaura Singh and Louis Fenech, The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies (2014); modern cosmology
courses.summary: This graduate-level course examines what the Guru Granth Sahib reveals about the nature, origin, and structure of the universe, situating Sikh cosmological thought within the broader landscape of world religions and modern astrophysics. Students engage primary Gurbani passages in Punjabi alongside scholarly commentary to understand how concepts such as Hukam, Kudrat, Nirgun, and Sargun constitute a coherent cosmological framework. The course maintains a non-concordist approach, exploring genuine convergences and irreducible differences between Sikh theology and contemporary scientific cosmology without forcing agreement.
outcomes: Analyze key Gurbani passages related to creation, cosmic order, and the infinite universe using Punjabi primary sources and English-language scholarship.
Explain core Sikh cosmological concepts — including Hukam, Kudrat, Nirgun, Sargun, and Brahmand — and distinguish them from analogous Hindu, Islamic, and secular cosmological frameworks.
Critically evaluate non-concordist methodology when comparing Sikh theology with modern astrophysics, identifying where genuine convergences exist and where the frameworks remain incommensurable.
Situate Sikh cosmological thought within the historiography of Sikh Studies, drawing on the Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies and other foundational scholarly works.
Articulate a philosophically informed personal position on living meaningfully within Waheguru's infinite creation, grounded in Gurbani and engaged with contemporary scientific knowledge.
references: Singh, Pashaura and Louis E. Fenech, eds. The Oxford Handbook of Sikh Studies. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014.

courses.title: Astrology, Fate, and Gurbani: What the Guru Actually Said
courses.source: SGGS; W.H. McLeod, Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion (1968); Kahn Singh Nabha, Mahan Kosh (1930)
courses.summary: This course examines what the Guru Granth Sahib actually teaches about astrology, fate, and auspicious timing, contrasting Gurmat's framework of Hukam with the astral determinism prevalent in the Guru's cultural milieu. Students engage primary Gurbani passages, janamsakhis, and modern scientific literature to develop a rigorous, evidence-based understanding of why Sikhi rejects horoscopes and ritual observance of planetary positions. The course equips learners to think critically about popular astrological claims and to articulate Sikh theology on fate, free will, and divine grace.
outcomes: Identify and interpret key Gurbani passages that address astrology, auspicious timing, and planetary influence.
Explain the theological distinction between Hukam (divine order) and astrological determinism within Gurmat.
Evaluate historical and modern astrological claims using critical-thinking and scientific-evidence frameworks.
Trace the cultural and historical context of astrology in the Indian subcontinent during the Guru period.
Apply Gurmat principles on karma, destiny, and divine grace to contemporary questions about fate and free will.
references: McLeod, W. H. *Guru Nanak and the Sikh Religion*. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1968.
Nabha, Kahn Singh. *Mahan Kosh*. Patiala: Language Department Punjab, 1930.

courses.title: Flat Earth Theory and Gurbani: A Critical Examination
courses.source: SGGS; Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot (1994); modern spherical Earth science; Sikh cosmology
courses.summary: This course provides a rigorous, graduate-quality critical examination of Flat Earth Theory, testing its claims against 2,500 years of scientific evidence while exploring what Gurbani actually teaches about the Earth and the cosmos. Students will discover that the Guru Granth Sahib's vision of countless infinite universes stands in direct opposition to the cramped, conspiratorial cosmology of the Flat Earth movement. The course also equips students with tools for critical thinking, logical analysis, and respectful dialogue — grounded firmly in Sikh values and the obligation of reason that Gurbani itself demands.
outcomes: Accurately describe the core claims of Flat Earth Theory and trace their historical and social origins.
Identify and analyze the primary scientific evidence for a spherical Earth, from Eratosthenes to satellite imagery.
Interpret key Gurbani passages describing the Earth and cosmos and explain why they are incompatible with Flat Earth claims.
Recognize common logical fallacies used in Flat Earth arguments and apply critical thinking frameworks to evaluate misinformation.
Apply Sikh values of reason, humility, and respectful dialogue when engaging with those who hold fringe cosmological beliefs.
references: Sagan, Carl. Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space. New York: Random House, 1994.

courses.title: Automation, AI, and Honest Work: A Sikh Ethics of Labour in the Age of Machines
courses.summary: As artificial intelligence automates millions of jobs, Sikh ethics offers a coherent and urgent framework for response. This course grounds the contemporary crisis of technological unemployment in the Gurmat teaching of ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ (honest, dignified labour), examines what automation and wealth concentration mean for Sikh workers and communities, and applies ਦਸਵੰਧ and ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ as policy frameworks for ensuring that the gains of AI are shared across all of humanity.

courses.title: AI, Energy, and the Earth: Gurbani's Call to Ecological Responsibility
courses.summary: Artificial intelligence carries a vast environmental footprint — data centers consume enormous quantities of electricity and water, AI hardware generates toxic e-waste, and the carbon cost of training frontier models rivals that of entire industries. This course reads that environmental crisis through the lens of Gurbani, placing the Sikh ecological ethic — rooted in Japji Sahib's declaration that air is Guru, water is father, and earth is mother — in direct conversation with the planetary costs of AI.

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence and Human Dignity: Gurmat Perspectives on the Soul, Consciousness, and Technology
courses.summary: As artificial intelligence systems exhibit increasingly sophisticated behaviour — passing professional exams, generating poetry, holding extended conversations, expressing what appears to be emotion — fundamental questions about the nature of consciousness and human uniqueness become urgent. This course examines those questions through the lens of Gurbani, with particular focus on the concept of ਜੋਤਿ (divine light within), the nature of ਆਤਮਾ (soul), ਮਨ (mind), and ਵਿਵੇਕੁ (discernment), and what these theological concepts say about human dignity in AI-mediated systems.

courses.title: The Hanuman Natak: An Introduction to Sikh Court Literature
courses.summary: This introductory course invites learners to encounter the Hanuman Natak — a Braj Bhasha dramatic poem composed by Hirdey Ram Bhalla in the early seventeenth century — as one of the earliest surviving literary works connected to the Sikh tradition's courtly milieu. Students will learn who Hirdey Ram was, what kind of text the Hanuman Natak is, how it draws on the Ramayana's Hanuman cycle while infusing bhakti devotion, and why it occupies a distinct and important place in the literary history of the Guru period. No prior knowledge of classical Indian literature is assumed.

courses.summary: This advanced course subjects the Hanuman Natak to sustained scholarly analysis across three interconnected domains: its Braj Bhasha language and literary craft, its devotional (bhakti) architecture and poetic theology, and the theological themes it shares with and distinguishes from Gurbani and the wider Sikh tradition. Students engage with the poem as a serious literary artifact, examine its metrical and rhetorical structures, interrogate its theological claims and their limits, and situate it within comparative bhakti scholarship. The course assumes familiarity with the introductory Hanuman Natak courses.

courses.title: Addiction and Freedom: Understanding Dependency Through Gurbani and Modern Recovery
courses.summary: This course offers a complete framework for understanding and overcoming addiction by holding two lenses at once: the diagnosis of Gurbani and the findings of modern recovery science. Gurmat locates the root of every dependency — substance, sexual, digital, financial — in ਤ੍ਰਿਸ਼ਨਾ, the infinite thirst governed by ਮਾਇਆ, ਲੋਭ, ਮੋਹ, and ਕਾਮ, and reads the addict not as a moral failure but as a soul reaching for the Infinite at the wrong address. Across twelve lessons we examine drugs and alcohol, pornography, social media, and gambling through both neuroscience and Gurbani, then turn to the prescription: ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ as neurological and spiritual healing, ਸੰਗਤ as recovery community, and ਸੇਵਾ as the outward focus that breaks the self-absorbed loop. Far from opposing professional care, the course integrates AA/NA, therapy, rehabilitation, and medication as complementary tools, and equips families to support struggling members with compassion and boundaries. It closes by framing relapse within ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ and Divine ਬਖਸ਼ਿਸ਼, charting the long, hopeful road from bondage to freedom…
outcomes: Explain addiction using both neuroscience and the Gurmat vocabulary of ਤ੍ਰਿਸ਼ਨਾ, ਮਾਇਆ, ਲੋਭ, ਮੋਹ, and ਕਾਮ.
Map the four-stage addiction cycle and identify Gurmat intervention points at each stage.
Analyse substance, pornography, digital, and gambling addictions through paired Gurbani and clinical lenses.
Articulate the central thesis that all addiction is the soul's misdirected search for the Infinite.
Describe ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, ਸੰਗਤ, and ਸੇਵਾ as a complete, evidence-aligned recovery triad.
Integrate professional resources — fellowships, therapy, rehabilitation, medication — with Gurmat practice.
Support a family or ਸੰਗਤ member with compassion, boundaries, and appropriate referral.
Respond to relapse through ਚੜ੍ਹਦੀ ਕਲਾ and Divine ਬਖਸ਼ਿਸ਼ rather than shame.

courses.title: ਆਤਮਾ and ਜੋਤਿ: The Soul Beyond All Physical Categories
courses.summary: This course examines a central theological claim of the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ: that the divisions humans impose on one another — gender, caste, race, and the shape and condition of the body — are ਮਾਇਆ, temporary illusions that obscure the one reality. Drawing on verified passages from ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ, ਸੁਖਮਨੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ, ਅਨੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ and the wider Granth, and reading them through the disciplined exegetical method of Prof. Sahib Singh, students learn that the ਜੋਤਿ within every being is the only identity that stands before ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. We trace the movement of Gurbani thought from ਹਉਮੈ — the ego that manufactures separation — toward the recognition of ਇਕੁ ਨੂਰ, the single Light from which all creation springs. Across twelve lessons the course builds from theology to ethics to daily ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ practice, so that the learner does not merely understand that the soul transcends the body but begins to see other people as the Gurus saw them…
outcomes: Explain the ਇਕੁ ਨੂਰ (One Light) theology and locate its scriptural basis in verified Gurbani.
Identify how the ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ treats gender, caste, race, and body as ਮਾਇਆ rather than ultimate identity.
Distinguish ਹਉਮੈ consciousness from ਜੋਤਿ consciousness and describe the spiritual mechanics of each.
Apply Prof. Sahib Singh's grammatical-contextual exegetical method to a Gurbani passage.
Describe ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ as the disciplined path toward knowing the ਆਤਮਾ beyond physical categories.
Articulate the characteristics of the liberated soul (ਜੀਵਨ ਮੁਕਤ) as drawn in Gurbani.
Translate the theology of the soul into concrete ethical practice in how one perceives and treats others.
Construct a personal daily practice for cultivating ਜੋਤਿ consciousness.

courses.title: Females in the Punj Pyare: History, Akal Takht, and Gurbani on Gender in Sikh Ceremony
courses.summary: This 300-level seminar offers an honest, balanced examination of one of the most debated questions in contemporary Sikh practice: whether women may serve among the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ (the Five Beloved Ones) who administer ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤ ਸੰਚਾਰ. The course presents four streams of evidence side by side — the historical record of ਵੈਸਾਖੀ 1699 and the centuries that followed, the institutional positions of the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ and the Sikh Rehat Maryada, the theology of gender equality embedded in ਸ੍ਰੀ ਗੁਰੂ ਗ੍ਰੰਥ ਸਾਹਿਬ, and the scholarly debate between traditional (ਟਕਸਾਲ) and reformist-feminist Sikh thinkers. Following the methodology of ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾ (shared belonging) and respectful ਵਿਚਾਰ (deliberation), the course deliberately takes no side. Students learn to distinguish ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ from ਰਹਿਤ, theology from history, and conviction from evidence, so that they may participate in the ਪੰਥ's ongoing collective discernment with rigor, humility, and ਪਿਆਰ…
outcomes: Reconstruct the historical narrative of ਵੈਸਾਖੀ 1699 and identify what the primary and traditional sources do and do not establish about the original ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ.
Cite and interpret verified passages of ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ that articulate the spiritual equality of women and men, distinguishing theological claims from ritual prescriptions.
Summarize the formal provisions of the Sikh Rehat Maryada that bear on gender and ceremonial roles, reading the document closely and accurately.
Explain the ਅਕਾਲ ਤਖ਼ਤ's institutional position on the composition of the ਪੰਜ ਪਿਆਰੇ and the theological and historical reasoning offered for it.
Fairly reconstruct both the conservative (ਟਕਸਾਲ / traditional) case and the reformist-feminist scholarly case, steelmanning each before evaluating it.
Analyze documented historical and modern cases in which women have served in ceremonial leadership, weighing their evidentiary status.
Apply the principle of ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾ to the question of ceremonial participation and articulate the tension between ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ's egalitarianism and inherited tradition.
Describe how the Sikh ਸੰਗਤ discerns contested questions collectively through ਗੁਰਮਤਾ, institutional authority, and scholarship.

courses.title: ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤ: The Sikh Householder Life as Spiritual Path
courses.summary: This course examines one of the most radical claims in the history of religion: that Guru Nanak Sahib rejected the ascetic flight from the world and proclaimed the householder's life — marriage, family, honest labour, child-rearing, and sanctified intimacy — as the supreme arena of spiritual realisation. Drawing on Gurbani, the Vaaran of Bhai Gurdas, and the encyclopaedic scholarship of Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha, students trace how ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤ becomes not a concession to weakness but the golden mean between barren worldliness and barren renunciation. We study the theology of the husband-wife bond as ਧਨ-ਪੀਉ, the home as a living ਸੰਗਤ, the integration of ਨਾਮ ਜਪੋ, ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰੋ and ਵੰਡ ਛਕੋ, the milestones from birth to death, and the gift — never the compromise — that family life represents on the path to the One…
outcomes: Explain why Guru Nanak Sahib rejected renunciation and articulate the textual basis for the householder ideal in Gurbani.
Distinguish ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤ from both ਸੰਨਿਆਸ (renunciation) and mere ਸੰਸਾਰ (worldliness) as a deliberate middle path.
Analyse the ਧਨ-ਪੀਉ (bride-Groom) metaphor and its application to the human husband-wife relationship.
Apply the three pillars — ਨਾਮ ਜਪੋ, ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰੋ, ਵੰਡ ਛਕੋ — to concrete decisions of family and economic life.
Describe the Sikh family as a ਸੰਗਤ and the home as a sacred space of ਸਿਮਰਨ and ਸੇਵਾ.
Survey the major Sikh family milestones and the customs Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha documents around them.
Evaluate Sikh approaches to grief, death, and multigenerational household life through a Gurmat lens.
Present contested questions of family ethics fairly, representing the range of scholarly and Panthic positions.
