courses.title: ਕੁਦਰਤਿ and ਹੁਕਮਿ: Gurbani's Theology of Creation
courses.summary: Sri Guru Granth Sahib contains one of the world's most sophisticated theologies of creation. This 250-level course undertakes the exegetical work of systematically studying what Gurbani actually says about ਕੁਦਰਤਿ (the created order as divine expression), ਹੁਕਮਿ (the divine command and law through which creation operates), and humanity's place within that order. Across twelve lessons we move from the cosmology of Japji Sahib through the panentheism implicit in Gurbani's vision of nature, into the five elemental building-blocks of the cosmos, the ਜੋਤਿ (divine light) that animates every creature, and the ethical consequences that follow: trusteeship over ownership, the ecological vice of ਅਹੰਕਾਰ, and the ecological virtue of ਸੰਤੋਖ. We then widen the canon to consider the Dasam Granth, the Sarbloh Granth, and the Vaaran of Bhai Gurdas, before closing with the implications of this theology for contemporary environmental ethics and action. The aim is not advocacy but disciplined reading — letting the Guru's own words shape a coherent account of why creation matters, what it reveals about the One, and how human beings are called to live within it…
outcomes: Reconstruct the cosmology of Japji Sahib and explain how multiplicity arises from the One through ਹੁਕਮਿ
Define ਹੁਕਮਿ and analyse how Gurbani frames creation as operating through a divine order rather than random chance
Articulate the panentheistic relationship between ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ and ਕੁਦਰਤਿ, distinguishing it from pantheism and classical theism
Identify the five elements in Gurbani and describe their role in the constitution of created life
Explain the doctrine that every creature bears ਜੋਤਿ and trace its implications for the equality of all life
Contrast the trustee and owner models of the human relationship to nature, grounding trusteeship in Gurbani
Evaluate ਅਹੰਕਾਰ as an ecological sin and ਸੰਤੋਖ as an ecological virtue
Apply Gurbani's theology of creation to construct a coherent Sikh environmental ethic

courses.title: Gurbani and Political Ideologies: Socialism, Nationalism, and the Halemi Raj Vision
courses.summary: This upper-division seminar examines how ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ relates to the major political ideologies that organize the modern world — socialism, communism, liberalism, progressivism, conservatism, nationalism, oligarchy, and nativism. Its governing thesis is that Gurmat does not align with any earthly political party; it transcends and critiques them all. The Gurus' vision of ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ — the realm of humility — is neither capitalist nor socialist, neither nationalist nor globalist. Each ideology carries a fragment of truth that Gurmat affirms and a fatal flaw that Gurmat rejects. Through close reading of ਜਪੁਜੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ, ਆਨੰਦ ਸਾਹਿਬ, ਸੁਖਮਨੀ ਸਾਹਿਬ, and the Sikh political tradition of ਮਿਸਲਾਂ and Khalsa Raj, students learn to evaluate political programs against the standard of ਨਿਆਉ (justice), ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ (welfare of all), and the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ ideal. The course is deliberately non-partisan: it equips Sikhs to be principled participants in any polity without surrendering Gurmat to the categories of left or right. We end by sketching a Gurmat political ethics adequate to the twenty-first century…
outcomes: Articulate the concept of ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ as a transcendent political vision that sits above the left-right spectrum.
Map eight major political ideologies against Gurmat, identifying in each both a genuine overlap and a decisive divergence.
Trace the historical Sikh political tradition from the ਮਿਸਲਾਂ through Khalsa Raj to the modern diaspora.
Apply ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ and ਨਿਆਉ as evaluative criteria for assessing political programs.
Distinguish ਸਾਂਝੀਵਾਲਤਾ (universal fraternity) from ethnic nationalism and nativism.
Explain the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ ideal as a meta-political stance that resists capture by any party.
Cite ਗੁਰਬਾਣੀ accurately by ਅੰਗ where certainty exists, and reason responsibly where it does not.
Construct a coherent, non-partisan Gurmat political ethics for contemporary civic life.

courses.title: First Peoples and Gurbani: Indigenous Wisdom and the Sikh Vision of Creation
courses.summary: This 200-level comparative course places the lived wisdom of Indigenous North American peoples in respectful dialogue with the teachings of Gurbani. It does not collapse two distinct civilizations into one, nor does it claim that Sikhi and any Indigenous nation are the same. Instead, it asks a careful question: where Indigenous peoples have long practised reverence for ਕੁਦਰਤਿ, communal ਸੇਵਾ, oral wisdom, and an intimate spiritual bond with the land, what does Gurbani say to those same human concerns? Students examine the diversity of First Nations rather than a single stereotype, study how Sikh values of ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ resonate with Indigenous communal feasting and council, and confront the shared history of colonial violence — Mughal and British pressure on the Sikh Panth alongside European settler destruction of Indigenous cultures. The course honours genuine differences in cosmology and identity, including Two-Spirit traditions, while modelling how Sikhs today might walk in solidarity with Indigenous land-rights movements. Throughout, every Gurbani reference is cited responsibly by ਅੰਗ only where certain, and parallels are offered as bridges of understanding, not as proof that one tradition contains the other…
outcomes: Describe the diversity of Indigenous North American nations and resist flattening them into a single stereotype
Explain the Indigenous concept of land stewardship and compare it with the Gurbani vision of ਕੁਦਰਤਿ
Analyze parallels between oral wisdom traditions and the Sikh practice of ਕੀਰਤਨ and ਕਥਾ
Compare communal structures such as ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ with Indigenous council and feasting practices
Evaluate both the genuine convergences and the real differences between Indigenous and Sikh concepts of the sacred
Trace shared histories of colonial violence and traditions of resilient response in both peoples
Reflect on Two-Spirit identities through a careful Gurmat lens that presents multiple positions fairly
Articulate how Sikh principles of ਸੇਵਾ and justice can inform solidarity with Indigenous land-rights movements

courses.title: Conquering Kaam: Spiritual Discipline Against Lust in the Sikh Tradition
courses.summary: This 300-level course undertakes a disciplined exegetical study of ਕਾਮ (lust, compulsive desire) as it is diagnosed and treated within Sri Guru Granth Sahib, the Dasam Granth, and the Vaaran of Bhai Gurdas. Rather than treating ਕਾਮ as a subject of moral scolding, the course follows Gurbani's own framing of it as a spiritual disorder — a force that fractures the ਮਨ, severs the soul from ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ, and binds it within ਮਾਇਆ. Working shabad by shabad and ਅੰਗ by ਅੰਗ where citation is certain, students learn how Gurbani names the symptom, explains the mechanism, and prescribes an antidote rooted in ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, ਸੰਗਤ, ਰਹਿਤ, and ਸੰਤੋਖ. The arc moves from method, through diagnosis, into the architecture of liberation, and finally to Gurbani's own portraits of the soul that has subdued desire. Throughout, the course honors the principle that one must never fabricate ਅੰਗ numbers or Gurbani phrases, citing only what is verified and naming a granth honestly when the precise ਅੰਗ is uncertain…
outcomes: Articulate Prof. Sahib Singh's exegetical method and apply it to passages of Gurbani concerning ਕਾਮ
Survey systematically the shabads in SGGS that diagnose ਕਾਮ, organized by ਅੰਗ ranges and raag
Explain the spiritual mechanics by which ਕਾਮ weakens the ਮਨ and separates the soul from ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ
Identify and explain the Gurbani-prescribed antidotes: ਨਾਮ ਸਿਮਰਨ, ਸੰਗਤ, ਰਹਿਤ, and ਸੰਤੋਖ
Reconstruct the liberation sequence by which the ਪੰਜ ਚੋਰ are defeated and their opposing virtues established
Interpret Gurbani's first-person testimonies of having overcome ਕਾਮ as descriptions of an attained state

Cite Gurbani responsibly, distinguishing verified ਅੰਗ references from passages that must be named without a fabricated ਅੰਗ

courses.title: Queer, Transgender, and LGBTQ+ Identities: A Sikh Theological Inquiry
courses.summary: This 300-level seminar undertakes a rigorous theological inquiry into how Sikh scripture and tradition speak to questions of gender, embodiment, and identity. Beginning from the conviction that the ਆਤਮਾ has no gender, that the ਜੋਤਿ dwells equally in all beings, and that ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ transcends every binary category, the course reads Gurbani as a literature that evaluates persons by their internal relationship with ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ rather than by their physical body or social labels. Students examine the nirgun and sargun registers of Sikh theology, the impermanence of the body, the gender-fluid imagery of the Dasam Granth, the universal-light theme of the Sarbloh Granth, and Guru Nanak's radical dismantling of social hierarchies. The seminar then turns to history, to the Sikh Rehat Maryada, to the Sikh critique of ਹਉਮੈ and ਮਾਇਆ, and finally to the practical ethics of ਸੇਵਾ and ਸੰਗਤ toward LGBTQ+ individuals. Throughout, contested questions are presented with multiple positions held in tension, never resolved by fiat, so that students learn to hold tradition and compassion together while reasoning from Gurmat itself…
outcomes: Articulate the Gurbani teaching that the ਆਤਮਾ is genderless and that the ਜੋਤਿ dwells equally in all beings.
Distinguish the nirgun and sargun registers of Sikh theology and explain how ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ transcends binary categories.
Analyze Gurbani passages on the impermanence of the physical body and the priority of inner devotion over outward form.
Interpret gender-fluid and divine-play imagery in the Dasam Granth and the universal-light theme of the Sarbloh Granth with scholarly care.
Trace Guru Nanak's critique of caste, ritual purity, and social hierarchy and apply it to contemporary identity questions.
Evaluate what the Sikh Rehat Maryada states explicitly and where it is silent regarding gender and sexual identity.
Apply the Sikh ethics of ਸੇਵਾ and ਸੰਗਤ to pastoral engagement with LGBTQ+ individuals while presenting contested positions fairly.
Construct a Gurmat-grounded pastoral framework that distinguishes cultural Punjabi attitudes from scriptural teaching.

courses.title: Same-Sex Marriage and Sikhi: Gurbani, Akal Takht, and the Scholarly Debate
courses.summary: This 300-level course offers an honest, rigorous, and impartial examination of one of the most contested questions facing the global Sikh community today: how does Sikhi understand same-sex marriage? Beginning with what Sri Guru Granth Sahib actually says about the purpose and theology of ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ, the course moves through the textual record of the Dasam and Sarbloh Granths, the historical practice of early Sikh communities, the explicit provisions of the ਸਿੱਖ ਰਹਿਤ ਮਰਯਾਦਾ, and the 2005 Akal Takht ruling. It then presents — fairly and without endorsement — the reformist scholarly critique, the conservative Gurmat defense of tradition, and the lived experiences of LGBTQ+ Sikhs. Students will not be told what to conclude. Instead they will be equipped with the textual, historical, and theological tools to engage the question with ਨਿਮਰਤਾ, intellectual honesty, and respect for the ongoing ਵੀਚਾਰ of the Panth. The course models how a tradition rooted in ਇੱਕ ਓਅੰਕਾਰ holds difficult conversations with integrity, presenting all positions accurately so that each student, family, and ਸੰਗਤ may discern with open eyes…
outcomes: Articulate what Sri Guru Granth Sahib affirms about the purpose, theology, and metaphysics of marriage in its own terms
Distinguish between the literal-textual, historical, juridical, and theological layers of the same-sex marriage question in Sikhi
Summarize the 2005 Akal Takht position and the theological reasoning offered in its defense
Summarize the reformist scholarly critique of that position with equal accuracy and fairness
Explain the conservative Gurmat case for upholding tradition on its own strongest grounds
Engage respectfully with the lived experiences of LGBTQ+ Sikhs and the pastoral question of belonging
Identify the core tension between a theology of inclusion and a theology of tradition without collapsing it prematurely
Apply Chicago-style citation and evidence standards to a sensitive intra-Panthic debate

courses.title: Sex Education and Gurbani: Kaam, Anand Karaj, and Ethical Intimacy
courses.summary: This course examines what Gurbani teaches about human sexuality, desire, and intimacy. Gurbani identifies ਕਾਮ (unbridled lust) as one of the ਪੰਜ ਚੋਰ — the five thieves that rob the soul of union with ਵਾਹਿਗੁਰੂ — yet it fully sanctifies physical intimacy within ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ, the sacred marriage covenant. Across twelve lessons, students trace how Guru Sahib distinguishes ਕਾਮ from ਪ੍ਰੇਮ, why ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤ (householder life) is honoured as the highest path rather than renunciation, and how the discipline of restraint is grounded in protecting people from emotional trauma, disease, and spiritual harm rather than in shame. The course situates Gurmat alongside Hindu, Muslim, Christian, and secular approaches to sex education, equips students to think about dating, pornography, hookup culture, and social media through a Gurmat lens, and closes by drawing out the distinctive contribution Sikhi offers to a confused world…

Distinguish ਕਾਮ (possessive lust) from ਪ੍ਰੇਮ (selfless love) using textual evidence from Gurbani.
Explain the theology of ਅਨੰਦ ਕਾਰਜ and why Sikhi sanctifies intimacy within marriage.
Articulate the four ਕੁਰਹਿਤ (cardinal prohibitions) and the principle of avoiding ਪਰ ਨਾਰੀ / ਪਰ ਪੁਰਖ.
Describe the Gurmat rationale for premarital abstinence in terms of health, emotional safety, and spiritual focus.
Apply Gurmat principles to contemporary questions of dating, pornography, hookup culture, and social media.
Explain why ਗ੍ਰਿਹਸਤ is honoured as the highest path and how Sikhi holds a positive view of marital sexuality.
Compare Sikh sex education with Hindu, Muslim, Christian, and secular frameworks and identify Gurmat distinctives.

courses.title: Sikh Democratic Engagement: Civic Duty, Voting, and Political Participation
courses.summary: This course argues that the Sikh tradition does not call its adherents to retreat from public life but to enter it with ਧਰਮ as their moral compass. Beginning with the ancient institution of the ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ — among humanity's oldest sustained experiments in participatory, consensus-based governance — the course traces a continuous Sikh political imagination from the eighteenth-century ਗੁਰਮਤਾ to contemporary voting, candidate evaluation, community organizing, accountability movements, and coalition-building. Students will learn to read civic participation as a form of ਸੇਵਾ, to evaluate candidates and parties through a Gurmat lens, to resist the idolatry of partisan loyalty, and to engage diverse coalitions without surrendering Sikh identity. Across twelve lessons the course combines primary-source Gurbani, the historical record of the Khalsa Commonwealth, and modern political science to equip students for grounded, ethical civic life…
outcomes: Explain the institution of the ਸਰਬੱਤ ਖ਼ਾਲਸਾ and assess its standing as an early model of participatory democracy.
Define ਗੁਰਮਤਾ and describe how the eighteenth-century Khalsa reached binding collective decisions.
Construct a Gurmat-grounded argument for why Sikhs ought to vote and participate in civic life.
Apply a Gurmat candidate-evaluation framework to real electoral choices.
Diagnose the dangers of party idolatry and distinguish loyalty to principle from loyalty to faction.
Compare the missions and methods of major Sikh political and advocacy organizations.
Analyze civic duty, accountability, and coalition-building as expressions of ਸੇਵਾ and ਸੰਗਤ.
Evaluate Sikh political representation and activism across multiple national contexts.

courses.title: The Duty to Defend: Standing Up for the Oppressed in the Sikh Tradition
courses.summary: This course argues that ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ — the welfare of all — is unconditional. Through the martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji for the Kashmiri Pandits, the liberation of 52 non-Sikh kings by Guru Hargobind Ji, and the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ ideal, students learn that the duty to defend the helpless carries no creed test and no agreement test. Sikhi defends without endorsing, refuses to abandon those it disagrees with, and treats capable silence before ਜ਼ੁਲਮ as complicity. The course distinguishes tolerance, endorsement, and active defense, and translates the classical duty into modern practice…
outcomes: Explain why ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ functions as an unconditional, creed-blind obligation rather than a sentiment limited to Sikhs.
Reconstruct the historical episode of the Kashmiri Pandits and analyse why Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji defended a faith Sikhi rejects theologically.
Distinguish clearly between tolerance, endorsement, abandonment, and active defense, and locate the Gurmat position among them.

Apply the principle that the duty to defend does not weaken when theological or political agreement disappears.
Identify when capable silence before ਜ਼ੁਲਮ crosses into complicity (ਮਿਲੀਭੁਗਤ).

lessons.title: The Aurangzeb Context: Forced Conversion and Religious Genocide

lessons.title: ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ as Active Defense — Not Passive Suffering

lessons.title: Guru Hargobind Ji and the 52 Kings: Bandi Chorh Divas

lessons.title: The ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ Ideal: When and For Whom to Act
lessons.summary: Defines the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ as the fusion of saint and soldier and sets out the thresholds of when, for what, and for whom force and protection are justified.

lessons.title: ਨਿਆਉ in Gurbani: The Moral Duty to Intervene

lessons.title: When Passive Witness Becomes Complicity

lessons.title: Modern Applications: What This Looks Like Today
lessons.summary: Translates the classical principles into contemporary practice and closes by returning the duty to the benediction of the ਅਰਦਾਸ.

courses.title: Sikh Economic Ethics: Dasvandh, Langar, and Justice in the Marketplace
courses.summary: This course argues that ਦਸਵੰਧ and ਲੰਗਰ are not merely devotional customs but the operational core of a complete economic philosophy — one that predates and transcends both socialism and capitalism. Drawing on Gurbani, the Sikh institutional tradition, and comparative political economy, students examine how the integrated triad of ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ, ਵੰਡ ਛਕੋ, and ਨਾਮ ਜਪੋ produces a system in which honest labour is sanctified, surplus is voluntarily redistributed, and the dignity of the poor is structurally protected. Across twelve lessons we trace the theology of tithing, the working mechanics of the communal kitchen, Gurbani's critique of ਲੋਭ and hoarding, and the vision of ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ as a polity of justice. We compare Gurmat economics rigorously against socialism, capitalism, and libertarianism, showing where each converges and diverges, and we ask what a contemporary Gurmat economic vision — grounded in ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ — might offer a world of widening inequality and ecological strain…
outcomes: Explain the integrated triad of ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ, ਵੰਡ ਛਕੋ, and ਨਾਮ ਜਪੋ as a single economic system rather than three separate ethics
Describe the theology and practical mechanics of ਦਸਵੰਧ and evaluate it as a voluntary redistributive instrument
Analyze ਲੰਗਰ as a functioning economic institution in terms of inputs, processes, outputs, and beneficiaries
Compare Gurmat economics with socialism, capitalism, and libertarianism across ownership, redistribution, the role of the state, incentives, and treatment of the poor
Trace Gurbani's critique of ਲੋਭ and hoarding alongside its affirmation of honest wealth
Articulate ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ and ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ as principles of distributive and political-economic justice
Assess the historical development of Sikh philanthropic institutions from local ਲੰਗਰ to global seva networks
Construct a defensible Gurmat economic vision for contemporary problems of inequality, work, and sustainability

courses.title: Sikh Land and Water Stewardship: Sacred Ecology in Practice
courses.summary: Punjab — the land of the ਪੰਜ ਆਬ (five waters) — is named for its rivers, and Sikh tradition holds water and land as sacred gifts of ਅਕਾਲ ਪੁਰਖ. Yet the Satluj, Beas, and Ravi are choking on industrial effluent, pesticide runoff, and over-extraction, while Punjab's water table collapses beneath a monoculture of wheat and paddy. This 150-level ethics course connects Gurbani's reverence for water (ਪਾਣੀ), air (ਪਵਣੁ), and earth (ਧਰਤਿ) to concrete, achievable stewardship that any Sikh can practice. Students study the sacred geography of Punjab's rivers, the ecological crisis facing them, the theology of the ਸਰੋਵਰ, Baba Seva Singh Ji's tree-planting ਸੇਵਾ, traditional and regenerative farming, kitchen gardening, water conservation at home and in the Gurdwara, langar-rooted food-waste reduction, biodiversity protection, and the organizations carrying this work forward. The course is practical above all: every lesson ends in action, so that ecological stewardship becomes a living expression of ਸੇਵਾ and of the Gurbani teaching that we are guests upon a sacred Earth…
outcomes: Explain the sacred status of water, air, and earth in Gurbani and connect it to the ਪੰਜ ਆਬ geography of Punjab
Describe the ecological crisis facing the Satluj, Beas, and Ravi rivers and Punjab's groundwater, with its agricultural and industrial drivers
Interpret the ਸਰੋਵਰ as both a theological symbol and a working model of water sanctuary
Evaluate traditional, organic, and regenerative farming through the lens of Gurmat ethics
Apply langar principles of ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ and waste-avoidance to household and community food systems
Design a personal and Gurdwara-level water-conservation and biodiversity plan
Identify Sikh environmental organizations and the specific work each performs
Construct a personal ecological-stewardship commitment grounded in ਸੇਵਾ

courses.title: Sikh Pastoral Care at the Margins: Welcoming All into the Sangat
courses.summary: This course offers a practical, scholarly guide for Sikh families and Gurdwaras seeking to welcome every person into the ਸੰਗਤ — including LGBTQ+ individuals, converts of any background, mixed-heritage Sikhs, and disabled members of the community. Grounded in the theology of ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ, and in the Guru Sahib's radical dismantling of ਜਾਤਿ-ਪਾਤਿ and social hierarchy, the course distinguishes between cultural Punjabi expectations and ਗੁਰਮਤਿ itself. Students will learn to build genuinely welcoming spaces, support family members through difficult conversations, attend to mental health and disability, and embody the model of belonging the world urgently needs. On contested ethical questions the course presents the full range of positions held within the Panth fairly and without taking sides, equipping families to act with both conviction and compassion…
outcomes: Articulate the theology of ਸੰਗਤ and ਪੰਗਤ and explain why it makes radical inclusion a Sikh obligation rather than a modern accommodation

courses.title: Sikh Social Justice and Modern Advocacy: The Sant-Sipahi in Action
courses.summary: This course examines how the Sikh ideal of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ — the saint-soldier who unites contemplative devotion with moral courage — translates into the institutions and practices of modern social justice advocacy. Drawing on Gurbani, Sikh history, and contemporary sociology, students trace the journey from the battlefield ethic of the Khalsa to the courtroom, the picket line, the refugee shelter, and the interfaith coalition. The course surveys Sikh civil rights movements across the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada; anti-discrimination law; the labor ethic rooted in ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ; the work of organizations such as the Sikh Coalition and United Sikhs; the long campaign for recognition of the 1984 violence; and the theology of solidarity that underwrites Sikh alliances with Muslim, Black, and Indigenous communities. Throughout, students learn to distinguish principled coalition-building from the dissolution of identity, and to read advocacy as an expression of ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ — the well-being of all. The arc closes with the Guru's vision of ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ, a polity of humility and justice, as the horizon toward which Sikh advocacy aims…
outcomes: Explain the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ principle and trace its translation from martial defense to modern civic advocacy
Compare Sikh civil rights movements in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada and their legal milestones
Analyze the theological grounding of labor rights in ਕਿਰਤ ਕਰਨੀ and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ
Evaluate the strategies of major Sikh advocacy and humanitarian organizations worldwide
Assess the campaign for recognition of the 1984 violence and the ethics of memory and justice
Construct principled frameworks for interfaith and cross-community solidarity grounded in ਸਰਬੱਤ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ

courses.title: Sikhi and Ecological Restoration: Living Green in a World of Rising Pollution
courses.summary: This course reads the ecological crisis through the lens of Gurbani, beginning from the foundational verse ਪਵਣੁ ਗੁਰੂ ਪਾਣੀ ਪਿਤਾ ਮਹਤਾ ਧਰਤਿ ਮਾਂ (Japji Sahib, Ang 8), which names air as Guru, water as father, and earth as mother. Across twelve lessons it argues that ਕੁਦਰਤਿ is the living expression of Waheguru unfolding through ਹੁਕਮਿ, not a warehouse of resources for human consumption. We examine corporate pollution as institutionalized ਲੋਭ, the hidden carbon and water costs of AI and data centers, the waste of fast fashion answered by ਸੰਤੋਖ, and the langar model as a working zero-waste, plant-forward ecology. We study Eco-Sikh activism, the river-restoration legacy of Baba Seva Singh Ji of Khadoor Sahib, the contested ethics of diet, and the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ as defender of creation. The course closes with a vision of the restored earth under ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ, insisting that a Sikh who watches the earth be destroyed in silence has abandoned ਧਰਮ…
outcomes: Explain the theology of ਕੁਦਰਤਿ as the manifest creation of Waheguru unfolding through ਹੁਕਮਿ, and articulate why this forbids treating nature as a mere resource.
Interpret ਪਵਣੁ ਗੁਰੂ ਪਾਣੀ ਪਿਤਾ ਮਹਤਾ ਧਰਤਿ ਮਾਂ (Japji Sahib, Ang 8) as the kinship foundation of a Sikh ecological ethic.
Analyze corporate pollution, fast fashion, and digital-economy emissions as expressions of ਲੋਭ, and contrast them with ਸੰਤੋਖ and Gurmat restraint.

lessons.title: The Langar Model as Ecological Practice: Zero Waste and Plant-Forward
lessons.summary: Analyzes langar as a working model of plant-forward, zero-waste, commons-based ecology rooted in ਸੇਵਾ and ਵੰਡ ਛਕਣਾ.

lessons.title: Sikh Ecological Activism: Eco-Sikh Movement and Baba Seva Singh Ji
lessons.summary: Surveys organized Sikh environmental action, from the Eco-Sikh movement to the river and tree restoration of Baba Seva Singh Ji of Khadoor Sahib.

lessons.title: Water as Sacred: Protecting Punjab's Rivers and Clean Water
lessons.summary: Frames water as the ਪਿਤਾ of Japji and examines the crisis of Punjab's rivers and aquifers as a ਧਰਮ obligation.

lessons.title: The Vegetarian Diet as Environmental Act
lessons.summary: Presents the contested ethics of diet in Sikhi fairly while examining the environmental dimension of plant-forward eating.

lessons.title: Sikh Climate Responsibility: The ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ Defends Creation
lessons.summary: Extends the saint-soldier ideal to climate, casting defense of creation as a contemporary front of the ਸੰਤ-ਸਿਪਾਹੀ's duty.

lessons.title: Practical Gurmat Living: Energy, Consumption, Waste, Transportation
lessons.summary: Translates the course's theology into a concrete household and sangat plan for energy, consumption, waste, and transportation.

lessons.title: The Restored Earth Vision: ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ and the Ecological Imagination
lessons.summary: Closes with Guru Arjan Sahib's vision of ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜ read as an ecological commonwealth and a horizon for restoration.

courses.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji and the Ethics of Interfaith Defense
courses.summary: This 300-level seminar reads the ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ of ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ਼ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਜੀ not as biography but as a sustained philosophical argument about the universality of religious freedom. The Ninth Master gave his life in 1675 at ਚਾਂਦਨੀ ਚੌਕ for the ਧਰਮ of the Kashmiri Pandits — a tradition whose theology the Gurus themselves had critiqued. The course treats this as the founding human-rights event of its kind: a defense of conscience offered to people one philosophically disagrees with. Students analyze the Gurmat concept of ਨਿਆਉ (justice) as standing above any single community's ਧਰਮ, compare the act with natural-law theory and the modern human-rights tradition, distinguish Sikh ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ from martyrdom in Islam, Christianity, and Hinduism, and build a Gurmat framework of unconditional defense applicable to 1984, the Rohingya, Gaza, and beyond…
outcomes: Reconstruct the philosophical argument for why one may be obligated to die for the religious freedom of a faith one disagrees with
Explain ਧਰਮ and ਨਿਆਉ in Gurmat and articulate why ਨਿਆਉ transcends any single community's interest
Compare Gurmat's grounding of religious freedom with natural-law theory and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Distinguish ਗੁਰੂ ਤੇਗ਼ ਬਹਾਦਰ ਜੀ's ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ from martyrdom traditions in Islam, Christianity, and Hinduism by motivation, beneficiary, and theological basis
Analyze why an interfaith defense of conscience was politically more dangerous to ਔਰੰਗਜ਼ੇਬ than armed rebellion
Apply a Sikh humanitarian-engagement framework to contemporary atrocities and identify the conditions that trigger a defense obligation
Cite verified Gurbani in support of an ethics of justice that transcends self-interest
Construct and defend a Gurmat philosophy of unconditional defense of conscience
references: Singh, Ganda. The Martyrdom of Guru Tegh Bahadur. Punjabi University Press, 1976.
Grewal, J. S. The Sikhs of the Punjab. Cambridge University Press, 1990.
Fenech, Louis E. Martyrdom in the Sikh Tradition: Playing the Game of Love. Oxford University Press, 2000.
McLeod, W. H. Sikhism. Penguin, 1997.
Singh, Nikky-Guninder Kaur. The Birth of the Khalsa: A Feminist Re-Memory of Sikh Identity. SUNY Press, 2005.
Mandair, Arvind-Pal Singh. Sikhism: A Guide for the Perplexed. Bloomsbury, 2013.
Finnis, John. Natural Law and Natural Rights. 2nd ed. Oxford University Press, 2011.
United Nations. Universal Declaration of Human Rights. United Nations, 1948.
Singh, Pashaura. The Guru Granth Sahib: Canon, Meaning and Authority. Oxford University Press, 2000.
Sen, Amartya. The Idea of Justice. Harvard University Press, 2009.

lessons.title: The Philosophical Question: Why Die for Another Religion?
lessons.summary: Frames the central puzzle: the ethical reasoning behind sacrificing one's life for the religious freedom of a tradition one disagrees with.

lessons.title: Religious Freedom as a Universal Right in Gurmat
lessons.summary: Examines how Gurmat grounds freedom of conscience as a universal entitlement rather than a concession to a favored group.

lessons.title: Comparing with Natural Law Theory and Modern Human Rights
lessons.summary: Sets Gurmat's grounding of conscience beside natural-law theory and the UDHR, mapping convergences and differences.

lessons.title: The "I Disagree But Will Die for Your Right" Principle
lessons.summary: Develops the core principle: defense of a right one disagrees with, distinguishing it from agreement, charity, and alliance.

lessons.title: How This Differs from Martyrdom in Islam, Christianity, and Hinduism
lessons.summary: Provides the comparative table distinguishing Sikh ਸ਼ਹੀਦੀ from martyrdom in three other traditions by motivation, beneficiary, and theological basis.

lessons.title: ਨਿਆਉ as Higher Than Any Single Community's ਧਰਮ
lessons.summary: Argues that justice (ਨਿਆਉ) in Gurmat functions as a meta-norm above any one community's particular ਧਰਮ.

lessons.title: Gurbani on Justice That Transcends Self-Interest
lessons.summary: Anchors the ethics of self-transcending justice in verified Gurbani, citing only by certain ਅੰਗ.

lessons.title: The Paradox Aurangzeb Feared Most: Why This Was More Dangerous Than Armed Resistance
lessons.summary: Analyzes why a sacrificial interfaith defense of conscience threatened imperial legitimacy more than rebellion could.

lessons.title: Human Rights Implications for Today
lessons.summary: Translates the ethics of unconditional interfaith defense into a general account of contemporary human-rights obligation.

lessons.title: 1984, Rohingya, Gaza — The Sikh Ethical Duty
lessons.summary: Applies the framework to three contemporary atrocities, modeling consistent reasoning across cases including one involving Sikhs as victims.

lessons.title: The Sikh Humanitarian Engagement Framework
lessons.summary: Consolidates the principles into an operational framework for Sikh humanitarian engagement, from disposition to action.

lessons.title: A Gurmat Philosophy of Unconditional Defense
lessons.summary: Synthesizes the course into a coherent Gurmat philosophy of unconditional defense of conscience, with its commitments and limits.
